tutorialData.title: AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner (CLF-C02)
tutorialData.lead: A chapter-by-chapter course for the AWS Cloud Practitioner exam, in a strict teaching order, with diagrams, a quiz on every lesson and community practice questions.

sections.title: Chapter 1: Foundations
sections.note: The plain basics every later chapter relies on: servers, the cloud, virtual machines, service models, APIs and four everyday words.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Every AWS service is, underneath, computers in buildings that other computers reach over a network. Once you can picture that, the later chapters stop feeling like magic.

This lesson names the physical and software pieces one by one, so every later lesson can use them without stopping to explain.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **data center** — a building full of computers, with its own power, cooling and network connections.
- **server** — a computer whose job is to answer requests from other computers.
- **on-premises** — IT equipment that a company keeps in its own buildings (often shortened to on-prem).
- **operating system** — the main program on a computer, such as Windows or Linux, that runs everything else and shares out the hardware.
- **application** — a program that does a job for people, such as email, a web shop or a photo editor.
- **data** — the information an application stores and uses, such as customer records or photos.
- **client and server** — the client is the program or device that asks, and the server is the computer that answers.
- **network** — computers connected so they can send messages to each other.
- **internet** — the huge public network that links millions of smaller networks together.
- **IP address** — a number that identifies one computer on a network, like a street address for a house.

**A server is just a computer with a job.** It has the same parts as a laptop. It runs an operating system, and on top of that runs an application. The application keeps its data on the server's disks.

**A data center is where many servers live.** Racks of servers share power, cooling and network cables. A company that keeps its own data center runs its IT on-premises: the building, the machines and the people who look after them all belong to that company.

**Computers talk as client and server.** Your phone or browser is the client: it sends a request. The server sends back an answer. To find each other, computers sit on a network, and each one has an IP address. The internet is the public network made of many networks joined together. Figure 0-1 below shows one request making that trip.

blocks.title: Picture to keep
blocks.content: A data center is a warehouse of servers. Your phone is a client. The internet is the road between them.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Before the cloud, getting a server meant buying it, installing it and housing it. Cloud computing replaces that with renting what you need, when you need it.

This lesson gives the definition of cloud computing that the rest of the course builds on.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **cloud computing** — the on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing.
- **on-demand self-service** — you ask for what you need yourself, at any time, and get it in minutes, without waiting for a person to deliver it.
- **pay-as-you-go** — you pay only for what you use, and billing stops when you stop using it.
- **cloud provider** — a company, such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), that owns data centers and rents out computing power and other services.
- **AWS account** — your own account with AWS: you create and manage your resources in it, and it is where sign-in and billing for them are handled.
- **resource** — anything you create and run in your account, such as a server or a place to keep files.

**Cloud computing means renting IT instead of owning it.** AWS describes it as the on-demand delivery of IT resources over the internet with pay-as-you-go pricing. Instead of buying, owning and maintaining physical data centers and servers, you get computing power and other services as needed from a cloud provider such as AWS.

Think of electricity. You do not run your own generator; you buy power from a utility and pay for what you use. AWS makes the same comparison: the capacity you get matches your needs, and you pay only for what you use. Figure 0-2 below puts the two ways side by side.

blocks.content:
**A small scenario.** A shop needs a server for its website. On-premises, it buys a machine, installs it and keeps it running. In the cloud, someone on the team asks for a server, has it within minutes, and stops paying when the server is switched off. That is on-demand self-service plus pay-as-you-go.

**Where your things live: the AWS account.** To use AWS you create an AWS account. It is the home of what you build, and it also carries your sign-in and your bill. Every server or file store you create inside it is a resource.

blocks.title: One-line definition
blocks.content: Cloud computing = renting IT over the internet, on demand, and paying only for what you use.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A physical server often sits mostly idle when it runs only one job. Virtualization lets one machine act as several, and it is the technology that makes renting servers from a provider practical.

This lesson explains virtual machines and the hypervisor that manages them.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **virtualization** — technology that creates virtual representations of servers, storage, networks and other physical machines in software.
- **virtual machine** — a software-defined computer that runs on a physical computer, with its own operating system and its own share of the resources.
- **hypervisor** — the software that manages the virtual machines on a computer and makes sure each one gets its allocated resources without interfering with the others.

**Virtualization lets one physical server act like several computers.** Picture a company that needs three servers: one for email, one for a customer-facing application and one for internal tools. Without virtualization it buys three physical machines. It then pays all the maintenance costs but uses only a fraction of each machine's capacity.

With virtualization, the company creates three virtual machines on a single physical server. Each virtual machine has its own operating system and runs like a separate computer. The physical computer is called the host, and the virtual machines are the guests.

The hypervisor does the sharing. It gives each virtual machine its allocated processor, memory and disk, and keeps one from disturbing another. Figure 0-3 below shows the layers.

blocks.content: **Why the cloud depends on this.** A cloud provider can run many customers' virtual machines on its hardware. AWS describes the next step: instead of owning the machines, a company can use a virtual machine from a cloud provider such as AWS, which manages all the underlying hardware.

items.text: A type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor is installed directly on the computer's hardware instead of on an operating system. It performs better and is common in enterprise use. A type 2 (hosted) hypervisor is installed on top of an operating system and suits end-user computing.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Cloud services differ in how much work they leave to you. IaaS, PaaS and SaaS are three common labels for that split, and you will meet them in almost every cloud conversation.

This lesson explains who manages what in each one.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **IaaS** — Infrastructure as a Service: the basic building blocks, such as networking, computers (virtual or dedicated hardware) and data storage space, with the most control left to you.
- **PaaS** — Platform as a Service: the provider manages the underlying infrastructure, usually hardware and operating systems, so you can focus on deploying and managing your application.
- **SaaS** — Software as a Service: a complete product that the provider runs and manages, so you only decide how to use it.

**The three labels answer one question: how much do you want to manage?**

- **IaaS** gives you building blocks such as virtual computers. It offers the highest flexibility and control, and it is closest to the IT that many teams already know. You choose and look after the operating system and the application.
- **PaaS** removes hardware and operating system work. You bring the application, and you skip chores such as buying capacity and patching, which means installing updates that fix bugs and security holes.
- **SaaS** is a finished product. Web-based email is the classic example: you send and receive mail without maintaining the servers or the operating systems behind it.

Figure 0-4 below shows who runs which layer.

blocks.content: **A small scenario.** Team A wants full control of a virtual computer and its operating system: IaaS. Team B only wants to deploy its application code and not patch servers: PaaS. Team C just needs email for staff: SaaS.

blocks.title: Careful with the labels
blocks.content: AWS says these are the traditional groupings, and that definitions vary from company to company. At AWS the focus is on solutions to your needs, which can span many service types. Use the labels to compare how much you manage, not as strict boxes.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Almost everything in the cloud is used by sending messages from one program to another. An API is the agreed way to do that, and you will see the word on nearly every page from here on.

This lesson explains what an API is and how a request and a response work.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **API** — Application Programming Interface: a set of definitions and protocols that lets two software components communicate, like a contract of service between two applications.
- **request and response** — a request is a message from the client asking for something, and the response is the answer the server sends back.

**An API is a contract between two programs.** It says how one program may ask and how the other will answer. AWS gives a simple example: a weather bureau keeps daily weather data in a software system. The weather app on your phone talks to that system through an API and shows you the forecast.

The same client and server idea from the first lesson applies. The application that sends the request is the client, and the application that sends the response is the server. In the example, the bureau's weather system is the server and the phone app is the client.

Because the contract is written down, the client does not need to know how the server works inside. It only needs to ask in the agreed format. Figure 0-5 below shows that exchange.

blocks.title: REST APIs
blocks.content: The most popular style of web API today is REST. Clients and servers exchange data using HTTP, the set of rules web browsers use to talk to web servers. A key feature is statelessness: the server does not save client data between requests, so each request must carry what the server needs.

items.term: Four words you will meet constantly

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Later chapters judge every design with two plain questions: is it fast, and is it up? Latency and availability are the words for those questions.

This lesson gives four short definitions you will keep using.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **latency** — the time delay between asking for something and getting it.
- **availability** — the percentage of time that a workload is available for use.
- **downtime** — the time when a workload is not available for use.
- **workload** — a set of components that together deliver business value, such as a website with its servers and its data.

**Latency is about speed.** When you click a link, a request travels over the network to a server, and the response travels back. The time delay is the latency. Latency is lower when the client and the server are closer together on the network.

**A workload is the thing you run.** One website with its servers and its data is a workload. A company may have many workloads, and each one is judged on its own.

**Availability is about being up.** Time when the workload can be used is uptime, and time when it cannot is downtime. Availability is the share of the total time that the workload is up. For example, a site that is up for 99 minutes out of every 100 is 99 percent available, and its downtime is one minute in every 100.

blocks.title: Two questions for every design
blocks.content: Is the latency low enough for the people using the workload? Is the availability high enough for what the business needs?

sections.title: Chapter 2: Global infrastructure
sections.note: How AWS places its computers around the world: Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations, and how to use them for speed and resilience.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Where your computers physically sit decides two things: how fast users get answers, and what happens when something goes wrong. Everything in this chapter is about those two choices.

This lesson names the two problems that one building in one place creates.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **single point of failure** — one part of a system that, if it fails, stops the whole system.

**Problem 1: distance.** If your users are far from your servers, every request and response has to travel farther, and latency goes up. AWS notes that putting applications closer to end users reduces latency and improves their experience.

**Problem 2: one place.** Suppose all your servers are in one data center. A power cut, a fire or a flood there would stop everything, because the data center is a single point of failure. The failing part is not always a building: a single server, a single network connection or a single power source can play the same role.

So a good design asks two questions. Where are the users, so latency stays low? And what is the single point of failure, so one event cannot stop the whole workload? The next lessons show how AWS organizes its infrastructure to answer both.

blocks.title: The two questions
blocks.content: Distance: are my servers close to my users? Failure: does one broken part stop everything?

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> AWS has to put its computers somewhere, and you have to choose where yours run. The unit AWS uses for that choice is the Region.

This lesson explains what a Region is, why Regions are isolated, and what to weigh when picking one.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Region** — a physical location in the world where AWS clusters data centers; each Region is a separate geographic area.
- **Region isolation** — each Region is designed to be isolated from the other Regions, and resources are not copied between Regions unless you set that up.
- **Region selection factors** — the four things to weigh when choosing a Region: compliance, latency, cost, and which services and features it offers.

**A Region is a separate geographic area where AWS clusters data centers.** AWS gives Regions names such as US East (Ohio) and Canada (Central).

**Regions are isolated from each other.** This design gives the greatest possible stability: one Region's trouble stays in that Region. It has a practical effect: when you view your resources, you see only those in the Region you selected, and resources are not copied to other Regions unless you set that up yourself.

Figure 1-1 below shows the idea as a schematic: a few Regions, each a cluster of data centers.

blocks.content:
**How to choose a Region.** AWS's architecture guidance names four factors:

- **Compliance.** Following the laws and rules that bind your data. If they apply, the Region that meets them overrides the other factors.
- **Latency.** A Region close to your users gives lower latency.
- **Cost.** AWS services are priced differently from one Region to another.
- **Services and features.** New services and features reach Regions gradually, so smaller Regions may not have them yet.

**Small scenario.** A shop whose customers are mostly in Canada has a reason to pick a Region near them for low latency, as long as the other three factors do not say otherwise.

blocks.title: Always check the current list
blocks.content: AWS adds Regions over time, so the number and names change. The AWS Global Infrastructure page has the current list.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> One data center is a single point of failure. AWS solves this inside every Region by splitting it into several separate locations, called Availability Zones.

This lesson explains what an Availability Zone is and why its separateness matters.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Availability Zone** — one or more discrete data centers, with redundant power, networking and connectivity, inside a Region. Often shortened to AZ.
- **AZ isolation (no shared single points of failure)** — each AZ runs on its own physically separate infrastructure, so things like generators and cooling equipment are not shared between AZs.
- **low-latency links between AZs** — the AZs in a Region are connected to each other by fast network links, so they can work together closely.

**An Availability Zone is one or more data centers.** It is not always exactly one building: AWS defines it as one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking and connectivity. (Redundant here means duplicated, so that one failure does not cut the supply.) Each Region has several of them, at least three according to AWS.

**AZs do not share single points of failure.** Each runs on its own physically separate, independent infrastructure. Common points of failure such as generators and cooling equipment are not shared. Because AZs are physically separate, even extremely uncommon disasters such as fires, tornadoes or flooding would affect only a single AZ.

**But they are linked.** The AZs in a Region are connected through low-latency links, so an application can use more than one at the same time. Figure 1-2 below shows one Region with three AZs.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.content: Region = a geographic area. Availability Zone = a separate location inside that Region. AZs fail separately, and they talk fast.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Zones that fail separately are only useful if your application actually uses more than one of them. High availability is the design habit that puts that to work.

This lesson shows how running in several AZs keeps an application up when one AZ has a problem.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **high availability** — designing a system so it keeps working, with as little downtime as possible, when parts of it fail.
- **redundancy** — keeping spare copies of a part, so that when one fails another can take over its work.
- **multi-AZ design** — running the same application in two or more Availability Zones of one Region.

**Redundancy is the tool, high availability is the goal.** If one server fails and a spare is ready, users keep going. That spare is redundancy. A system built so that it keeps working through failures has high availability.

**Multi-AZ design applies this to AZs.** You run the same application in at least two AZs. If one AZ has a problem, the other still works, because the AZs do not share single points of failure. AWS describes distributing applications across multiple AZs as a way to remain resilient in the face of most failure modes, including natural disasters or system failures. The switch of work to the healthy copy is called failover, and it can be automated.

Figure 1-3 below shows two copies of an application, one per AZ, and one AZ failing.

blocks.content:
**Compare the alternative.** An application in one AZ has a single point of failure. The same application in two AZs does not, so downtime from a failure in one AZ is avoided or cut short.

**Who spreads the copies?** For some services AWS spreads across AZs for you. For others you choose which AZ to use. That is part of design, and later chapters show it service by service.

blocks.title: Limit of multi-AZ
blocks.content: All the AZs of a Region are in one Region. Multi-AZ design protects against an AZ problem, but it does not protect against a problem that affects the whole Region. The next lessons cover that.

items.term: When to use more than one Region

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Several AZs protect you from a problem in one location, but not from a problem across a whole Region, or from laws and distances that a single Region cannot answer. For those, you use more than one Region.

This lesson lists the reasons that justify running in several Regions.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **multi-Region use cases** — situations where one Region is not enough: disaster recovery, business continuity, low latency for users in different places, and data sovereignty.
- **disaster recovery** — preparing for and recovering from a disaster, meaning an event that prevents a workload from doing its job in its primary location.
- **business continuity** — keeping the business running through a disaster.
- **data sovereignty** — the rule that data must stay under the laws of a country, which can require storing it in a Region located in that country.

**Disaster recovery (DR).** A disaster is an event that prevents a workload from doing its job where it normally runs. DR is the preparation for that, and the recovery from it. A second Region, separate from the first, is a place to recover to.

**Business continuity.** The goal behind DR: the business keeps running. AWS treats DR as part of business continuity planning.

**Low latency for users.** One Region may be far from some of your users. Placing the workload in a Region near each group lowers latency for everyone.

**Data sovereignty.** Some laws bind data to a country. Choosing a Region located in that country can be mandatory for data covered by such laws.

Figure 1-4 below shows a primary Region, a recovery Region and users near each.

blocks.title: What it costs you
blocks.content: Because Regions are isolated, nothing is copied from one Region to another unless you set it up. Using several Regions means you build and run those copies yourself, so use them when you have one of these four reasons.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A user on the other side of the world from your Region will see high latency, however good your design is. Edge locations put copies of content next to users, so the answer comes from nearby.

This lesson explains edge locations and content caching.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **edge location** — a site in AWS's worldwide network, close to users, that holds copies of content so it can be delivered quickly.
- **content caching** — keeping copies of content in places closer to users, so a request is served from the copy instead of travelling to the original.

**An edge location is a site close to users that keeps copies.** AWS names Amazon CloudFront as its content delivery service (a service that delivers files, such as web pages and images, to users quickly). It delivers content through a worldwide network of data centers called edge locations.

When a user asks for content, the request goes to the edge location that gives the lowest latency. If the content is already there, CloudFront delivers it immediately. If not, CloudFront fetches it from the origin, which is the source you defined as the definitive version of your content, and keeps a copy. Figure 1-5 below shows both cases.

blocks.content: **Benefits.** Copies held in multiple edge locations around the world mean lower latency, because the answer comes from nearby, and higher reliability and availability, because the content exists in many places. The original content stays at its origin, in a Region or elsewhere, and edge locations keep copies of it.

blocks.title: Not the same as a Region
blocks.content: Edge locations are many and close to users, and they hold cached copies. Regions are fewer, are where you run your workloads, and are made of AZs.

items.term: How Regions, AZs and edge locations relate

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You now have three physical building blocks. Cloud design questions often boil down to which block to use, so it helps to see how they fit together.

This lesson puts Regions, Availability Zones and edge locations into one picture.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **relationships among Region, AZ and edge location** — a Region contains several AZs; edge locations are separate sites around the world that keep copies of content close to users, and the AWS global network connects them to the Regions.

**Containment.** A Region is a geographic area. Inside each Region are several Availability Zones, and inside each AZ are one or more data centers. An AZ never spans Regions.

**Edge locations are a different kind of site.** They are not inside a Region's AZs. They are spread around the world, close to users, and they hold cached copies of content. They connect to Regions over the AWS global network.

Figure 1-6 below draws the three together.

blocks.caption: Regions contain AZs, and AZs contain data centers. Edge locations are separate sites near users, connected to Regions by the AWS global network.

blocks.content:
**Which block answers which question?**

- Need to pick where a workload lives, for latency, law, cost or services? Choose a **Region**.
- Need the workload to survive a data center problem? Use more than one **AZ** in that Region.
- Need to survive a Region-wide problem, or to serve distant users and meet sovereignty rules? Use more than one **Region**.
- Need fast delivery of content to users everywhere? Use **edge locations**.

items.term: Why not make every AZ its own Region?
items.text: Regions are isolated: nothing is copied between them unless you set it up. AZs in one Region are linked by low-latency links, which is what lets an application use several AZs closely. The two levels give you different trade-offs: simple, close cooperation between AZs, and strong isolation between Regions.

sections.title: Chapter 3: Benefits of the AWS Cloud
sections.note: This chapter explains why organizations choose the AWS Cloud: the value proposition, capacity, scalability, elasticity, speed, agility, global reach and fault tolerance.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Before you learn the parts of the cloud one by one, you need the whole promise in one place.
> Every lesson in this chapter is one piece of it.

The cloud value proposition is what you get in return for choosing the cloud instead of owning your own servers.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **cloud value proposition** — the promise of what you get from using the cloud: the reasons a company would choose it over running its own data centers.

A *value proposition* is the promise a product makes: what you get in exchange for choosing it.

The cloud value proposition is that you rent computing power from a provider and pay only for what you use, instead of buying and running it all yourself.

AWS spells that promise out as six advantages. The card below lists them. This lesson only names them. The next lessons teach the ones the exam asks about, one at a time.

blocks.title: AWS's six advantages of cloud computing
blocks.content:
1. Pay only for what you consume, instead of paying up front for data centers and servers before you know how you will use them.
2. Usage from very many customers is added together, so a provider like AWS can run at a lower cost for each unit and pass that on as lower pay-as-you-go prices.
3. Stop guessing capacity: you can use as much or as little computing power as you need and change it with only a few minutes' notice.
4. Increase speed: new resources are only a click away, so the time to make them available to your developers drops from weeks to just minutes.
5. Stop spending money running and maintaining data centers: you focus on your own customers instead of racking, stacking and powering servers. (Racking and stacking is the physical work of mounting servers in racks and wiring them up.)
6. Go global in minutes: you can deploy your application in several Regions around the world with a few clicks, which lowers latency for your customers.

items.text: It is AWS's own summary of why customers move. When an exam or a colleague asks for the benefits of the cloud, these six are the shared starting point. The rest of this chapter turns each one into something you can explain in your own words.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> On your own servers you must decide how much power you need before you know the real demand.
> Guess wrong and you either waste money or let users down.

In the cloud you no longer have to guess: you take what you need and change it later.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **capacity** — how much work your servers can do at the same moment.
- **capacity planning** — deciding in advance how much capacity you will need.
- **over-provisioning** — having more capacity than the work needs, so some of it sits idle and you still pay for it.
- **under-provisioning** — having less capacity than the work needs, so work is slow or fails.

A *workload* needs servers, and *capacity* is how much work those servers can do together. Capacity planning means deciding in advance how much computing power you will need.

On-premises, capacity planning is hard because you must buy servers before the demand arrives, and they take time to buy and install. That leaves two ways to be wrong.

- If you guess too high, you pay for machines that sit idle: this is called over-provisioning.
- If you guess too low, there is not enough power for the work and users get slow or failed responses: this is called under-provisioning.

A small shop planning a sale shows the problem. It does not know whether a few visitors or very many will come. Buy for the many and most of the machines sit idle. Buy for the few and the site fails on the busy day.

blocks.title: The cloud answer
blocks.content:
AWS lists this as its advantage 'stop guessing capacity'. In the cloud you can use as much or as little capacity as you need, and change it with only a few minutes' notice.

- Start small and add more when demand grows.
- Give capacity back when demand drops.
- You do not have to pick one number in advance and live with it.

items.text: You still think about how much you expect to need. What changes is the cost of being wrong: a bad guess is corrected in minutes by changing what you use, not fixed by buying hardware.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Your workload will not stay the same size.
> You need words for the two ways to handle more work, because they behave very differently.

Scalability is the ability to grow to handle more work. There are two ways to grow.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **scalability** — the ability of a system to handle more or less work by changing how many resources it uses.
- **scale up** — make one machine bigger or more powerful (also called vertical scaling).
- **scale out** — add more machines and share the work between them (also called horizontal scaling).

Scalability is the ability of a system to handle more (or less) work by changing the amount of resources it uses.

There are two ways to add power.

- Scaling up (also called vertical scaling) means moving to a bigger machine.
- Scaling out (also called horizontal scaling) means adding more machines and sharing the work between them.

Think of a shop with a busy checkout. Scaling up is buying one faster, bigger till. Scaling out is opening more tills side by side.

blocks.title: Which one grows further?
blocks.content:
On physical hardware, AWS notes that scaling up needs powerful hardware, can be expensive, and demand could outgrow it. Scaling out spreads the investment over many smaller machines and is usually more effective.

| | Scale up | Scale out |
|---|---|---|
| What you do | Make one machine bigger | Add more machines |
| Also called | Vertical | Horizontal |
| Risk | One machine has a top size | Work must be shared between machines |

items.text: AWS sometimes says 'scale up and down' just to mean 'get bigger and smaller'. In this module, scale up always means a bigger machine and scale out means more machines. Read the context when the words are used loosely.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Being able to grow is good, but demand also drops.
> Elasticity is what stops you paying all day for the capacity you only need at the peak.

Elasticity is scalability that follows demand in both directions.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **elasticity** — the ability to add resources when demand rises and give them back when it falls, so your resources match the demand.

Elasticity means matching the resources you have to the demand for them, growing when demand rises and shrinking when it falls. Because you pay as you go, shrinking again also shrinks the bill.

Figure 2-1 below shows one day of demand. The flat line is on-premises capacity, bought for the peak. The stepped line is cloud capacity that follows demand.

blocks.title: Figure 2-1

blocks.caption: Demand over time. Fixed capacity is paid for all day. Elastic capacity follows demand, so the idle gap shrinks.

blocks.content:
Scalability and elasticity are close but not the same.

| | Scalability | Elasticity |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Can it handle more work? | Does it follow demand up and down? |
| Direction | Mostly growing | Growing and shrinking |
| Money | Not about the bill | Idle capacity is given back, so you stop paying for it |

AWS describes elasticity as matching the supply of resources to the demand for them.

items.text: A system you can enlarge by buying more machines is scalable. If you cannot give the machines back when demand drops, it is not elastic. The cloud makes both easy: you add and remove capacity in minutes and pay only while you use it.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A good idea waits while the servers are being bought and installed.
> Speed of deployment decides how long that wait is.

In the cloud the wait shrinks from weeks to minutes.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **speed of deployment** — how long it takes to go from needing a resource to having it running and ready to use.

Speed of deployment is how long it takes to go from needing a resource to having it running.

On-premises that path includes ordering the hardware, waiting for delivery, then racking, stacking and powering the servers. Each step takes time and a person.

In the cloud the provider has already built the data centers. In the cloud new resources are only a click away, so the time drops from weeks to just minutes.

AWS also describes it this way: businesses no longer need to plan for and buy servers weeks or months in advance, and can spin up hundreds or thousands of servers in minutes.

blocks.title: Worked scenario
blocks.content:
A team has an idea on Monday and needs five servers to try it.

- On-premises: order, wait for delivery, rack, cable, install. The team waits.
- In the cloud: ask for the resources and they are running within minutes.

Same idea, very different start.

items.term: Speed is a global benefit too
items.text: The same speed applies to places. Deploying to a new Region is also a few clicks, not a new building. A later lesson in this chapter picks this up.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Most ideas do not work the first time.
> The faster and cheaper it is to try one, the more you can learn and the sooner you find the ones that do.

Agility is the freedom to experiment, because trying is quick and cheap.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **agility** — how quickly and cheaply an organization can try an idea, learn from it and change direction.

Agility is how quickly and cheaply an organization can try an idea, learn from it, and change direction. AWS says that in the cloud the cost and time it takes to experiment and develop is significantly lower.

Two earlier ideas make this possible.

- **Speed of deployment:** resources arrive in minutes, so a trial can start today.
- **Pay-as-you-go:** you pay only while the trial runs, so a failed trial costs little.

Speed of deployment is about the wait for resources. Agility is what an organization does with that speed: more experiments, shorter cycles.

blocks.title: Worked scenario
blocks.content:
A team wants to test a new feature.

1. It asks for the resources it needs and they are ready in minutes.
2. It tries the idea for a few days and pays only for that time.
3. The idea does not work. The team gives the resources back and stops paying.
4. It starts the next idea the same day.

On-premises, step 1 alone could take weeks, and the servers would stay on the bill.

items.text: You cannot buy agility directly. It appears when resources are fast to get and cheap to give back. That is why AWS lists it together with speed in one advantage.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Customers far from your servers wait longer for every answer.
> With cloud Regions you can move your application to where your customers are.

Global reach is serving the world without building anything in the world.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **global reach** — the ability to deploy your application in places around the world, near your customers, quickly and at low cost.

Global reach is the ability to put your application close to customers anywhere in the world, quickly and at low cost. AWS says you can deploy an application in multiple Regions around the world with just a few clicks, which gives lower latency and a better experience for customers.

Remember the pieces from the global infrastructure chapter.

- **Latency** is the delay between a request and its answer. A Region near your users cuts it.
- **Multi-Region use cases:** disaster recovery, business continuity, low latency for end users and data sovereignty.
- Edge locations keep copies of content close to users, which also lowers latency.

Before the cloud, reaching a new country meant leasing space and installing servers there. Now it means choosing another Region.

blocks.title: Worked scenario
blocks.content:
A company has customers in two distant parts of the world and its application runs in one Region.

- Far customers get slower answers.
- The company deploys the same application in a second Region near them.
- Latency drops for those customers, and it did not build a data center.

items.term: Not every Region is for everyone
items.text: Which Regions to use depends on more than distance: laws about where data may live (data sovereignty) and service availability also matter, as in the earlier lesson on choosing a Region.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Parts of any system will fail sooner or later.
> The question is whether your users notice.

Fault tolerance is how a system keeps going when a part breaks.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **fault tolerance** — the ability of a system to keep working when part of it fails, because spare parts take over their work.

Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to keep working when part of it fails, because spare parts take over. AWS describes spares as subsystems that can take over the work of a failed one, typically almost seamlessly. With true spares, several parts would have to fail before the workload is affected.

High availability, from the global infrastructure chapter, is the goal of staying available with little downtime. Fault tolerance is a way to reach it: add redundancy, which means extra copies of the parts that matter, and let them take over.

Because Availability Zones do not share single points of failure, copies in different Availability Zones are spares in separate places.

blocks.title: Worked scenario
blocks.content:
An application runs one copy in Availability Zone A and one in Availability Zone B.

1. Both copies serve users.
2. Availability Zone A has a problem and its copy stops.
3. The copy in Availability Zone B takes over the work.
4. Users keep being served, with little or no downtime.

No single point of failure remains between the two copies.

items.text: High availability and fault tolerance protect what users see: the application stays up. The cloud makes this easier because you can create the extra copies in separate Availability Zones within minutes and pay only for them.

sections.title: Chapter 4: Deploying and operating in AWS
sections.note: This chapter covers the ways to reach and operate AWS (console, API, SDK, CLI, infrastructure as code with CloudFormation) and the three deployment models.

items.term: Ways to reach AWS, and the console

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Before you can build anything on AWS you need to know the doors into it.
> There is more than one door, and the right one depends on the job.

The AWS Management Console is the door you click through in a web browser.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **ways to provision and operate** — the different ways to create AWS resources and then manage them: clicking in a browser, typing commands, writing code, or describing the result in a file.
- **provision** — create a resource and set it up so it is ready to use.
- **AWS Management Console** — the web-based application that gives you one place in your browser to reach all AWS services.
- **sign-in credentials** — the secret details, such as a username and a password, that you use to prove who you are.

To provision a resource means to create it and set it up so it is ready to use. To operate a resource means to look after it afterwards: check it, change it, stop it.

AWS offers several ways to do both.

- **Click** in a browser: the console, taught in this lesson.
- **Type** text commands.
- **Write code** that talks to AWS.
- **Call AWS directly** with web requests that your own program signs.
- **Describe** the result you want in a file and let AWS build it.

The next lessons teach each one. All of them are ways to reach the same AWS account and resources.

blocks.title: The AWS Management Console
blocks.content:
You reach it with your sign-in credentials. The AWS Management Console is a web-based application that gives you one place, in your browser, to reach every AWS service. What it gives you:

- **Search** for services and features.
- **Settings** such as language and default Region.
- **Individual service consoles**, one for each AWS service, all reached from AWS Console Home.

It is visual, so it is the easiest place to look around and learn what a service does.

items.term: What the console does not do for you
items.text: A person clicks, so results depend on that person's memory and care. That is fine for exploring. It is a weakness when the same job must be done again and again; later lessons give better ways.

items.term: Every action is an API call

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> It looks like clicking, typing and coding are three different things.
> Underneath they are one thing, and knowing that makes every way into AWS easier to understand.

Every way into AWS ends at the same door: the API.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **AWS API** — the door each AWS service offers to programs: you send a request, AWS does the work and sends back a response.
- **AWS SDK** — a set of libraries for a programming language that makes AWS API calls for you.
- **access key** — secret values a program uses to prove who is making a request.

An AWS API is the door that each AWS service offers to programs: you send a request, AWS does the work and sends back a response. Every action you take on AWS ends up as a call to an AWS API.

Figure 3-1 below shows the three ways so far ending at the same API.

blocks.caption: The console, typed commands and an SDK all end in the same AWS API, which acts on your resources.

blocks.content:
The console is the API with buttons on top: AWS's own records of API calls include calls from the console and calls made by code. Typed commands, taught in a later lesson, also reach the API directly.

You could call the API yourself, but you would have to digitally sign every request with your credentials (signing means attaching a proof of who sent the request, made with your secret credentials). An AWS SDK is a set of libraries for a programming language, such as Python or Java, that makes those API calls for you. The SDKs take care of tasks such as cryptographically signing requests, managing errors and retrying requests automatically. For a program, the signing needs an *access key* to prove who is asking.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.content: Because the API is the single door, almost anything you can click you can also do from code. A program must prove who it is too, using credentials such as an access key.

items.text: AWS lists SDKs for programming languages and platforms such as Java, Python, Ruby, .NET, iOS and Android. You pick the one that matches the language your application is written in.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Clicking is slow when you do the same job fifty times.
> Typed commands can be saved and run again.

The AWS CLI is AWS from a text window.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **command line** — a text window where you type a command and press Enter to run it.
- **AWS CLI** — the AWS Command Line Interface: a tool that lets you use AWS services by typing commands.
- **script** — a file of commands that a computer runs in order.

A command line is a text window where you type a command and press Enter to run it. The AWS Command Line Interface, or AWS CLI, is an open source tool that lets you use AWS services by typing commands in your command-line shell. (A shell is the program that reads what you type.)

It gives you direct access to the public APIs of AWS services. It runs in the shells you may already use on Linux or macOS, and at the Windows command prompt or in PowerShell. AWS also offers a second set of command line tools, AWS Tools for PowerShell.

blocks.title: What typed commands give you
blocks.content:
AWS says command line tools can be faster and more convenient than the console, and useful for building scripts. A script is a file of commands that a computer runs in order.

- Save the steps you used once.
- Run the same steps again later, the same way each time.
- Share them with a colleague.

A script is a **repeatable** way to do the job, where clicking depends on a person.

items.text: The CLI does not unlock anything new. It reaches the same API as the console and the SDK. What changes is how you work: typing and saving instead of clicking.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You now know three handles on the same door.
> Choosing the wrong one wastes time or causes mistakes, so you need a way to choose.

Match the way in to the shape of the job.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **one-time operation** — a job you do once, by hand, and probably will not do again.
- **repeatable process** — a job you will do again and again, so it should run the same way every time.
- **programmatic access** — reaching AWS from a program or script through the API, an SDK or the CLI instead of clicking.

A one-time operation is a job you do once, by hand, and probably will not do again. A repeatable process is a job you will do again and again, so it should run the same way every time. Programmatic access means a program or a script, not a person clicking, calls AWS through the API, an SDK or the CLI.

Figure 3-2 below turns the choice into three questions.

blocks.caption: Three questions pick the way in: once and by hand, repeated from typed commands, or inside an application.

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.content:
- One look or one change: use the console.
- The same job again and again: put the commands in a script and use the CLI.
- AWS must be called from inside an application: use an SDK.

This is guidance, not a law: the CLI and SDK are both programmatic access.

items.text: A learner wants to see what a service looks like: the console. An admin must create the same set of resources for every new team: a script. A web application must save a customer's upload: an SDK in the application's own code.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A script repeats steps, but you still have to write every step in the right order.
> There is a simpler idea: describe what you want and let software work out the steps.

Infrastructure as code means your resources are described in a file.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **infrastructure as code** — describing your resources in files, the way programmers write code, and letting software create them from those files.
- **template** — the file that describes the resources you want and their settings.
- **automation** — letting software do the steps instead of a person.
- **declarative** — describing the end result you want, not the steps to get there.

Infrastructure as code is the practice of describing your resources in files, the way programmers write code, and letting software create them from those files. A template is the file that describes the resources you want and their settings.

The style is *declarative*. Declarative means you describe the end result you want, not the steps to get there. Compare a recipe card that lists steps with an order form that lists what you want on the table.

Automation means letting software do the steps instead of a person. With a template, the software does the creating, so the same template gives the same result each time.

blocks.title: What you gain
blocks.content:
- **Repeatable:** use one template again and again.
- **Consistent:** every copy matches, because a person is not typing each one.
- **Trackable:** templates are text files, so a history of changes (version control) shows what changed, who changed it and when, and lets you go back to an older version.
- **Less manual work:** the person describes, the software builds.

items.text: An imperative approach lists every step and the order of steps. Declarative lists only the end state. Declarative is simpler when you know which parts and settings you need. This module focuses on declarative templates.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A template is only a file until something reads it.
> AWS CloudFormation is the AWS service that reads a template and builds what it describes.

You write the template. CloudFormation does the building.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **AWS CloudFormation** — the AWS service that creates and configures resources from a template.
- **stack** — the collection of resources created from one template, managed together as one unit.

AWS CloudFormation is an AWS service that builds your resources from a template: you describe what you want, and CloudFormation creates and configures it for you.

Figure 3-3 below shows the flow: a template becomes a stack, and the stack holds the resources.

blocks.caption: A template goes into CloudFormation, which creates a stack: the group of resources the template describes.

blocks.content:
A stack is the collection of resources that CloudFormation creates from one template, managed together as a single unit. When you delete the stack, CloudFormation deletes all the resources in it.

The template does not need to say which resource must exist first: AWS says you do not have to figure out what depends on what, because CloudFormation handles that.

Templates can be reused, so the same template can build the same resources in several Regions. CloudFormation is available through its console, API, the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs.

blocks.title: Worked scenario
blocks.content:
A team wants the same test environment in two Regions.

1. It writes one template that describes the resources.
2. It creates a stack from the template in the first Region, then another stack from the same template in the second Region.
3. When the test ends, it deletes each stack and the resources in it are deleted too.

Nothing is rebuilt by hand.

items.text: The template is the plan. The stack is the plan in action. The resources are the real things. Change the plan, update the stack, and the resources follow.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Not every system can move to the cloud on day one.
> Three deployment models describe where a system can live: all in the cloud, all in your data center, or in both at once.

The model describes where it runs, not how you reach it.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this module in this lesson.

- **cloud deployment model** — all parts of the application run in the cloud.
- **on-premises deployment model** — the resources run in your own data center.
- **hybrid deployment model** — cloud resources connected to resources that are not in the cloud, most often your own data center.

A deployment model is the place where your application and its resources run: in the cloud, in your own data center, or in both.

Figure 3-4 below shows the three.

blocks.content:
- In the cloud model, all parts of the application run in the cloud. Such an application was built in the cloud or moved there from older infrastructure.
- In the on-premises model, the resources are in your own data center. AWS notes this does not give many of the cloud's benefits but may be chosen for dedicated resources. It is sometimes called a private cloud.
- A hybrid deployment connects resources in the cloud with resources that are not in the cloud, most often your own data center. It lets an organization extend its infrastructure into the cloud while connecting it to its internal systems.

blocks.title: Worked scenario
blocks.content:
A company keeps a system in its own data center. It builds a new web application in the cloud and connects the two so they can exchange data.

That company is using the hybrid deployment model.

items.term: Models and ways in are different questions
items.text: A deployment model says where the application runs. The console, CLI, SDK and templates are ways to build and operate it. A cloud application can be built with any of them.

sections.title: Chapter 5: The Well-Architected Framework
sections.note: Six pillars AWS uses to judge whether a design is good, plus the free tool that runs the review.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Every choice you make while building on AWS has pros and cons. The Framework gives you one shared list of questions, so you can judge a design instead of guessing.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Well-Architected Framework**: AWS's collection of best practices and questions for judging how good a design is. It comes from AWS's experience designing and reviewing thousands of customer architectures.
- **pillar**: one of the six areas the Framework is split into.
- **best practice**: a way of doing something that experience has shown works well.

The **AWS Well-Architected Framework** helps you understand the pros and cons of the decisions you make while building systems on AWS. It documents a set of foundational questions that show whether a specific design lines up with cloud best practices.

The Framework is built on **six pillars**: operational excellence, security, reliability, performance efficiency, cost optimization and sustainability. Figure 4-1 below shows them as six blocks that all apply to one workload.

blocks.content:
You apply the pillars to one workload at a time. A workload is a set of components that together deliver business value, such as a website. Each pillar holds its own best practices and its own questions, so a review walks through the workload six times, once per pillar.

The review is meant to be a constructive conversation about architectural decisions, and it is not an audit. The goal is to find what to improve, not to hand out a pass or a fail.

**One-liner for your notes:** the Framework is six pillars of questions for judging any workload.

items.text: AWS compares creating a software system to constructing a building. If the foundation is not solid, structural problems can undermine the whole building. In the same way, if you neglect one of the six pillars, it becomes hard to build a system that delivers what you expect. Using the pillars lets you produce stable and efficient systems, so you can focus on other parts of the design.
It is written for people in technology roles, such as chief technology officers, architects, developers and operations team members. You do not need to be an architect to use its questions.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A good design still fails if the people running it cannot see what is happening, cannot change it safely, or never learn from mistakes. This pillar is about running the workload well, day after day.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **operational excellence pillar**: the pillar about supporting development, running workloads effectively, gaining insight into how they behave, and continuously improving the processes around them.
- **observability**: collecting enough data from a workload, such as measurements and records of events, to understand how it behaves and stay in control.
- **blast radius**: how much of a system is hurt when one change goes wrong.

Operational excellence is a commitment to build software correctly while consistently delivering a great customer experience. The **operational excellence pillar** contains best practices for organizing your team, designing your workload, operating it at scale, and evolving it over time.

The key idea is that operations are part of the design. You plan how the workload will be changed, watched and repaired before it goes live, not afterwards.

blocks.title: Design principles of the pillar
blocks.content:
- **Organize teams around business outcomes**: teams, leaders and goals point at the same results.
- **Implement observability for actionable insights**: collect data so you can act when business results are at risk.
- **Safely automate where possible**: treat the whole environment like code.
- **Make frequent, small, reversible changes**: small steps are easier to undo.
- **Refine operations procedures frequently**: keep improving how you work.
- **Anticipate failure**: practise failure scenarios and test your response.
- **Learn from all operational events and metrics**: share lessons across teams.
- **Use managed services**: reduce operational burden by handing routine work to AWS-run services.

**Safely automate** builds directly on infrastructure as code. In the cloud you can define your entire workload and its operations (applications, infrastructure, configuration and procedures) as code, and update it. You can then start operations automatically in response to events. Automation gives consistent responses, limits human error and reduces operator toil, meaning boring repeated manual work. Guardrails such as approvals and error thresholds keep automation safe.

**Example.** A team that ships one huge update every quarter risks a large failure. A team that ships small automated changes every day has a small blast radius, and it can reverse a bad change quickly.

items.text: Designing a workload so its parts are loosely coupled (each part works on its own and depends little on the others) lets you update components regularly. Automated deployment together with smaller, incremental changes reduces the blast radius and allows faster reversal when failures occur. That gives a team confidence to deliver improvements while keeping quality.

Anticipating failure means driving failure scenarios on purpose to understand the workload's risk profile. You then test whether your procedures and your team's response work, and you make informed decisions about the risks you find.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A workload is only useful if its data and systems stay safe. The security pillar lists the habits that keep them safe while you keep building quickly.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **security pillar**: the pillar about protecting data, systems and assets while taking advantage of cloud technologies to improve your security.
- **least privilege**: giving each person or program only the permissions it needs, and nothing more. You will study this in the access management chapter.
- **encryption**: scrambling data so that only someone holding the right key can read it. You will study this in the security chapters.
- **defense in depth**: using several layers of security controls, so that one failed layer does not expose everything.

The **security pillar** encompasses the ability to protect data, systems and assets while taking advantage of cloud technologies to improve your security.

Its first principle is to **implement a strong identity foundation**. Apply the principle of least privilege and enforce separation of duties, which means no single person controls a whole sensitive process. Centralize identity management, meaning one central place decides who is who and what they may do, and aim to eliminate long-term static credentials, meaning passwords or keys that stay valid for a long time.

**Example.** An intern needs to read one report. Least privilege says to grant read access to that report only, and not to the whole system.

blocks.title: Design principles of the pillar
blocks.content:
- **Implement a strong identity foundation**: least privilege, separation of duties, central identity management.
- **Maintain traceability**: monitor, alert and audit actions and changes in real time.
- **Apply security at all layers**: defense in depth with several controls.
- **Automate security best practices**: define controls as code in templates whose changes are saved and tracked.
- **Protect data in transit and at rest**: classify data and use encryption and access control as fitting.
- **Keep people away from data**: reduce direct access and manual handling.
- **Prepare for security events**: have incident processes and run response simulations.

Two principles protect data directly. **In transit** means while data travels across a network, and **at rest** means while it is stored. Both need protection, and encryption is one of the main tools.

Two more principles are about people and process. **Keep people away from data** lowers the risk of mistakes and mishandling, because tools do the work instead of humans. **Prepare for security events** means having a plan and practising it, so detection, investigation and recovery are fast.

items.term: What does apply security at all layers cover?
items.text: AWS lists layers such as the edge of the network, load balancing, every service that runs code, the operating system, the application and the code. Defense in depth means each layer has its own controls.

Software-based security mechanisms help you scale securely, faster and at lower cost. When controls are defined as code in version-controlled templates, you can create secure architectures the same way every time.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Customers judge a system by whether it works when they need it. The reliability pillar is about designing so that failures happen without hurting users, and recovery is routine.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **reliability pillar**: the pillar about a workload performing its intended function correctly and consistently when it is expected to, including operating and testing it through its whole lifecycle.
- **scale horizontally**: replace one large resource with several smaller ones that share the work.

The **reliability pillar** encompasses the ability of a workload to perform its intended function correctly and consistently when it is expected to. That includes the ability to operate and test the workload through its total lifecycle.

You already know the building blocks: high availability, disaster recovery and elasticity. This pillar asks whether your design actually uses them, and whether you have proved that it works.

blocks.title: Design principles of the pillar
blocks.content:
- **Automatically recover from failure**: watch business measures, and start automation when a limit is crossed.
- **Test recovery procedures**: in the cloud you can test how your workload fails and check your recovery steps.
- **Scale horizontally to increase aggregate workload availability**: many small resources instead of one large one.
- **Stop guessing capacity**: monitor demand and add or remove resources automatically.
- **Manage change through automation**: make infrastructure changes with automation that can be tracked and reviewed.

**Scale horizontally** is the principle that links most directly to earlier lessons. Replace one large resource with multiple small resources to reduce the impact of a single failure. Distribute requests across the smaller resources so that they do not share a common point of failure.

**Example.** One big server in one data center is a single point of failure. Four smaller servers spread over two Availability Zones keep serving users when one server, or one zone, is lost.

**Test recovery procedures** is a change from on-premises habits. On premises, testing usually proves that a workload works in one scenario. In the cloud you can use automation to simulate failures and to recreate the scenarios that caused failures before, so you fix weak spots before a real failure.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Users notice slow systems quickly, but fast systems that waste resources are costly. This pillar is about matching resources to what you need, and keeping that match as things change.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **performance efficiency pillar**: the pillar about using cloud resources efficiently to meet performance requirements, and keeping that efficiency as demand changes and technologies evolve.
- **serverless**: a style where AWS runs and manages the servers, and you only supply your code or data. The next chapter covers this.
- **mechanical sympathy**: choosing the technology that fits how you will really use it, for example picking storage by how your data is accessed.

The **performance efficiency pillar** includes the ability to use cloud resources efficiently to meet performance requirements, and to maintain that efficiency as demand changes and technologies evolve.

Two words from earlier lessons matter here. **Latency** is how long a response takes. **Elasticity** is how a workload grows and shrinks with demand. This pillar asks whether you chose resources well and keep checking that the choice is still right.

blocks.title: Design principles of the pillar
blocks.content:
- **Democratize advanced technologies**: consume hard technology as a service, instead of learning to run it yourself.
- **Go global in minutes**: deploy in several AWS Regions for lower latency and a better customer experience.
- **Use serverless architectures**: remove the need to run and maintain servers for routine tasks.
- **Experiment more often**: try different server sizes, storage and settings, and compare.
- **Consider mechanical sympathy**: choose the approach that fits how the service is used.

**Go global in minutes** connects to Regions and edge locations. Deploying your workload in multiple Regions around the world lets you give customers lower latency and a better experience, at minimal cost.

**Example.** Most of your users are far from your Region and pages load slowly. You deploy the workload in a Region near them, and latency drops.

**Democratize advanced technologies** means a small team can use specialized technology, such as converting video formats, as a service. The team focuses on its product instead of provisioning and managing resources.

**Experiment more often** works because resources are virtual and can be automated. You can quickly compare different server types or configurations, keep the best, and discard the rest.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> The cloud makes it easy to spend money by accident, and just as easy to save it. This pillar teaches you to pay for value, and nothing else.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **cost optimization pillar**: the pillar about running systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point.
- **undifferentiated heavy lifting**: routine infrastructure work, like racking, stacking and powering servers, that every company must do but that does not set your business apart.
- **Cloud Financial Management**: building the knowledge, programs and processes an organization needs to manage cloud spending well.

The **cost optimization pillar** includes the ability to run systems to deliver business value at the lowest price point. It builds on pay-as-you-go pricing and on the idea of not over-provisioning, which you met earlier.

**Adopt a consumption model** is the principle that puts pay-as-you-go into practice. Pay only for the computing resources you require, and increase or decrease usage depending on business requirements, instead of relying on elaborate forecasting.

**Worked example.** Development and test environments are typically only used for eight hours a day during the work week. You can stop these resources when they are not in use for a potential cost savings of 75% (40 hours versus 168 hours). The 40 is the working hours in a week, and the 168 is every hour in a week.

blocks.title: Design principles of the pillar
blocks.content:
- **Implement Cloud Financial Management**: build the skills and processes to manage cloud spending.
- **Adopt a consumption model**: pay for what you use, and stop what you do not.
- **Measure overall efficiency**: compare the business output of a workload with what it costs.
- **Stop spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting**: let AWS do data center work, and let AWS-run services take over operating system and application chores.
- **Analyze and attribute expenditure**: see usage and cost for each system and charge it to the workload owner.

**Measure overall efficiency** and **analyze and attribute expenditure** are about knowing where money goes. The cloud makes it simple to identify the usage and cost of each system, so costs can be assigned clearly to individual workload owners. That helps measure return on investment (ROI), meaning the gain you get for the money you spend, and it gives owners a reason to reduce waste.

**Stop spending money on undifferentiated heavy lifting** reminds you why the cloud can be cheaper than running your own data center. AWS handles racking, stacking and powering servers, so your team spends time on customers and projects.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Running computers uses energy, and wasted capacity wastes energy. This pillar asks you to deliver the same results with fewer resources.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **sustainability pillar**: the pillar about environmental impact, especially energy consumption and efficiency, and acting to reduce the resources a workload uses.
- **utilization**: how much of a resource's capacity is actually in use.
- **host**: a physical server that runs your workloads.

The **sustainability pillar** focuses on environmental impacts, especially energy consumption and efficiency, because they are important levers for architects to take direct action to reduce resource usage.

AWS describes the pillar as the ability to keep improving sustainability impacts by reducing energy consumption and increasing efficiency across all parts of a workload. It does this by getting the full benefit from the resources you provision and by minimizing the total resources you need.

blocks.title: Focus areas of the pillar
blocks.content:
- **Understand your impact**: measure what your workload uses and estimate its future impact.
- **Establish sustainability goals**: for example, fewer servers and less storage per transaction.
- **Maximize utilization**: right-size and design for high use, and remove idle resources.
- **Adopt new, more efficient hardware and software**: keep evaluating better options.
- **Use managed services**: the same idea as in the operational excellence pillar.
- **Reduce downstream impact**: AWS also names this as a focus area for the pillar.

**Maximize utilization** ties back to over-provisioning. AWS explains that two hosts running at 30% utilization are less efficient than one host running at 60%, because each host has a baseline power consumption. Idle capacity still uses energy, so unused resources are waste for both cost and the environment.

**Example.** A workload keeps ten servers running all night at low use. Right-sizing it to fewer, busier servers does the same work with less energy.

The cost and sustainability pillars often agree, because both reward removing idle resources. They can still pull against reliability, which the next lesson explains.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Exam questions and real design talks describe a situation and leave you to name the pillar. Practise matching the situation to the question each pillar asks.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **pillar trade-offs**: choices where improving one pillar makes another worse, so you decide which matters more for your business.

Each pillar asks one main question about a workload:

| Pillar | The question it asks |
|---|---|
| Operational excellence | Can we run it, see it and keep improving it? |
| Security | Are data and systems protected? |
| Reliability | Does it keep working, and recover? |
| Performance efficiency | Does it meet speed needs without waste? |
| Cost optimization | Are we paying the lowest price for the value? |
| Sustainability | Are we using the least energy and resources? |
