blocks.content:
When you design, the pillars sometimes pull against each other. AWS says you make **trade-offs between pillars** based on your business context. You might favour sustainability and cost over reliability in a development environment. For a mission-critical system you might favour reliability, accepting higher cost and sustainability impact. In an online shop, performance can affect revenue.

AWS says security and operational excellence are generally not traded off against the other pillars. They stay strong while you balance the rest.

**One-liner for your notes:** match the situation to the pillar's question, and remember that business context decides the trade-offs.

items.term: A tip for telling similar pillars apart
items.text: Cost optimization and sustainability both reward removing waste, but one measures money and the other measures energy and resources. Reliability and operational excellence both involve failure, but reliability is about the design surviving failures, while operational excellence is about how people run, watch and improve the workload.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Reading the Framework once does not tell you how your own workload scores. The Tool turns the questions into a guided review you can repeat and track.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Well-Architected Tool**: a service in the cloud that gives you a consistent process to review and measure a workload against the Framework.
- **high risk issue (HRI)**: an architectural or operational choice AWS has found might cause a significant negative impact to a business.
- **medium risk issue (MRI)**: a choice that also might hurt the business, but to a lesser extent.
- **milestone**: a saved point in time that marks a key change in your architecture, such as going live.

The **AWS Well-Architected Tool** is a service in the cloud that provides a consistent process for you to review and measure your architecture using the Framework. AWS provides this service for reviewing your workloads at no charge.

You start by defining a workload in the Tool: a name, a description, whether it runs in production or pre-production, and the Regions it uses. Then you answer questions for each pillar. The Tool shows the risks it found and an improvement plan based on your answers.

blocks.title: High and medium risks
blocks.content:
- A **high risk issue (HRI)** is an architectural or operational choice that AWS has found might result in significant negative impact to a business.
- A **medium risk issue (MRI)** also might negatively impact a business, but to a lesser extent.
- Both come from your own answers. They are guidance, so you judge the real impact for your business.
- For each issue you can fix it and mark the best practice as met, or document why you chose not to.

**Milestones** let you save the state of a review at key moments in a workload's life, such as design, testing and go live. Comparing milestones shows whether the workload is improving. The Tool counts questions answered and the number of high and medium risks for each workload, so progress is easy to see.

**Example.** Before launching an online shop, a team defines it as a workload and answers the questions for all six pillars. The Tool lists several high risk issues. The team fixes them, saves a milestone, and repeats the review after launch.

**One-liner for your notes:** the Well-Architected Tool is the free guided review that finds risks in a workload.

items.term: A newer option: the Well-Architected Agent
items.text: AWS also describes an AI-powered AWS Well-Architected Agent that analyzes your deployed resources and infrastructure as code templates and suggests improvements. When this lesson was written, AWS marked the Agent as a preview release that is subject to change, so check the current AWS page before relying on it. The Tool, by contrast, is a manual, guided self-review.

sections.title: Chapter 6: Compute
sections.note: The AWS services that run your code: virtual servers, containers, serverless functions, and the tools that scale and connect them.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Almost every application needs somewhere to run its code. AWS offers several ways to do that, so you first need a map of the choices before you meet each service.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **compute**: the processing power, meaning CPU and memory, that runs your application's code. On AWS you rent it instead of buying servers.
- **compute categories**: the three styles of AWS compute: virtual machines, containers and serverless.
- **container**: a package that holds an application and everything it needs to run. The lessons on containers explain it fully.
- **serverless**: a style where AWS fully manages the servers, so you do not set up, maintain or provision them.

**Compute** is the processing power that runs your code. AWS compute services fall into three styles, called **compute categories**. They differ in how much you manage yourself and how much AWS manages for you.

1. **Virtual machines.** You rent a virtual server and choose its operating system and software. You have the most control, and the most to look after. This is the infrastructure as a service (IaaS) idea from the foundations chapter.
2. **Containers.** You package your application and what it needs into a container, and a service runs those containers for you.
3. **Serverless.** You supply code, and AWS runs it on servers you never see. You have the least control, and the least to look after.

blocks.title: The three styles side by side
blocks.content:
| Style | What you get | What you look after |
|---|---|---|
| Virtual machine | A virtual server | The operating system and software |
| Container | A packaged application | The package, and sometimes the machines |
| Serverless | Your code runs when needed | Only your code |

**Example.** A team must run old software that needs one exact operating system setting. They need control of the operating system, so a virtual machine fits. Another team only wants a small piece of code to run when a customer uploads a photo. They do not want any server to look after, so serverless fits.

The next lessons walk through each style in turn, starting with virtual machines.

**One-liner for your notes:** more control means more work, and less control means less work.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many applications simply need a server with an operating system, the way they would on your own hardware. EC2 gives you that in minutes, without buying anything.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Amazon EC2**: short for Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud. A service that provides on-demand, scalable computing capacity in the AWS Cloud.
- **EC2 instance**: one virtual server that you launch in EC2.
- **AMI**: short for Amazon Machine Image. A preconfigured template that packages the operating system and extra software needed to start an instance.
- **security group**: a virtual firewall that controls which traffic can reach your instances. The networking chapter covers it fully.
- **VPC**: your own private network section inside AWS. The networking chapter covers it fully.
- **S3**: an AWS service for storing files, called objects. The storage chapter covers it fully.

**Amazon EC2** provides on-demand, scalable computing capacity in the AWS Cloud. You use it to launch as many or as few virtual servers as you need, configure security and networking, and manage storage. Each virtual server is an **EC2 instance**.

EC2 is infrastructure as a service. You pick the operating system and the software, and you look after them. AWS looks after the physical hardware, the data center and the virtualization.

To launch an instance you pick an **AMI**, which is a preconfigured template that packages the operating system and additional software. You also pick an instance type, which the next lesson explains. Figure 5-1 below shows an instance launched from an AMI inside one Availability Zone.

blocks.content:
You can launch many instances from one AMI when you need servers with the same setup. You can also use different AMIs for servers that need different setups. You must specify an AMI when you launch an instance.

An AMI belongs to one Region. You can copy it to another Region to launch instances there. An instance runs in one Availability Zone inside that Region.

blocks.title: Helpers you will meet again
blocks.content:
- **Security group**: a virtual firewall in front of your instances. It lists the protocols, ports and source addresses that may reach them.
- **VPC**: the private network your instances live in.
- **S3**: a place to keep files outside of any single instance.

You meet each of these properly in the later chapters. For now it is enough to know that an instance is protected and connected through them.

items.term: You already know how to manage EC2
items.text: You can create and manage EC2 instances with the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, CloudFormation templates and the AWS SDKs. These are the ways to operate AWS that you met in the deploying and operating chapter.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A tiny website and a video converter need very different machines. Choosing the right type of machine is how you avoid paying for hardware you do not need.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **EC2 instance type**: the configuration of CPU, memory, storage and networking that an instance gets.
- **general purpose**: instance types with a balance of compute, memory and networking.
- **compute optimized**: instance types for tasks that need strong processors.
- **memory optimized**: instance types for workloads that hold large data sets in memory.
- **storage optimized**: instance types for workloads that read and write a lot of data on local storage.
- **accelerated computing**: instance types that use hardware accelerators, called co-processors, for special jobs.

When you launch an instance, the **EC2 instance type** you choose determines the hardware of the host computer. Each type offers a different balance of compute, memory, network and storage. Types are grouped into instance families based on these abilities.

A type also comes in different sizes, so you can scale the resources to the work. AWS groups the types into categories. Figure 5-2 below matches five of them to the kind of work each suits.

blocks.caption: Match the shape of your workload to an instance family.

blocks.content:
Here is each category in plain words:

- **General purpose** gives a balance of compute, memory and networking. It suits web servers, code repositories and small to medium databases.
- **Compute optimized** suits compute bound work that benefits from high-performance processors, such as batch processing, media transcoding and dedicated game servers.
- **Memory optimized** suits workloads that process large data sets in memory, such as in-memory databases.
- **Storage optimized** delivers many low-latency, random reads and writes on local storage. It suits high-throughput databases and data streaming.
- **Accelerated computing** uses co-processors to do some jobs more efficiently, such as floating point calculations (math with decimal numbers), graphics processing or data pattern matching.

**Example.** A video site converts every uploaded video into other formats. The work keeps the processor busy and needs little extra memory, so it is compute bound (held back mainly by processor speed) and a compute optimized type fits.

You are not locked in. AWS suggests launching an instance and testing with your own application, and you can change the instance type later if your needs change.

**One-liner for your notes:** pick the instance family that matches what your workload is short of, whether that is balance, processor, memory, disk or special hardware.

items.term: A sixth category and the processors
items.text: AWS also lists an HPC optimized category for high performance computing, such as complex simulations. Instance types also differ in the processor inside, such as Intel, AMD or AWS Graviton.

Names are based on the instance family, generation, processor family, capabilities and size. In AWS lists, for example, types starting with C are compute optimized and types starting with R are memory optimized.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Traffic is rarely steady. Auto Scaling adds servers when your application is busy and removes them when it is quiet, so you stop guessing capacity.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Auto Scaling**: a feature that keeps the right number of EC2 instances running for the load on your application.
- **scaling policy**: a rule that tells the group when to add or remove instances.
- **min, max and desired capacity**: the smallest allowed, largest allowed and wanted number of instances in the group.

**Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling** helps you ensure that you have the correct number of EC2 instances available to handle the load for your application. You create collections of instances called **Auto Scaling groups**. This is how EC2 becomes elastic.

You give each group three numbers. The **minimum** is the size it never goes below. The **maximum** is the size it never goes above. The **desired capacity** is how many instances you want right now. AWS gives this example: a group with a minimum of four instances, a desired capacity of six and a maximum of twelve. Figure 5-3 below shows that group at three moments.

blocks.caption: The scaling policies move the group size up and down, and the group stays between the minimum and the maximum.

blocks.content:
A **scaling policy** decides when the number changes. With **target tracking**, you pick a target for a measurement, such as average processor use, and the group adds or removes instances to stay near it. AWS compares this to a thermostat: you choose the temperature and the thermostat does the rest. AWS also offers step scaling and simple scaling.

The group also looks after health. It monitors instances and replaces ones that are impaired or terminated, to keep the desired capacity. You can spread a group over several Availability Zones, and it balances instances evenly across them, which gives high availability.

There is no additional fee for Auto Scaling. You pay only for the resources you use, such as the instances.

items.term: Where do new instances get their settings?
items.text: Auto Scaling groups use launch templates as configuration templates for the instances they launch. A launch template is a saved set of settings for new instances, so each one starts the same way.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Several servers are no use if every user is sent to the same one. A load balancer spreads the traffic and skips servers that are broken.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Elastic Load Balancing**: the AWS service that automatically distributes incoming traffic across multiple targets.
- **load balancer**: a component that receives traffic and shares it among several targets, such as instances.
- **load balancer health check**: a regular test of each target, so the load balancer only sends requests to healthy ones.
- **ALB and NLB**: the Application Load Balancer, which works with web requests, and the Network Load Balancer, which works with network connections.
- **layer 7 and layer 4**: layer 7 means the balancer reads web requests such as HTTP. Layer 4 means it handles network connections such as TCP and UDP without reading the web request.

**Elastic Load Balancing** automatically distributes your incoming traffic across multiple targets, such as EC2 instances, containers and IP addresses, in one or more Availability Zones. A **load balancer** is the part that receives the traffic. Using one increases the availability and fault tolerance of your applications.

Figure 5-4 below shows a load balancer in front of four instances spread over two Availability Zones, inside an Auto Scaling group.

blocks.content:
Health checks keep users away from broken servers. A **load balancer health check** monitors each target, so the load balancer sends requests only to the healthy ones. Elastic Load Balancing also scales its own capacity automatically as incoming traffic changes.

Load balancing and Auto Scaling work as a pair. Instances that Auto Scaling launches are registered with the load balancer automatically. Instances that it terminates are deregistered. So the group changes size and the traffic keeps flowing.

blocks.title: Two load balancer types to know
blocks.content:
| | Application Load Balancer (ALB) | Network Load Balancer (NLB) |
|---|---|---|
| Layer | 7, web requests | 4, connections |
| Protocols (ways computers talk over a network) | HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC | TCP, UDP, TLS |
| AWS suggests it for | flexible application management | extreme performance and a static IP |

An ALB can route by what is in the web request. An NLB passes connections through quickly. AWS suggests an ALB for flexible application management, and an NLB when you need extreme performance and a static IP address (one that never changes).

items.text: Elastic Load Balancing also has a Gateway Load Balancer. The Classic Load Balancer is the previous generation, and AWS recommends migrating to a current generation load balancer.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> An application that works on one machine often breaks on another because something small differs. A container packs the application with what it needs, so it runs the same way everywhere.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **container**: a package that holds an application and the files and libraries it needs to run, isolated from other containers on the same host.
- **container image**: a read-only file that holds what is needed to run a containerized application. A running container is created from an image.
- **container orchestration**: automating the starting, stopping, scaling and management of many containers.
- **Docker**: a popular open-source tool and runtime for building and running containers.

**Containerization** bundles an application's code with all the files and libraries it needs to run on any infrastructure. The result is a **container**. It sets up the same environment each time, so you can build once and run it on many machines.

Containers use operating system level virtualization. Multiple containers can run on a single host operating system without needing a hypervisor, and each stays isolated from its neighbors. Figure 5-5 below compares this with virtual machines, which use a hypervisor to virtualize hardware.

blocks.content:
A **container image** is the starting point. It is a file with the information needed to run the application, and it is read-only. You build the image once and start as many containers from it as you need. A container starts fast because it does not need to boot a whole operating system.

**Docker** is a popular open-source container runtime that lets developers build, deploy and test containerized applications on many platforms.

One container is easy to manage. A large application can have hundreds or thousands. **Container orchestration** automates their whole life, from provisioning and scheduling to deployment and deletion. Without it you would start, stop and restart every container by hand.

items.text: A container shields the application from differences in software installed on the host, because the application and its dependencies travel together. This is why the same container can move from a laptop to a server to the cloud.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Once your application is in a container image, you need a safe place to keep the image and a service that runs the containers for you. AWS provides both.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Amazon ECR**: Amazon Elastic Container Registry. A managed place to store, share and deploy container images.
- **Amazon ECS**: Amazon Elastic Container Service. A fully managed container orchestration service that deploys, manages and scales containerized applications.

**Amazon ECR** is an AWS managed container image registry. A registry is a store of images. ECR supports private repositories (named places in the registry that hold images) with permissions, so only the people and instances you choose can use your images. It can also scan images for software vulnerabilities (weak spots attackers could use), and replicate them to other Regions.

**Amazon ECS** is a fully managed container orchestration service that helps you deploy, manage and scale containerized applications. Figure 5-6 below shows how the two fit together: ECR stores the image, and ECS pulls it and runs it.

blocks.title: ECS words to know
blocks.content:
- **Task definition**: the blueprint for your application.
- **Cluster**: the infrastructure your application runs on.
- **Task**: a piece of work that runs and then stops.
- **Service**: a long-running application that ECS keeps running.

ECS can run your containers on EC2 instances in your account. You choose the instance type and the number of instances, and you manage that capacity. ECS can also add instances to the cluster as needed, and increase or decrease the number of tasks in a service automatically.

ECS works with services you already know. It can use Elastic Load Balancing to spread traffic across the containers of a service, and Auto Scaling to manage the EC2 instances of its cluster.

**One-liner for your notes:** ECR stores container images and ECS runs them.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many teams already use Kubernetes to run containers. EKS lets them keep using it on AWS without running the hardest part themselves.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Kubernetes**: a popular open-source container orchestrator for deploying, scaling and managing many containers.
- **Amazon EKS**: Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service. A managed AWS service for running Kubernetes.
- **control plane**: the part of Kubernetes that schedules workloads and keeps track of the state of the cluster.

**Kubernetes** is a popular open-source container orchestrator that software developers use to deploy, scale and manage a large number of containers. It works in a declarative style. You describe what you want in configuration files, and Kubernetes takes action to match it.

**Amazon EKS** provides a fully managed Kubernetes service. With EKS, AWS manages the Kubernetes control plane for you. That covers the components that schedule workloads, integrate with AWS and store the cluster information. EKS runs in the AWS cloud, and also in your own data centers.

blocks.title: ECS or EKS?
blocks.content:
| | Amazon ECS | Amazon EKS |
|---|---|---|
| Orchestrator | An AWS service built for AWS | Open-source Kubernetes |
| A good fit when | You want to stay with AWS-managed tools | You already use Kubernetes |
| Your tools | Learn ECS | Reuse Kubernetes tools |

EKS is certified Kubernetes-conformant. So you can deploy Kubernetes-compatible applications without refactoring (rewriting them), and you can use Kubernetes community tools and plugins.

**Example.** A company runs Kubernetes in its own data center and wants to use the same tools in AWS. EKS fits, because the team keeps its Kubernetes knowledge. A small team with no Kubernetes experience, which only wants to run containers on AWS, may prefer ECS, because it needs no Kubernetes knowledge.

Both services use container images, and ECR can hold the images for either one.

**One-liner for your notes:** ECS is the AWS way to orchestrate containers and EKS is managed Kubernetes.

items.term: What does AWS manage in standard EKS?
items.text: In the standard approach, AWS manages the Kubernetes control plane when you create a cluster. With EKS Auto Mode, EKS also manages the nodes, which are the machines that run your containers.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many jobs are small and happen only now and then. Running a server around the clock for them wastes money and time. Lambda runs your code only when something happens.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **serverless**: a style where the cloud provider fully manages the servers behind an application, so you do not configure, maintain or provision them.
- **AWS Lambda**: AWS's serverless compute service. It runs your code without you provisioning or managing servers.
- **event-driven function**: a piece of code that runs in response to an event, such as a file arriving or a web request.

**Serverless** computing means the cloud provider fully manages the servers that run your application. You do not configure, maintain or provision them. The service scales automatically with the workload.

**AWS Lambda** is a serverless compute service. You run code without provisioning or managing servers. Lambda manages server maintenance, capacity provisioning, scaling and patching for you, so you can focus on your application logic.

The original kind of Lambda function is an **event-driven function**. You write a handler function and connect it to a trigger, which is the event that starts it. When the trigger fires, Lambda runs the function. Figure 5-7 below shows the flow.

blocks.content:
Each run is independent, and Lambda scales by running more copies as demand grows. With no events, nothing runs. This fits the pay-as-you-go idea. Lambda charges per request, plus the time your code runs weighted by the memory you give it (called GB-seconds).

**Limits matter.** By default, one run can last up to 15 minutes. So Lambda suits short, event-driven jobs, such as making a thumbnail when a photo is uploaded. A single job that must run for hours is usually a better fit for the other compute services in this chapter.

**One-liner for your notes:** Lambda runs short pieces of code in response to events, and AWS handles every server.

items.term: Lambda now has three compute types
items.text: AWS describes three Lambda compute primitives. Event Functions are the original type and run code in response to events. Web Functions run web applications as HTTP servers. MicroVMs are isolated environments for workloads that need a dedicated environment per user or job. All three share a serverless foundation with no server management and pay-per-use billing.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Containers still need machines to run on, and looking after those machines is real work. Fargate gives you the containers without the machines.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Fargate**: a serverless compute engine for containers that works with Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, so you run containers without managing servers.

**AWS Fargate** is a technology that you use with Amazon ECS or Amazon EKS to run containers without having to manage servers or clusters of EC2 instances. You no longer provision, configure or scale clusters of virtual machines. That removes the need to choose server types, decide when to scale a cluster, or optimize cluster packing (fitting containers onto servers without wasting space).

You package the application in containers, say how much CPU and memory it needs, define networking and permissions, and launch it. Fargate is a serverless, pay-as-you-go compute engine.

blocks.title: ECS with EC2 or with Fargate
blocks.content:
| | Containers on EC2 instances | Containers on Fargate |
|---|---|---|
| Who picks servers | You | AWS |
| Who scales the cluster | You, with Auto Scaling | AWS |
| You still define | Image, CPU, memory | Image, CPU, memory |

Each Fargate task has its own isolation boundary. It does not share the underlying kernel (the core of the operating system), CPU, memory or network interface with another task.

**Choosing between the three.** Use **EC2** when you need full control of the server. Use **Lambda** for short, event-driven code. Use **Fargate** when your application is already in containers and you do not want to manage servers. For example, a team with a containerized web service and no wish to patch servers can run it on Fargate.

**One-liner for your notes:** Fargate is serverless compute for containers, and it works with ECS and EKS.

items.text: EKS lets you choose per pod where compute comes from, EC2 or Fargate. A pod is the smallest unit Kubernetes runs, and it holds one or more containers. You can even have a cluster where some pods run on EC2 while others run on Fargate.

items.term: Easier compute: Elastic Beanstalk and Lightsail

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Not everyone wants to design servers, scaling and load balancing. Two services hide that work so you can get an application online quickly.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Elastic Beanstalk**: a service that deploys your web application and sets up the servers, load balancing, health monitoring and scaling around it.
- **Amazon Lightsail**: a simple way to start on AWS for websites and web apps, bundling servers and extras for a low, predictable monthly price.

**AWS Elastic Beanstalk** lets you deploy web applications into the AWS Cloud. You build and deploy your application, and Beanstalk provisions EC2 instances or EKS clusters, configures load balancing, sets up health monitoring and dynamically scales your environment. It is a platform as a service (PaaS) idea.

Beanstalk supports Go, Java, .NET, Node.js, PHP, Python and Ruby, and also Docker containers. There is no additional charge for Beanstalk itself. You pay only for the underlying AWS resources your application uses.

**Amazon Lightsail** is described by AWS as the easiest way to get started with AWS for anyone who needs to build websites or web applications. It includes what you need to launch quickly, such as instances (virtual private servers), container services and load balancers, for a low, predictable monthly price. You click to launch a simple operating system, a ready-made application such as WordPress, or a development stack.

Lightsail suits individual developers, hobbyists and people learning cloud basics. As a project grows, it can connect to other AWS services.

blocks.title: Choosing the easier option
blocks.content:
| Service | What you do | Good for |
|---|---|---|
| EC2 | Set up and run everything | Full control |
| Elastic Beanstalk | Upload the application | Web apps without wiring servers |
| Lightsail | Click to launch a bundle | Simple projects, fixed monthly price |

Example: a hobbyist wants a WordPress blog this afternoon. Lightsail fits. A small team has a Python web app and wants load balancing and scaling set up for them. Beanstalk fits.

items.text: Beanstalk has two modes. Standard runs applications directly on EC2 and supports Windows applications. Cluster runs applications on Amazon EKS and supports faster deployments and autoscaling.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some work is not a website or a quick event. It is a big pile of jobs that must all run, then stop. Batch finds and releases the computers for you.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Batch**: a service that runs batch computing workloads on AWS and provisions the resources needed for submitted jobs.
- **batch job**: a unit of work that runs from start to finish without anyone waiting on it, such as processing a large set of files.

A **batch job** is a unit of work that runs to completion on its own, such as processing a large set of files overnight. **AWS Batch** helps you run batch computing workloads on AWS. It removes the heavy lifting of configuring and managing the infrastructure, and it provisions resources in response to the jobs you submit.

Batch runs on top of Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, so your jobs run as containers. It can scale compute capacity on EC2 instances and on Fargate resources. You do not install or manage batch software.

**Example.** A research team must process a very large set of files. They submit the work as jobs. Batch starts the compute capacity the jobs need, runs them, and scales back when they finish. The team looks at results instead of managing servers.

**Batch or Lambda?** Lambda suits short, event-driven functions, with a default limit of 15 minutes per run. Batch suits large, compute-intensive workloads of any scale made up of many jobs.

**One-liner for your notes:** Batch runs big piles of jobs and manages the compute for them.

items.text: AWS Batch plans, schedules and runs containerized batch workloads across AWS compute, such as ECS, EKS, Fargate and EC2 instances.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Sometimes data or applications must stay close to a factory, a hospital or an office. AWS Outposts brings AWS to your building instead of sending everything to a Region.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Outposts**: a service, fully run by AWS, that places AWS infrastructure, services and APIs at your own site.

**AWS Outposts** is a service, fully run by AWS, that extends AWS infrastructure, services, APIs and tools to your premises. You build and run applications on premises with the same programming interfaces as in AWS Regions. It uses local compute and storage for lower latency and local data processing.

An Outpost is a pool of AWS compute and storage capacity deployed at your site. AWS operates, monitors and manages it as part of an AWS Region. Figure 5-8 below shows an Outpost in your data center, linked back to the Region.

blocks.content:
This is the hybrid deployment model you met earlier: some resources are on premises and others are in the cloud. With Outposts, the on-premises part uses AWS tools.

Outposts comes in two forms. An **Outposts rack** is an industry-standard 42U rack (U is a standard unit of rack height). An **Outposts server** is a 1U or 2U server for sites with limited space. On an Outpost you can create resources such as EC2 instances and ECS clusters. Outposts racks also support Amazon EKS nodes. AWS manages the hardware and keeps it connected to the Region over a service link.

**Example.** A factory must react to machine data in very short time and cannot wait for a round trip to a distant Region. It installs an Outpost on site, runs EC2 instances there for local processing, and still manages everything with AWS tools.

**One-liner for your notes:** Outposts is AWS infrastructure in your building, managed by AWS.

items.text: Each Outpost is an extension of an Availability Zone and its associated Region. Instances in Outpost subnets communicate with other instances in the Region using private IP addresses within the same VPC.

sections.title: Chapter 7: Storage
sections.note: Object, block and file storage on AWS, S3 classes and lifecycle, EBS, EFS and FSx, hybrid storage and backup.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Every storage service in this chapter is one of three shapes.
> Learn the shapes first and each service becomes easy to place.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **object storage**: storage that keeps each piece of data as one whole item, with a unique identifier and labels that describe it.
- **block storage**: storage that cuts data into equal-sized blocks and acts like a raw disk for one server.
- **file storage**: storage that keeps files in folders and shares them over the network.

Storage is where data is kept so a server and its applications can read it later. There are three basic shapes, and each answers a different need.

**Block storage** divides data into equal-sized blocks and stores them for fast access. A server uses it like a local hard drive: the operating system puts its own file system on top and treats it as its own disk. A file system is the way an operating system organises files on a disk.

**File storage** keeps data as files inside folders and shares it over the network. Many servers can open the same folder at once, like a shared office drive.

**Object storage** keeps unstructured data as whole items. Each item has a unique identifier and metadata, which means labels that describe the content. You ask for an item by its identifier, not by a disk position or a folder path. Think of a coat check: hand in the whole coat, get a ticket, and show the ticket to get the same coat back.

Figure 6-1 below shows the three shapes side by side.

blocks.title: Which shape fits?
blocks.content:
- A server needs its own fast disk to install an application on: **block storage**.
- Several servers must read and write the same folder of documents: **file storage**.
- A website keeps millions of photos and asks for each one by name through an API: **object storage**.

Object storage is reached through an API, so an application that only knows how to open folders needs new code to use it.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Amazon S3 is the first AWS service most people use, and the base for much of what follows.
> Two words, bucket and object, unlock the whole service.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon S3**: AWS's object storage service (Simple Storage Service).
- **bucket**: the container that holds your objects in S3.
- **object**: one stored item in S3: the data plus the metadata that describes it.
- **durability**: how unlikely it is that stored data is lost.

Amazon S3 is an object storage service. You can store any amount of data in it and use it for websites, mobile applications, backup and restore, and archive.

A **bucket** is a container for objects. An **object** is a file plus its metadata. Every object has a **key**, its unique name inside the bucket, for example photos/puppy.jpg.

To start, you create a bucket and give it a name and a Region. After that you cannot change the name or the Region. By default the name must be unique across all AWS accounts. Buckets and the objects in them are private until you grant access.

You can reach S3 through the console, the CLI, the SDKs or its REST API (a web interface that programs call), so everything you learned about ways to operate AWS applies.

**Durability** is how unlikely it is that your data is lost. S3 is designed for 99.999999999% durability, often called eleven nines, and in its default setup it stores your data across at least three Availability Zones. "Designed for" is AWS's wording: it is a design target, so read it that way.

Durability is not the same as availability. Availability is whether you can reach the data right now; durability is whether it still exists.

blocks.title: Bucket, object, key
blocks.content:
| Word | Plain meaning |
|---|---|
| Bucket | the container, created in one Region |
| Object | the data plus its metadata |
| Key | the object's unique name in its bucket |

items.text: The usual bucket is called a general purpose bucket. S3 also has directory buckets (for very low latency), table buckets (for tabular data) and vector buckets (for vector data). This course uses general purpose buckets.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Keeping all data in one class wastes money, because most data gets colder with age.
> A storage class lets you pay for the access speed you really need.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **S3 storage class**: a setting on each object that decides its storage price and its access cost.
- **S3 Standard**: the default class, for data you read often.
- **S3 Intelligent-Tiering**: a class that moves objects between cheaper and costlier tiers by itself.
- **S3 Standard-IA and One Zone-IA**: classes for data read rarely; IA means infrequent access.
- **retrieval time vs cost**: the trade-off: the colder the class, the cheaper to store but the more it costs to read.

Every object in S3 has a storage class. The class sets what you pay to store the object and what it costs to read it. If you do not choose, S3 uses **S3 Standard**.

The rule behind every class is **retrieval time vs cost**. The less often you need data, the cheaper it is to keep, but the more it costs to read it back, in fees or in waiting. Figure 6-2 below places four classes on that scale.

blocks.content:
**S3 Standard** is for data you access often. It has no minimum storage duration and no retrieval fee.

**S3 Intelligent-Tiering** is for data with unknown or changing access patterns. It moves each object between tiers automatically, for example to the Infrequent Access tier after 30 days without access. There are no retrieval fees, but a small monthly monitoring and automation fee applies.

**S3 Standard-IA** is for long-lived data you read about once a month. Reads are still fast (milliseconds), but there is a retrieval fee per GB, a 30-day minimum storage duration (you pay for 30 days even if you delete sooner) and a 128 KB minimum billable size (smaller objects are billed as 128 KB). It keeps data in at least three Availability Zones.

**S3 One Zone-IA** has the same fees but stores data in only one Availability Zone. That makes it cheaper, but the data is lost if that zone is destroyed.

blocks.title: Which class for which data?
blocks.content:
- Product images read every day: Standard.
- Data nobody can predict: Intelligent-Tiering.
- Backup that cannot be re-created, read rarely: Standard-IA.
- Thumbnails you can re-create at any time, read rarely: One Zone-IA.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some data must be kept for years but is almost never read, such as old records.
> The Glacier classes make that data very cheap to keep, in exchange for slower reads.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon S3 Glacier**: the family of three S3 storage classes built for long-term archive.
- **archive storage**: storage for data you keep but rarely read, which may not be readable instantly.
- **S3 Glacier retrieval options**: the speed choices when you restore archived data: faster costs more, slower costs less.

The **Amazon S3 Glacier** classes are part of S3. Your data stays in your buckets, as objects. There are three classes:

- **Glacier Instant Retrieval**: read about once a quarter, still in milliseconds. Minimum storage duration 90 days.
- **Glacier Flexible Retrieval**: read once or twice a year, with retrieval from minutes to hours. Minimum 90 days.
- **Glacier Deep Archive**: read less than once a year. AWS calls it the lowest-cost storage option in AWS. Minimum 180 days.

The two cheaper classes are **archive storage**: objects are archived and not available for real-time access. To read one you first send a restore request, which makes a temporary copy you can then access.

When you restore, you pick a **retrieval option**. Faster options cost more.

- Flexible Retrieval: Expedited (typically 1 to 5 minutes), Standard (3 to 5 hours) and Bulk (5 to 12 hours, free).
- Deep Archive: Standard (typically within 12 hours) and Bulk (typically within 48 hours).

This is the same rule as before. The colder the class, the cheaper to store and the longer you wait.

blocks.title: Pick the Glacier class
blocks.content:
| Class | Read it | Wait |
|---|---|---|
| Instant Retrieval | about quarterly | milliseconds |
| Flexible Retrieval | once or twice a year | minutes to hours |
| Deep Archive | less than yearly | hours |

items.text: AWS also has a separate, older service called Amazon Glacier that stores data in vaults. AWS recommends the Glacier classes inside S3 for long-term data. When this course says Glacier, it means the S3 classes.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Data gets colder with age, and nobody wants to move millions of objects by hand.
> A lifecycle policy lets S3 change classes and delete data on a schedule.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **lifecycle policy**: a set of rules on a bucket that moves objects to cheaper classes or deletes them as they age.

A **lifecycle policy** (an S3 Lifecycle configuration) is a set of rules for a bucket. S3 applies the rules to a group of objects automatically. There are two kinds of action.

- **Transition**: move objects to another storage class after some time, for example to Standard-IA 30 days after creation, or to Glacier Flexible Retrieval one year after creation.
- **Expiration**: delete objects after some time. S3 deletes them for you, for example after a regulatory retention period ends.

Figure 6-3 below shows one rule set that uses both.

blocks.content:
When you add rules to a bucket, they apply to the objects already there and to objects you add later.

Transitions cost a little: AWS notes there are charges for lifecycle transition requests, and a minimum storage duration can add charges if you move or delete an object early. Check the current S3 pricing page before you design a rule.

blocks.title: Use cases
blocks.content:
- Reports kept for a month, then deleted.
- Documents read often for a few weeks, then rarely, then archived for a legal period, then deleted.
- Data kept only for archive from day one.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> An EC2 instance needs a disk that keeps its data even when the instance stops or fails.
> Amazon EBS is that disk, and a snapshot is its backup.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon EBS**: Elastic Block Store: block storage you attach to EC2 instances.
- **volume**: one EBS disk; you attach it to an instance and use it like a local hard drive.
- **snapshot**: a point-in-time backup of a volume that lives on after the volume is gone.

**Amazon EBS** (Elastic Block Store) is block storage for EC2 instances. An EBS **volume** is a disk you attach to an instance. After you attach it, you use it like a local hard drive, to store files or install applications.

A volume lives in one Availability Zone and can be attached only to an instance in the same zone. It exists independently of the instance, so its data stays when the instance stops. AWS also stores volume data on multiple servers within the zone, so one failed server does not lose it. Figure 6-4 below shows the layout.

blocks.content:
A **snapshot** is a point-in-time backup of a volume. It persists independently from the volume. You can restore a new volume from a snapshot at any time, and you can use snapshots to move data to another account, Region or Availability Zone.

You can grow a volume or tune its performance with no downtime. Volume types fall into two groups: SSD-backed (solid-state drives) for transactional work, which means many small reads and writes, and HDD-backed (spinning hard disk drives) for work that needs high throughput, which means moving large amounts of data steadily. You pay for what you provision, which means the size you set, not the amount you fill.

blocks.title: Volume vs snapshot
blocks.content:
| | Volume | Snapshot |
|---|---|---|
| Is | a live disk | a backup copy |
| Attached to an instance | yes | no |
| Restores to | n/a | a new volume |

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Sometimes you need a very fast disk for data you can afford to lose, such as scratch work.
> Instance store is that disk, and knowing when it vanishes avoids data-loss surprises.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **instance store**: temporary block storage on disks physically attached to the host computer an EC2 instance runs on.

An **instance store** is temporary block-level storage for an EC2 instance. The disks are physically attached to the host computer that runs the instance. It suits temporary data that changes often, such as buffers and scratch data, or temporary data that you copy across a fleet of instances. A fleet is a group of instances, and scratch data is working data you can easily rebuild.

There is no extra charge: instance store volumes are included in the price of the instance. Not every instance type has them, and you can attach them only when the instance launches.

The key fact is lifetime. The data survives a reboot. It does **not** survive a stop, hibernate or terminate, and it is lost if the underlying disk fails. Never keep valuable, long-term data there. To hibernate an instance means to pause it and save its memory so it can resume later.

blocks.title: Instance store vs EBS
blocks.content:
| | Instance store | EBS volume |
|---|---|---|
| Where | disks in the host computer | a separate volume attached to the instance |
| Survives stop or terminate | no | yes |
| Extra charge | none, in instance price | pay for what you provision |
| Best for | scratch and temporary data | data you must keep |

items.term: If you need to keep it
items.text: AWS says to copy any instance store data you need to keep onto something persistent, such as an EBS volume, an S3 bucket or an EFS file system.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Several servers often need to read and write the same files at once.
> EFS gives them one shared file system that grows by itself.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **Amazon EFS**: Elastic File System: shared file storage that grows and shrinks automatically.

**Amazon EFS** (Elastic File System) is serverless, fully elastic file storage. You share file data without provisioning or managing capacity. It grows and shrinks automatically as you add and remove files, and can scale to petabytes.

EFS speaks the NFS protocol (versions 4.1 and 4.0), so ordinary tools work with it. It is reachable from EC2, ECS, EKS, Lambda and Fargate, and it uses POSIX permissions. AWS notes it is not supported on Windows-based EC2 instances. NFS (Network File System) is a standard way to share files over a network, and POSIX permissions are the permission style used on Linux and similar systems. To mount a file system means to connect it to a server so that it appears as a folder.

Figure 6-5 below shows its main strength: instances in several Availability Zones mount the same file system at once.

blocks.content:
EFS has two file system types.

- **Regional** (recommended): data is stored across multiple Availability Zones in the Region, so it stays available even if a zone is down.
- **One Zone**: data is stored in a single Availability Zone, so damage to that zone can lose data.

Compare with EBS. An EBS volume is a disk tied to one zone. EFS is a shared set of folders that many instances can open together.

blocks.title: EFS in one line
blocks.content: Many servers, one set of folders, no capacity to plan, Linux-style access (NFS).

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some applications need a specific kind of file system, not just any shared folder.
> FSx runs well-known file systems for you, so you can move such applications without rewriting them.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **Amazon FSx**: a family of fully managed file systems built on popular third-party technologies.

**Amazon FSx** is a family of fully managed shared file systems. AWS runs each one for you. There are four, named after the technology they are built on:

- **FSx for Windows File Server**: a real Windows file server. It uses the SMB protocol, which Windows applications and tools expect. SMB (Server Message Block) is an industry-standard way to access file storage over a network.
- **FSx for NetApp ONTAP**: shared storage built on NetApp's ONTAP file system.
- **FSx for OpenZFS**: shared storage built on the OpenZFS file system.
- **FSx for Lustre**: shared storage built on Lustre, a high-performance file system for applications where storage speed matters.

FSx for Lustre can also link to an S3 bucket, so it presents S3 objects as files.

blocks.title: EFS or FSx?
blocks.content:
| If you need | Pick |
|---|---|
| Plain shared Linux-style folders (NFS), growing automatically | Amazon EFS |
| A Windows file server for Windows applications (SMB) | FSx for Windows File Server |
| A file system tuned for storage speed | FSx for Lustre |

items.text: Many companies already run applications built around a specific file system. FSx lets them keep that file system but hand the servers, patching and hardware failures to AWS.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many companies keep some applications on-premises but want cloud storage behind them.
> Storage Gateway lets those applications use S3 as if it were a local file share.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Storage Gateway**: a service that gives on-premises applications access to AWS cloud storage.
- **cached file system**: a file share that keeps recently used data local for speed, while the full data lives in the cloud.

**AWS Storage Gateway** gives on-premises applications access to AWS cloud storage. It fits a hybrid deployment model. You run the gateway in your data center as a virtual machine or a hardware appliance. It talks to your applications with the usual protocols: NFS, SMB and iSCSI. (iSCSI makes remote storage look like a local disk.)

AWS lists three gateway types:

- **File Gateway** (AWS calls it S3 File Gateway): files over NFS or SMB. Each file is stored as an object in S3.
- **Volume Gateway**: block volumes over iSCSI, backed by S3.
- **Tape Gateway**: a virtual tape library for backup software, with tapes stored in AWS.

blocks.content:
The gateway acts as a **cached file system**. It keeps a local copy of recently used data for low-latency access, while all the data lives in S3. Volume Gateway has the same idea in its cached volumes: data is stored in S3 and frequently used data is kept locally.

Because the data is in S3, you can manage it with S3 features such as lifecycle policies.

blocks.title: When to think Storage Gateway
blocks.content: Pick it when applications stay on-premises, the data should end up in AWS, and you want local speed without rewriting the applications.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Backing up each service by hand, with its own tool and schedule, is easy to forget.
> AWS Backup sets one policy and applies it across many services.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Backup**: a service, run for you by AWS, that centralizes and automates backups across AWS services.
- **backup plan**: a policy that says what to back up, how often, how long to keep it and where to copy it.

**AWS Backup** is a service, run for you by AWS, that centralizes and automates data protection across AWS services, in the cloud and on premises. You set policies and watch activity in one place, instead of backing up service by service with custom scripts.

The policy is called a **backup plan**. It defines your backup requirements, and you apply it to the resources you want to protect across the services you use. Figure 6-7 below shows one plan covering several services.

blocks.content:
AWS Backup can protect Amazon EC2 instances, EBS volumes, S3 data, EFS and FSx file systems, Storage Gateway volumes and Amazon RDS (a service for structured business data that you will meet in the next chapter), among others. The list grows, so check the current AWS page.

Useful features: lifecycle rules that move older backups to low-cost cold storage, copies of backups to other Regions, and incremental backups, which store only what changed after the first full copy for resource types that support it.

blocks.title: Snapshot or AWS Backup?
blocks.content: A snapshot protects one EBS volume. AWS Backup applies one schedule and one rule for how long to keep backups to many services at once and gives one place to review them.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> When a whole site fails, restoring a backup can take too long to get applications running again.
> Elastic Disaster Recovery keeps a ready-to-start copy of your servers in AWS.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery**: a service that continuously replicates (keeps an up-to-date copy of) servers to AWS so you can launch them quickly after a disaster.

**AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery** (DRS) minimizes downtime and data loss with fast, reliable recovery of on-premises and cloud-based applications. This is the disaster recovery idea from the global infrastructure chapter, made into a service.

You install it on your source servers. It replicates their data to a staging area in your AWS account, in the Region you select. The staging area uses affordable storage and minimal compute, which keeps cost low while you wait.

If disaster strikes, you launch recovery instances on AWS within minutes, from the latest server state or from an earlier point in time. Later you can fail back, which means switch back, to your original site.

You can also run non-disruptive drills, so you know recovery works before you need it.

**AWS Backup or DRS?** AWS Backup protects copies of data, which you restore when needed. DRS keeps whole servers replicated so applications can be running again on AWS within minutes.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.content: Backup protects data from loss. Elastic Disaster Recovery gets applications running again after a site is lost.

sections.title: Chapter 8: Databases
sections.note: Relational and NoSQL databases on AWS, managed versus self-run, caching, and moving a database with DMS and SCT.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Almost every application must store data and find it again quickly and safely.
> A database does that job, and the first split to learn is relational versus NoSQL.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **database**: an organized collection of data that an application can store, search and change.
- **table, row and column**: in a relational database a table holds one kind of thing, each row is one record, each column is one attribute.
- **SQL**: the language used to ask a relational database questions and change its data.
- **relational database**: a database that organizes data into tables with the same columns in every row.
- **NoSQL database**: a database that does not use the table layout; it stores data in other shapes and does not require SQL.

A **database** is an organized collection of data that an application can store, search and change. Applications use one instead of loose files so that finding and updating data stays fast and reliable.

A **relational database** organizes data into tables. A **table** holds one kind of thing, such as customers. Each **row** is one record, such as one customer. Each **column** is one attribute, such as the city. Every row has the same structure, much like a spreadsheet. You work with the data using **SQL**, a language for asking questions like "which customers live in Hanoi?" and for changing the data.

A **NoSQL database** does not use that table layout. Its data may be stored as simple name and value pairs, as JSON (a text format for nested name and value data), as a graph or in other shapes. AWS also calls these non-relational databases.

blocks.title: Relational or NoSQL?
blocks.content:
| | Relational | NoSQL |
|---|---|---|
| Shape of data | tables, same columns in every row | flexible; depends on the type |
| How you ask | SQL | the database's own methods |
| Fits | structured data with clear relations | flexible data, huge scale, special shapes |

The next lessons show one AWS service for each case.

items.text: Many applications use both. A shop can keep orders in a relational database and its fast-changing session data in a NoSQL database. AWS offers a different service for each shape, so you choose per job.

items.term: Database on EC2 or a managed database

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You can run a database yourself on an EC2 instance, or let AWS run it. The choice decides how much of your week goes to chores.
> This lesson shows exactly which chores move to AWS.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **managed service**: a service where AWS handles most of the management tasks, so you focus on using it.
- **self-managed database on EC2**: a database you install and run yourself on an EC2 instance, with an EBS volume holding the data.
- **database administration tasks**: the recurring chores of running a database: installing software, patching, backups, scaling and keeping it available.

There are two ways to run a database on AWS.

**Self-managed database on EC2.** You launch an EC2 instance, install the database software, and store the data on an EBS volume. This is IaaS: AWS runs the hardware, and you run everything above it.

**Managed service.** A **managed service** is one where AWS handles most of the management tasks. AWS has such a service for relational databases, covered in the next lesson.

The recurring chores are the **database administration tasks**: installing software, patching the operating system and the database software, taking backups, scaling and keeping the database available. Figure 7-1 below shows who does what in each setup.

blocks.caption: Responsibility for database chores on-premises, on EC2 and with a managed service.

blocks.content:
On EC2, AWS removes the hardware burden, but every task above it is still yours. AWS notes that this makes you more prone to user errors: updating the operating system or database software by hand can accidentally cause application downtime.

AWS recommends a managed relational database as the default choice for most relational database deployments, because the alternatives make you spend more time managing software and hardware. In every setup, tuning your own application remains your job.

blocks.title: The decision in one line
blocks.content: Choose a managed database unless you have a specific reason to take on all the chores yourself. Choose EC2 only when you accept those chores.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Most business applications use a relational database, and running one reliably is hard work.
> Amazon RDS runs it for you and gives two features, Multi-AZ and read replicas, that are easy to confuse.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon RDS**: Relational Database Service: a managed service for running relational databases.
- **database engine**: the specific database software that runs inside RDS, such as MySQL or PostgreSQL.
- **Multi-AZ deployment**: an RDS setup that keeps a standby copy in another Availability Zone for failover.
- **read replica**: an extra copy of the database used to serve read requests, so reads scale.

**Amazon RDS** makes it easier to set up, operate and scale a relational database in the cloud. It is a managed service: it handles backups, software patching, automatic failure detection and recovery.

You pick a **database engine**, the specific software that runs your database. RDS supports IBM Db2, MariaDB, Microsoft SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle Database and PostgreSQL. You can keep using the engine you already know. Behind the scenes, RDS stores database data on Amazon EBS storage.

RDS offers two features that are often mixed up.

blocks.title: Multi-AZ versus read replica
blocks.content:
| | Multi-AZ deployment | Read replica |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | availability and failover | more read capacity |
| What it is | a standby copy in another Availability Zone | an extra copy that serves reads |
| Think of it as | a spare tire | extra checkout lanes |

A **Multi-AZ deployment** automatically provisions and maintains a standby in a different Availability Zone. In the standard DB instance setup, the standby is synchronous, which means it is updated together with the primary, and it does not serve read traffic. It is there for data redundancy and failover.

A **read replica** is an extra copy that serves read requests. AWS lists read replicas as the way to increase read scaling. Use a Multi-AZ deployment to survive the loss of a zone, and read replicas to handle many readers.

items.text: RDS also offers Multi-AZ DB clusters, where the extra instances in other zones can serve read traffic too. The exam level idea stays the same: Multi-AZ is about availability.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some applications outgrow ordinary relational databases on speed and size.
> Aurora is AWS's own relational engine inside RDS, built to be faster and to grow its storage on its own.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **Amazon Aurora**: a fully managed relational database engine from AWS that is compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL.

**Amazon Aurora** is a fully managed relational database engine compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL. The code, tools and applications you use with those databases can be used with Aurora.

Aurora is part of Amazon RDS. When you set up a new database through RDS, you can choose Aurora MySQL or Aurora PostgreSQL as the engine, and you use the same console and tools to provision, patch, back up and recover it.

What Aurora adds:

- **Speed.** AWS states it delivers up to 6 times the throughput of stock (standard, unmodified) MySQL and of stock PostgreSQL on similar hardware.
- **Storage that grows itself.** The underlying storage grows automatically, up to 256 TiB (a tebibyte is a little over one terabyte) for a cluster volume.
- **Clusters.** It automates clustering and replication (several database servers working together, with copies of the data kept in step), which are among the hardest parts of database administration.

blocks.title: RDS engines or Aurora?
blocks.content:
| | Other RDS engines | Aurora |
|---|---|---|
| Relational | yes | yes |
| Managed by AWS | yes | yes |
| Built by | MySQL, Oracle and others | AWS, compatible with MySQL and PostgreSQL |

items.text: "Compatible" means existing MySQL or PostgreSQL applications work with Aurora without a rewrite. Aurora's engine and storage are AWS's own design, which is why its numbers differ from the stock engines.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some applications, such as carts and game scores, need the same fast answer whether they have ten users or a hundred million.
> DynamoDB is the NoSQL service built for that, with no servers to run.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon DynamoDB**: AWS's serverless, fully managed NoSQL database.
- **key-value**: a way of storing data where each item is found by a unique key.

**Amazon DynamoDB** is a serverless, fully managed, distributed NoSQL database with single-digit millisecond performance at any scale. Serverless means you do not provision servers or patch software, and there are no maintenance windows.

It stores data as **key-value** pairs (it can also store documents). Each item has a unique key, and you fetch it by that key, like looking up a word in a dictionary. AWS gives a shopping cart as an example: the same fast performance whether you have 10 or 100 million users.

DynamoDB does not support a JOIN, the SQL operation that combines tables. AWS recommends designing your data so that one lookup returns what you need.

In on-demand capacity mode you pay per read and write request, and it scales down to zero when idle.

blocks.title: DynamoDB in short
blocks.content:
| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Relational? | no, NoSQL |
| Servers to manage? | none, it is serverless |
| Best at | fast lookups by key at any scale |
| Weak at | JOINs across tables |

items.text: DynamoDB also offers ACID transactions (groups of changes that all succeed or all fail together), global tables that replicate across Regions, and backups with point-in-time recovery. For this exam the key facts are serverless, NoSQL and key-value.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A database that reads from disk is slower than memory, and popular questions get asked again and again.
> ElastiCache keeps the popular answers in memory so the database is asked less.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon ElastiCache**: a managed in-memory data store and cache service.
- **in-memory database**: a data store that keeps its data in memory (RAM) instead of on disk, for very fast reads.
- **cache**: a fast place that holds frequently used data so it does not have to be fetched from the slower source again.

A **cache** is a high-speed layer that holds frequently accessed data so an application does not have to ask the slower main data source every time. It reduces latency and the load on the database.

**Amazon ElastiCache** is a managed service for setting up and scaling a distributed **in-memory** data store or cache in the cloud. It works with the Valkey, Memcached and Redis OSS engines. You can start with a serverless cache or create a node-based cluster. Reads from a remote cache like this typically take under a millisecond, which is faster than a disk-based database.

Figure 7-2 below shows the usual pattern. The application asks the cache first. If the answer is there (a cache hit), it is returned quickly. If not (a cache miss), the application asks the database and stores the answer in the cache for next time.

blocks.content:
Note who does the work: the cache is used next to the database, not wired into it. AWS says the application, or the processes that use it, manages when to cache data and whether it is still valid.

So ElastiCache does not replace your database. It sits in front of one to make popular reads fast.

blocks.title: Database or cache?
blocks.content: A database is where data lives permanently. A cache holds copies of the hot data so reads are faster.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many applications already store data as JSON-like documents, and rows and columns fit them badly.
> DocumentDB is AWS's managed database for that shape, compatible with MongoDB.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon DocumentDB**: AWS's managed document database, compatible with MongoDB.
- **document database**: a NoSQL database that stores data as flexible, nested documents, usually in JSON.

A **document database** stores data as documents. A document is a JSON object: flexible, semi-structured and hierarchical. One customer document can hold a name, an address with a street and a city inside it, and a list of interests. Another customer document can have different fields.

**Amazon DocumentDB** (with MongoDB compatibility) is a fast, reliable, fully managed database service for these documents. You can run the same application code and use the same drivers and tools that you use with MongoDB.

AWS lists these features:

- Storage grows automatically as the data grows.
- Up to 15 replica instances share the same storage, which raises read throughput.
- Failover goes to a replica in another Availability Zone.
- Continuous backups to Amazon S3 allow restoring to any second in the retention period, up to 35 days.

blocks.title: Which NoSQL shape?
blocks.content:
| Shape | AWS service |
|---|---|
| key-value | Amazon DynamoDB |
| document | Amazon DocumentDB |

DynamoDB can also store documents. Pick DocumentDB when an application is built for MongoDB.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some questions are about relationships: who knows whom, which account is linked to which.
> Neptune is the graph database that follows relationships quickly.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Neptune**: AWS's fast, fully managed graph database service.
- **graph database**: a NoSQL database that stores things (nodes) and the relationships between them (edges).

A **graph database** is built to store and navigate relationships. It uses **nodes** to store things, such as people, and **edges** to store the relationships between them, such as "follows" or "owns". An edge has a start node, an end node, a type and a direction.

**Amazon Neptune** is a fast, reliable, fully managed graph database service for highly connected data. AWS says it is optimized for storing billions of relationships and querying them with millisecond latency.

Neptune supports the graph query languages Gremlin and openCypher, and SPARQL for RDF graphs (a W3C standard graph format). AWS names recommendation engines, fraud detection, knowledge graphs and network security among its use cases.

It is highly available: a cluster can have up to 15 read replicas, continuous backup to Amazon S3, and its data is copied across Availability Zones.

blocks.title: Why not tables?
blocks.content: SQL queries for highly connected data are complex and hard to tune. A graph database makes "friends of friends" a short, natural query.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Most companies already have databases somewhere else, and moving to AWS is a project of its own.
> This lesson names the two kinds of move so you know which tool a move needs.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **database migration**: moving a database, its structure and its data, from one place or setup to another, for example from on-premises to AWS.
- **homogeneous and heterogeneous migration**: homogeneous means both sides use the same database engine; heterogeneous means the engines differ.

**Database migration** means moving a database to a new place, for example from your data center to Amazon RDS. A migration has to carry three things: the structure (the tables and their columns), the data itself, and the changes people keep making while the move is running.

Migrations come in two kinds. In a **homogeneous migration** the source and the target use the same database engine, for example Oracle to Oracle. In a **heterogeneous migration** the engines are different, for example Oracle to MySQL.

The difference matters because two engines do not speak exactly the same dialect. Moving between the same engine is mostly a copy. Moving between different engines also requires converting the structure and code so the new engine understands them.

AWS has a tool for the data and a tool for the conversion. They are the next two lessons.

blocks.title: Homogeneous or heterogeneous?
blocks.content:
| | Homogeneous | Heterogeneous |
|---|---|---|
| Engines | same | different |
| Example | Oracle to Oracle | Oracle to MySQL |
| Structure conversion | usually not needed | needed |

items.text: Companies move to a managed service such as Amazon RDS or Aurora, or to a cheaper or more modern engine. AWS says its migration service can help with either a change of engine or a move that keeps the same one.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Copying a live database by hand risks long downtime and lost changes.
> AWS DMS moves the data and keeps source and target in sync while you switch over.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS DMS**: Database Migration Service: a cloud service that moves data between databases and other data stores.
- **database replication**: continuously copying changes from one database to another so the two stay in sync.

**AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS)** is a cloud service for migrating relational databases, NoSQL databases and other data stores. You can migrate into AWS or between combinations of cloud and on-premises setups. Either the source or the target must be on an AWS service.

At a basic level, AWS DMS is a server in the AWS Cloud that runs replication software. You create a source connection and a target connection, then schedule a task that moves the data. AWS DMS creates the tables and primary keys (the column that identifies each row) on the target if they do not exist.

You can run a one-time migration or use **database replication**: continuously copying ongoing changes so the source and the target stay in sync until you switch over.

DMS supports homogeneous migrations and heterogeneous migrations. For a heterogeneous move, DMS moves the data but you convert the structure first with a separate tool, the subject of the next lesson.

AWS DMS manages the infrastructure behind it, uses pay-as-you-go pricing, and can fail over to a backup replication server if the main one fails.

blocks.title: AWS DMS in one line
blocks.content: It moves the data (once, or continuously), and it works for the same engine or different engines.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> When the engine changes, the table structure and code must be rewritten for the new engine, and doing that by hand is slow.
> AWS SCT converts it automatically and tells you what is left to fix.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS SCT**: Schema Conversion Tool: a tool that converts a database's structure from one engine to another.
- **schema conversion**: rewriting a database's structure and code objects so a different engine understands them.

The **AWS Schema Conversion Tool (AWS SCT)** converts an existing database schema, its structure and code objects, from one database engine to another. This is **schema conversion**. The converted schema can be used with an Amazon RDS database, an Aurora cluster or a database on an EC2 instance.

For example, AWS SCT supports converting Oracle sources to targets such as Aurora PostgreSQL, MySQL and PostgreSQL. If part of a schema cannot be converted automatically, AWS SCT gives guidance on how to build the equivalent yourself.

Figure 7-3 below shows how the two tools split the work in a heterogeneous migration: SCT converts the structure, DMS moves the data.
