blocks.content:
You download AWS SCT to your local PC. DMS now also offers a web-based option called DMS Schema Conversion, which assesses and converts source schemas to a new target engine. Check the current AWS pages for which option and which engines suit your case.

For a homogeneous migration you usually do not need conversion; AWS says native tools can move the structure.

blocks.title: Which tool?
blocks.content:
- Moving the data: AWS DMS.
- Converting the structure for a different engine: AWS SCT.
- Same engine: DMS, often with native tools for the structure.

sections.title: Chapter 9: Networking
sections.note: How AWS builds networks (VPC, subnets, gateways, firewalls), names and routes traffic, and links your offices and users to AWS.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Every server you run on AWS has to live in a network. The VPC is that network, and every other lesson in this chapter builds on it.

An **Amazon VPC** (Virtual Private Cloud) is your own private network inside AWS. AWS describes it as a logically isolated virtual network that you define, and it closely resembles a traditional network you would run in your own data center. You launch resources, such as EC2 instances, inside it.

Picture a fenced plot of land in a very large shared city. Other customers have their own plots. Nobody walks into yours unless you build a door.

Your AWS account already has a default VPC in each Region, set up so you can launch EC2 instances straight away. You can also create more VPCs with the settings you need. There is no extra charge for a VPC itself, but some extra components you can add to it do cost money, so check the pricing page before you build.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon VPC** — your own isolated virtual network inside AWS, where you launch resources such as EC2 instances.
- **CIDR block** — the range of IP addresses a network may use, written like 10.0.0.0/16.
- **private IP address** — an address used inside your VPC; it is not reachable from the public internet.
- **public IP address** — an address that can be reached from the internet.

### Choosing the address range

When you create a VPC you must choose its range of IP addresses. The range is written as a **CIDR block**, for example 10.0.0.0/16.

The number after the slash sets the size. A /16 range holds 65,536 addresses and a /28 range holds 16 addresses, so a bigger number after the slash means a smaller range. AWS allows a VPC block from /16 down to /28.

AWS recommends choosing from the private ranges in RFC 1918 (the internet standard that sets aside address ranges for private networks). One of them starts at 10.0.0.0. You cannot make an existing CIDR block bigger or smaller afterwards, so choose with growth in mind.

### Private and public addresses

Nearly every resource in a VPC gets an IP address. Most of them use private IPv4 addresses (IPv4 is the common style of IP address, such as 10.0.1.25), which come from the VPC's own range and are not charged.

A resource that must be reachable directly from the internet over IPv4 needs a **public IP address**, an address that the internet can route to. AWS charges for public IPv4 addresses, with a limited free allowance for some usage, so check the current pricing page.

Figure 8-1 below shows a VPC in a Region with an EC2 instance in each of two Availability Zones. Each instance has a private address taken from the VPC range.

items.text: Each Region of your account already has a default VPC that is ready to use, so you can launch instances at once. It suits getting started and simple public sites. You can still change its parts later, and you can create more VPCs of your own.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> One big network is hard to protect. Subnets split the VPC into smaller parts, so web servers can face the internet while databases stay hidden.

A **subnet** is a range of IP addresses inside your VPC. You place resources, such as EC2 instances, into a specific subnet.

Each subnet must sit entirely inside one Availability Zone and cannot span zones. That gives you a simple recipe for high availability: create subnets in several Availability Zones and spread your servers across them, so the failure of one zone does not take everything down.

Think of the VPC as an office floor and the subnets as rooms. Each room is on exactly one floor of the building (one Availability Zone), and you decide which rooms have a door to the street.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **subnet** — a smaller range of addresses inside a VPC; it lives in exactly one Availability Zone.
- **public subnet** — a subnet whose resources can reach the internet and can be reached from it.
- **private subnet** — a subnet whose resources cannot be reached directly from the internet.

### Public and private subnets

A **public subnet** is a subnet whose resources can access the public internet. A **private subnet** is a subnet that does not have that direct route, so the internet cannot reach its resources directly.

AWS recommends private subnets to protect your resources. A typical shop puts its web servers in a public subnet, because customers must reach them, and its database in a private subnet, because only your own servers should talk to it.

What actually makes a subnet public or private is how its traffic is routed. The next lesson shows exactly how.

blocks.title: Why two zones?
blocks.content: Each subnet is tied to one Availability Zone. If you build the same pair of subnets in a second zone and run a copy of your servers there, the shop keeps working when one zone fails.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Calling a subnet "public" does not open it to the internet by itself. Two things do: a door out (the internet gateway) and a rule that points at the door (a route).

An **internet gateway** is a VPC component that allows communication between your VPC and the internet. You attach it to the VPC. AWS describes it as redundant and highly available, so it is not a single point of failure. There is no charge for the gateway itself, but there are data transfer charges for EC2 instances that use it.

A **route table** is the traffic controller of your VPC. It holds rules, called routes. Each route has a destination (a range of addresses) and a target (where to send that traffic, such as an internet gateway). Traffic is sent by looking at its destination address.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **internet gateway** — the door that connects a VPC to the internet.
- **route table** — a list of rules that says where traffic from a subnet is sent.

### What makes a subnet public

Every subnet is associated with a route table. A new subnet uses the VPC's main route table unless you change it.

A subnet is public when its route table has a route that sends internet-bound traffic to the internet gateway. That route is usually written 0.0.0.0/0, which means every address not matched by a more specific route. A subnet whose route table has no such route is private.

The instance also needs a public IP address. Without one, the internet cannot find it. In a private subnet, even an instance with a public IP address cannot talk to the internet, because no route leads to the gateway.

Figure 8-3 below shows a route table in a public subnet. The first route keeps traffic inside the VPC (local). The second sends everything else to the internet gateway.

blocks.title: Default VPC versus your own VPC
blocks.content: A default VPC already has an internet gateway and a route to it. A VPC you create yourself does not: you must add the internet gateway and the route before any subnet becomes public.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Servers in a private subnet still need to download updates. A NAT gateway lets them call out to the internet without letting anyone call in.

A **NAT gateway** is a Network Address Translation (NAT) service. It lets instances in a private subnet connect to services outside the VPC, while outside services cannot start a connection with those instances.

Think of a company switchboard. Staff can phone out through it, but strangers cannot dial a staff member directly.

The usual setup is a public NAT gateway. You create it in a public subnet and give it a public address (an Elastic IP address, a fixed public IP address) when you create it. In the private subnet's route table you add a route that sends internet-bound traffic to the NAT gateway. The NAT gateway then sends it out through the internet gateway.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **NAT gateway** — a service that lets private instances start connections to the internet while blocking connections started from outside.

### One rule to remember

With a NAT gateway, connections must always start from inside the VPC. Answers to those connections come back, but nobody outside can open a new conversation.

NAT gateways cost money. AWS lists them among the VPC parts that are charged, so use one only when private resources need to go out.

AWS also offers a private NAT gateway. It lets private instances reach other VPCs or your on-premises network, but not the internet, and it has no public address.

blocks.title: Internet gateway versus NAT gateway
blocks.content:
| | Instance in a public subnet | Instance in a private subnet with NAT |
|---|---|---|
| Can start a connection to the internet | Yes | Yes, through the NAT gateway |
| Can receive a new connection from the internet | Yes, if it has a public IP address | No |
| Typical use | Web servers | Databases that need patches |

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A route to the internet does not mean everyone should reach your server. Security groups decide which traffic may reach each instance.

A **security group** is a virtual firewall for a resource such as an EC2 instance. (A firewall is software that allows or blocks network traffic by rules.) It controls the traffic allowed to reach the resource and to leave it. The only traffic that reaches the instance is traffic that a rule allows.

Each rule names a source (or destination), a port range and a protocol (the set of rules a kind of traffic follows, such as SSH). A port is like a numbered door on a server. Remote login with SSH uses port 22, and remote desktop on Windows (RDP) uses port 3389. If no rule allows SSH, nobody can connect to the instance with SSH.

Security groups cost nothing. Every VPC comes with a default security group, and you can create more. You can attach several security groups to one resource.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **security group** — a virtual firewall attached to a resource such as an EC2 instance, with rules for what traffic is allowed.
- **stateful firewall** — a firewall that remembers a connection, so answers to allowed traffic are let through automatically.

### Stateful: the answer comes back automatically

Security groups are **stateful**. If an instance sends a request out, the response is allowed back in, whatever the inbound rules say. And responses to allowed inbound traffic are allowed to leave, whatever the outbound rules say.

That saves you from writing a second rule for every answer.

### Safe habits from AWS

- When you open port 22 (SSH) or 3389 (RDP), allow only specific IP address ranges. The range 0.0.0.0/0 lets anyone on the internet try to connect.
- Do not open large port ranges. Open only the ports that are needed, to the sources that need them.
- Use the fewest security groups you can, one per group of resources with similar needs.

blocks.title: Small scenario
blocks.content: A web server must serve visitors, and you want to connect to it from your office only. Rule 1 allows web traffic from anywhere. Rule 2 allows SSH only from your office's address range. Everything else is blocked, and the answers to allowed requests flow back automatically because the security group is stateful.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Security groups guard each instance. A network ACL adds a second layer at the edge of the whole subnet, and it behaves differently. The difference is a favourite exam question.

A **network ACL** (access control list, NACL) allows or denies specific traffic at the subnet level. It checks traffic as it enters and as it leaves the subnet.

Every subnet must be associated with a network ACL. If you do not choose one, the subnet gets the VPC's default network ACL, which allows all inbound and outbound traffic. You can create custom network ACLs. One network ACL can serve many subnets, but a subnet has only one network ACL at a time.

Rules are numbered from 1 to 32766. AWS checks them in order, lowest number first, and stops at the first rule that matches. Each rule either allows or denies. AWS suggests numbering in steps of 10 or 100 so you can insert rules later.

Network ACLs cost nothing.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **network ACL** — a numbered list of allow and deny rules that guards the edge of a subnet.
- **stateless firewall** — a firewall that does not remember connections, so answers need their own rules.

### Stateless: answers need rules too

Network ACLs are **stateless**. They do not save information about traffic they saw before. If a rule allows some traffic into the subnet, the answers are not automatically allowed back out. You need a rule for each direction.

### Where each tool sits

Figure 8-4 below shows traffic arriving at a subnet. The network ACL checks it at the subnet edge first. The security group then checks it at the instance.

blocks.title: Security group versus network ACL
blocks.content:
| | Security group | Network ACL |
|---|---|---|
| Guards | An instance (a resource) | A whole subnet |
| Remembers connections | Yes, stateful | No, stateless |
| A rule can | Allow traffic | Allow or deny traffic |
| Default | Comes with the VPC | Default allows all traffic |

AWS says security groups meet your needs in most cases. Use network ACLs when you want an additional layer.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Firewalls control who may connect. They do not tell you that the software inside a server is out of date. Amazon Inspector looks inside.

A **vulnerability** is a weakness in software that an attacker could use. **Amazon Inspector** is a vulnerability management service. It automatically discovers workloads and continually scans them for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure (for example, a path from the internet that you did not mean to open).

Inspector scans three kinds of resources: Amazon EC2 instances, container images in Amazon ECR, and AWS Lambda functions.

When it finds a problem, it creates a **finding**, a detailed report that names the affected resource and recommends how to fix it. You work with findings in the Inspector console or API.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Inspector** — a service that scans EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.
- **vulnerability** — a weakness in software that an attacker could use.

### Always scanning

You do not schedule scans by hand. Inspector finds eligible resources and scans them. It scans again when something changes that could add a new weakness: a new package installed on an instance, a patch installed, or a new CVE published (a CVE is a public identifier for a known weakness).

Inspector also gives each finding a risk score adjusted to your environment. For example, it can lower the score when a weakness is reachable over the network but the instance has no open path to the internet.

If you fix the problem, Inspector sees it and closes the finding.

blocks.title: Inspector in the security picture
blocks.content: Security groups and network ACLs control the traffic that may enter. Inspector checks the software and the network exposure of the resources behind them. AWS describes it as finding and reporting problems, not as blocking traffic.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> People type names like example.com. Computers need IP addresses. Route 53 turns the name into the address, and can steer visitors away from a broken server.

**DNS** (the Domain Name System) is the worldwide system that translates names that are easy to remember into the IP addresses computers use to find each other. Think of a phone book: you look up a name and get a number.

A **domain name** is the name of your site, such as example.com. A **hosted zone** is a container for the records that say how to route traffic for a domain and its subdomains. A record might say that www.example.com goes to the web server with a given IP address.

**Amazon Route 53** is a highly available and scalable DNS web service.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Route 53** — AWS's DNS service. It registers domain names, answers lookups and checks health.
- **DNS** — the system that turns a name like example.com into an IP address.
- **domain name** — the name of your site, such as example.com.
- **hosted zone** — a container for the records that say how to route traffic for one domain.
- **DNS health check** — an automatic test that sends requests to a resource to see whether it is reachable and working.
- **routing policy** — the rule that decides which answer Route 53 gives to a lookup.

### Three jobs

Route 53 can do three things, in any combination:

1. **Register domain names.** You can buy a name for your site.
2. **Route internet traffic.** When a visitor enters your name, Route 53 connects the browser to your website or application.
3. **Check health.** Route 53 sends automated requests to a resource, such as a web server, to verify that it is reachable, available and working. It can notify you when a resource fails, and it can route traffic away from unhealthy resources.

### Routing policies

When you create a record you choose a routing policy. It decides how Route 53 answers.

blocks.title: The routing policies
blocks.content:
| Policy | Use it when |
|---|---|
| Simple | one resource does the job |
| Failover | you want active-passive failover (one server works while a standby waits) |
| Weighted | traffic should be split in set proportions |
| Latency | resources are in several Regions and you want the best latency |
| Geolocation | answers depend on where the user is |
| Geoproximity | answers depend on where your resources are |
| IP-based | answers depend on the user's IP address range |
| Multivalue answer | up to eight healthy records, chosen at random |

Figure 8-5 below shows failover. Normally Route 53 answers with the primary server's address. If the health check fails, it answers with the standby server's address instead, and visitors keep reaching your site.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many companies keep some systems on-premises and some on AWS (a hybrid setup). Those two networks must talk to each other privately, and a VPN is the quickest way.

**AWS VPN** is a family of two services that connect to AWS over an **encrypted tunnel**. A tunnel is a private path through a bigger network. Encrypted means the data is scrambled, so anyone who intercepts it cannot read it.

**Site-to-Site VPN** joins your on-premises network to your VPC. It uses IPsec, a standard way to build encrypted connections. Each VPN connection includes two VPN tunnels that you can use at the same time for high availability.

**Client VPN** is a managed service for people. A user runs an OpenVPN-based client program on a laptop and connects securely to AWS resources and to resources in your on-premises network, from any location.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS VPN** — the AWS services that connect networks and people to AWS over encrypted tunnels.
- **Site-to-Site VPN** — a VPN that joins your on-premises network to your VPC.
- **Client VPN** — a VPN that lets individual users connect from their own devices.
- **encrypted tunnel** — a private path whose data is scrambled so outsiders cannot read it.

### How the pieces fit

For Site-to-Site VPN you need a device or program on your side (the customer gateway device) and an endpoint on the AWS side. The tunnels run between them.

The tunnels run over the public internet. AWS describes a VPN as faster to set up than a dedicated private connection, and cheaper when you do not need a very fast link. Because the traffic crosses the public internet, performance and reliability can vary.

### Which VPN for which job

blocks.title: Site-to-Site versus Client VPN
blocks.content:
| | Site-to-Site VPN | Client VPN |
|---|---|---|
| Connects | a whole network to a VPC | one person's device to AWS |
| Typical user | a company office or data center | a remote worker |
| Built on | IPsec tunnels | an OpenVPN-based client |

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A VPN travels over the internet, and the internet is sometimes slow or uneven. Some companies need a steadier private line to AWS.

**AWS Direct Connect** links your internal network to a Direct Connect location (a facility where your network meets AWS's) over a standard Ethernet fibre-optic cable. One end of the cable plugs into your router, the other into an AWS router. This **dedicated connection** is private: it bypasses internet service providers in your network path.

On top of the connection you create virtual interfaces. A private virtual interface reaches your VPC using private IP addresses. A public virtual interface reaches AWS public services, such as Amazon S3. A transit virtual interface reaches transit gateways, which a later lesson explains.

To use it, your network must be in a Direct Connect location, or you must work with a partner company or another service provider. Plan ahead: it involves a physical cable.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Direct Connect** — a private, dedicated network link between your network and AWS.
- **dedicated connection** — a physical fibre cable reserved for your traffic, instead of the shared internet.

### Cost and security

AWS bills Direct Connect by two things: port hours and outbound data transfer. A port is the connection point at the Direct Connect location, and the port-hour price depends on its capacity and connection type.

Direct Connect is private, but it is not automatically encrypted. When you need the data scrambled on the line, AWS documents two ways: MACsec (a standard for encrypting the link itself) on supported connections, or a Site-to-Site VPN over Direct Connect.

### VPN or Direct Connect?

Figure 8-6 below puts the two side by side. The VPN rides the public internet. Direct Connect uses a dedicated line.

blocks.title: Comparing the two
blocks.content:
| | AWS VPN | Direct Connect |
|---|---|---|
| Path | public internet | dedicated private connection |
| Setup | faster to set up | needs a physical connection |
| Performance | varies with the internet | low latency and a consistent experience |
| Encrypted | yes, in the tunnel | not by default |

A common setup uses both to reach the same VPC: the Direct Connect path is preferred, and a VPN acts as the backup that takes over if it fails.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> If your files sit in one Region, a user on the other side of the world waits longer. CloudFront keeps copies close to your users.

A **content delivery network** (CDN) is a network of servers spread around the world that keep copies of your content close to your users. **Amazon CloudFront** is the AWS content delivery network. It speeds up delivery of static and dynamic web content, such as web pages, style files, scripts and images.

CloudFront delivers content through edge locations. When someone asks for a file, CloudFront routes the request to the edge location with the lowest latency.

- If the file is already cached there, CloudFront delivers it at once.
- If not, CloudFront fetches it from your **origin**, the place that holds the original version, and keeps a copy.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon CloudFront** — the AWS service that delivers your content from edge locations close to your users.
- **content delivery network** — a worldwide network of servers that cache copies of content near users.

### Setting it up

You tell CloudFront where the originals live. An origin can be an Amazon S3 bucket or an HTTP server, such as a web server on an EC2 instance or on a machine you manage. You create a CloudFront **distribution**, the setting that tells CloudFront which origins to use. CloudFront gives the distribution its own domain name, and you can use your own domain name instead.

By default, a file stays in an edge location for 24 hours before it expires. Your origin can add headers that change how long files stay cached.

Because copies are held in many edge locations, you also get better reliability and availability. If you keep objects in a private S3 bucket, you can control who gets them with signed URLs and signed cookies (special links and cookies that prove a viewer may fetch the file).

blocks.title: Small scenario
blocks.content: Your shop stores product images in an S3 bucket. Visitors in far-away cities wait too long. You create a CloudFront distribution with the bucket as origin. The first visitor in a city makes CloudFront fetch the image and keep a copy. The next visitors nearby get it from the nearby edge location.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some applications are not files to cache. They are live services, and their users are spread around the world. Global Accelerator sends each user to the best endpoint over AWS's own network.

**AWS Global Accelerator** lets you create accelerators that improve the performance and availability of your application for local and global users. With a standard accelerator, Global Accelerator directs traffic over the AWS global network to endpoints in the nearest Region to the client.

Endpoints can be Network Load Balancers, Application Load Balancers, EC2 instances or Elastic IP addresses, in one or several Regions.

Global Accelerator gives you static IP addresses, addresses that do not change while the accelerator exists. For IPv4 you get two. Your users, and your firewall rules, can rely on those fixed addresses even if you change what sits behind them.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **AWS Global Accelerator** — a service that sends users to the best healthy endpoint over the AWS global network, using fixed IP addresses.

### It reacts to health

Global Accelerator chooses the endpoint using health, client location and the policies you set. It reacts to changes in health so that traffic goes to healthy endpoints.

If you delete an accelerator you lose its static IP addresses. Disabling it keeps them.

AWS also describes a custom routing accelerator, which maps one or more users to a specific destination among many.

### CloudFront or Global Accelerator?

blocks.title: Two services, two jobs
blocks.content:
| | Amazon CloudFront | AWS Global Accelerator |
|---|---|---|
| Main job | deliver web content from edge locations | send traffic to your endpoints over the AWS network |
| Keeps copies of your content | Yes, cached at edge locations | AWS describes it as routing traffic to endpoints |
| Gives you | a distribution with its own domain name | two static IPv4 addresses by default |
| Example | images and web pages | a live application in several Regions |

items.term: AWS PrivateLink and AWS Transit Gateway

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> As you add VPCs and offices, connecting each pair by hand becomes a mess. And sometimes you want to use a service without sending traffic over the internet at all.

**AWS Transit Gateway** is a network transit hub that interconnects VPCs and on-premises networks. Instead of linking every network to every other, you attach each network once to the hub. That is a hub-and-spoke layout. You can attach VPCs, VPN connections and Direct Connect links (through a Direct Connect gateway), among other things.

A transit gateway has its own route table, and you pay for each attachment per hour plus the traffic it processes.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Transit Gateway** — a hub that joins many VPCs and on-premises networks through one central point.
- **AWS PrivateLink** — a way to reach a service from your VPC privately, as if it were inside your VPC.

### AWS PrivateLink

**AWS PrivateLink** lets you privately connect your VPC to services and resources as if they were in your VPC. You do not need an internet gateway, a NAT device, a public IP address, Direct Connect or a VPN to reach the service from your private subnets.

You create a VPC endpoint in your VPC, a private door that leads to the service. You control which endpoints, services and resources your VPC can reach. The service can be an AWS service, a service hosted by another AWS account, or a partner service offered through AWS.

Figure 8-7 below shows both ideas: a transit gateway joining several networks, and PrivateLink giving a private subnet access to a service.

sections.title: Chapter 10: Access management (IAM)
sections.note: Who may do what in AWS: the root user, IAM users, groups, policies and roles, how to protect and store credentials, and how to manage many accounts and identities.

items.term: Who are you and what may you do

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Everything in this chapter answers two questions about every request to your AWS account. Learn the two words first and the rest falls into place.

**Authentication** means proving who you are. You sign in with credentials (a secret that only you should have, such as a password) and AWS matches them against an identity it trusts.

**Authorization** means deciding what you may do once AWS knows who you are. A request is allowed only if the identity has been given permission for that resource.

An **identity** is a "who" that AWS can recognise: a person, or an application that makes requests.

Think of an airport. The passport check proves who you are (authentication). Your boarding pass says which flight you may board (authorization). Having a valid passport does not let you board every plane.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **authentication** — proving who you are, for example by signing in.
- **authorization** — deciding what an identity is allowed to do.
- **identity** — a person or application that AWS can recognise and that can make requests.

### Where this meets AWS

Actions in AWS are carried out as API requests (a request sent to a service, such as "launch an instance" or "delete a bucket"). It does not matter whether you click in the console, run a command or call it from code. AWS first checks who sent the request, then checks whether that identity has permission for that action on that resource.

So when you add a new person or application to your AWS account, you do two jobs: give it an identity so it can authenticate, and give it permissions so it can be authorized. The rest of this chapter shows the tools for both.

blocks.title: Small scenario
blocks.content: A new analyst joins. She signs in with her own credentials, so AWS knows it is her (authentication). You allow her to read one report bucket and nothing else, so AWS lets her read that bucket and refuses everything else (authorization).

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> The first identity in every account can do everything, including closing the account. Protecting it is the single most important security habit.

When you create an AWS account you begin with one sign-in identity, the **root user**. It has complete access to all AWS services and resources in the account. You sign in as the root user with the email address and password you used to create the account.

AWS strongly recommends that you do not use the root user for everyday tasks. Use it only for the few tasks that need it, and do your daily work with other identities.

**Root user protection** means making that one powerful identity hard to steal and rarely used.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **root user** — the first identity of an account, with complete access to everything in it.
- **root user protection** — the habits that keep the root user safe: strong sign-in, an extra sign-in check, rare use.
- **root-only tasks** — the few jobs that only the root user can do.

### How to protect it

- Add an extra sign-in check beyond the password, such as a code from a phone app or a physical security key. AWS now enforces this for root users by default, but it needs you to set it up when you create the account or when prompted at sign-in.
- Guard the email address, because it is part of the root credentials.
- Use the root user only for the tasks that need it.
- Do your daily work with a separate administrator identity. The next lessons show how to create one.

### Root-only tasks

Some jobs can be done only by signing in as the root user. Examples from AWS's list:

blocks.title: Examples of tasks that need the root user
blocks.content:
- Close your account (for a standalone account, one that is not grouped with other accounts).
- Change the account's root settings, such as the root email address and password.
- Restore permissions if the only administrator accidentally removed their own.
- Activate access for other identities to the Billing and Cost Management console (where you see and manage your AWS bill).
- Fix a rule on an S3 bucket that accidentally blocks access for everyone.

AWS's full list is longer, but most daily administration does not need the root user.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> The root user should stay locked away. Everyone else needs their own identity, and groups stop you from managing permissions one person at a time.

**AWS IAM** (Identity and Access Management) is the AWS service that helps you securely control access to AWS resources. It controls who is authenticated (signed in) and who is authorized (has permissions) to use resources. IAM itself is offered at no additional charge.

An **IAM user** is an identity that you create in your account. It represents one person or one application. A user consists of a name and credentials, so that each person signs in with their own.

Never share one user between several people. Separate users mean each person can be given exactly the access they need and removed on their own.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS IAM** — the AWS service for creating identities and controlling what they may do.
- **IAM user** — an identity you create in your account for one person or application.
- **IAM group** — a collection of IAM users that share the same permissions.

### Groups

An **IAM group** is a collection of IAM users. You give permissions to the group, and every user in it receives them. When a new developer joins, add them to the Developers group. When someone changes jobs, move them to another group, with no need to edit their permissions one by one.

Facts to remember:

- A user can belong to several groups.
- Groups cannot be nested: a group holds users, not other groups.
- There is no default group with all users. You create it yourself if you want one.
- A group is for permissions. It is not an identity that can sign in.

blocks.title: A note on today's best practice
blocks.content: AWS recommends that people who work for your organization use federation (signing in through a company identity system) to get temporary access, and that IAM users are kept for the specific cases that federation does not cover. Later lessons explain federation and temporary access.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Users and groups say who. A policy says what they may do. Without a policy, an identity can do nothing useful.

An **IAM policy** is an object in AWS that defines permissions. You attach it to an identity, such as a user or a group. When that identity makes a request, AWS looks at the policy to decide whether to allow or deny it. Most policies are stored as JSON documents (a plain text format with named fields).

A policy statement has three main parts: the **effect** (Allow or Deny), the **action** (what may be done), and the **resource** (what it applies to).

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **IAM policy** — a document that lists what an identity is allowed or denied to do.
- **AWS managed policy** — a ready-made policy that AWS creates and maintains; you cannot change it.
- **customer managed policy** — a policy that you create and maintain in your own account.
Figure 9-1 below shows one statement. It allows reading objects from one bucket. The names are examples, and the long resource name is an ARN, the unique name AWS gives every resource.

blocks.content:
### Two kinds of managed policy

**AWS managed policies** are created and administered by AWS. They are convenient: AdministratorAccess, PowerUserAccess and ReadOnlyAccess are examples. You cannot change them. AWS sometimes updates them, for example when it launches a new service, and the update reaches everything the policy is attached to.

**Customer managed policies** are policies you create in your own account. You can change them as often as you like, and a change reaches everything the policy is attached to. They give you more precise control than AWS managed policies.

A good way to start is to copy an AWS managed policy and then trim it to your needs.

blocks.title: Which to use?
blocks.content:
| | AWS managed policy | Customer managed policy |
|---|---|---|
| Created by | AWS | You |
| Can you edit it? | No | Yes |
| Good for | Getting started fast | Exact permissions for your use case |

items.text: A policy can also be attached directly to a single user or group, called an inline policy. It belongs to that one identity and is deleted with it. If a policy could apply to more than one identity, a managed policy is the better choice.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> If a stolen password can do everything, a small mistake becomes a disaster. If it can do only one small job, the damage stays small.

The **principle of least privilege** means granting only the permissions needed to do a task, no more. You do this by naming the actions that may be taken, on specific resources, under specific conditions.

Think of a hotel key card. The cleaner's card opens the rooms to clean, not the safe in the office.

A request only works if a policy allows it, so least privilege is a habit of writing small, exact policies for each user or group.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **principle of least privilege** — give each identity only the permissions it needs for its job, and nothing more.

### How to get there

AWS gives a practical path:

1. **Start broad while you learn.** You might begin with wider permissions to explore what a workload needs. AWS managed policies help you start.
2. **Narrow down.** AWS managed policies are shared by all customers, so they may grant more than you need. Write customer managed policies that fit your use case.
3. **Use what AWS recorded.** IAM Access Analyzer can look at the activity AWS recorded and generate a fine-grained policy based on what an identity actually used.
4. **Review and remove.** Use last accessed information to find users, permissions and credentials that nobody uses, then remove them.

blocks.title: Small scenario
blocks.content: An analyst only needs to read one report bucket. A least-privilege policy allows only read actions on that bucket. An over-broad one allows every action on every resource. If her sign-in is stolen, the first policy exposes one bucket for reading. The second exposes the whole account.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Applications and other accounts need access too, but handing out passwords is risky. A role gives short-lived access without a password to lose.

An **IAM role** is an identity with permissions, like a user, but it is not tied to one person. Anyone who needs it, and is allowed to, can **assume** it (take it on for a while). A role has no password or other long-term credentials. When you assume it you receive **temporary credentials** for that role session, which stop working after a limited time.

Roles delegate access to people, applications or services that do not normally have it. For example, an application on an EC2 instance can use a role: AWS hands the instance the role's temporary credentials, and an application that uses an AWS SDK finds and uses them. No secret has to be stored on the server.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **IAM role** — an identity with permissions that anyone allowed to can assume, without a password of its own.
- **temporary credentials** — short-lived access credentials that stop working after a limited time.
- **cross-account role** — a role in one account that identities from another account are allowed to assume.

### Cross-account access

A role can also give users in one AWS account access to resources in another account. The account that owns the resources creates a role and says which other account may assume it.

Figure 9-2 below shows this. A user in account B asks to assume the role in account A, gets temporary credentials, and uses them to reach a resource in account A.

blocks.title: Roles versus users
blocks.content:
| | IAM user | IAM role |
|---|---|---|
| Tied to | one person or application | whoever assumes it |
| Long-term credentials | Yes | No |
| Typical use | specific cases that need them | applications on AWS, other accounts, temporary access |

AWS recommends that workloads use temporary credentials from roles rather than long-term credentials.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Passwords get guessed, reused and stolen. A second proof, plus rules for stronger passwords, makes a stolen password far less useful.

**Multi-factor authentication** (MFA) means signing in with more than one proof. The first is your sign-in credentials. The second is something you have, such as a device that produces a code or answers a challenge. With MFA, a thief who steals your password still cannot sign in.

This is the extra sign-in check from the root user lesson. AWS supports these types:

- **Passkeys and security keys.** Based on FIDO standards, they resist phishing (tricks that fool you into giving away a login). Security keys are physical devices; synced passkeys use a credential manager.
- **Virtual authenticator apps.** A phone app that makes time-based one-time codes.
- **Hardware TOTP tokens.** A small physical device that shows time-based codes (TOTP means time-based one-time password).

AWS recommends phishing-resistant MFA where you can.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **multi-factor authentication** — signing in with more than one proof, such as a password plus a code from a device.
- **password policy** — rules that every IAM user's password must follow, such as minimum length.

### Where MFA applies

The root user and IAM users can each register up to eight MFA devices of any type. You need only one device to sign in. Each user has its own MFA settings. Turning on MFA for the root user affects only the root user.

### Password policies

A **password policy** sets rules for IAM users' passwords. If you set none, AWS applies a default: 8 to 128 characters, at least three of four character types, not the same as the account name or email, and no expiry. A custom policy can set a minimum length from 6 to 128, require character types, and make passwords expire after 1 to 1,095 days.

Two limits matter. The password policy does not apply to the root user's password. And you cannot create a lockout rule that locks a user out after failed attempts, so combine a strong password policy with MFA.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Programs and command-line tools cannot type a password. They use access keys. Leaked keys are one of the most common ways accounts are attacked.

An **access key** is a long-term credential for an IAM user (or the root user). You use it to sign programmatic requests made through the AWS CLI or API, directly or through an AWS SDK.

An access key has two parts that must be used together: an **access key ID** and a **secret access key**. The secret key can be retrieved only when you create it. If you lose it, delete that access key and create a new one.

AWS says that IAM users with access keys are an account security risk. Wherever possible, use temporary credentials from a role instead. A user can have at most two access keys.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **access key** — a long-term credential made of an ID and a secret, used by programs and command-line tools.
- **credential rotation** — replacing a credential with a new one on a regular basis or when needed.
- **credential storage risks** — the dangers of keeping secrets where others can find them, such as inside code.

### Credential storage risks

AWS lists things you must not do:

- Do not create access keys with the root user's credentials.
- Do not put access keys or credential information in your application files.
- Do not include files with access keys in your project area, where they could be shared or copied by mistake.
- Remember that keys saved in the shared AWS credentials file are stored in plaintext (readable text).

### Rotation: replace without a break

When someone leaves, or a key might have leaked, **rotate** it: create a second key while the first still works, switch your applications to the new key, check the old key's last-used information, then deactivate it, and delete it after you are sure nothing needs it. The limit of two keys per user makes this swap possible.

items.term: Storing secrets: Secrets Manager and Systems Manager

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> An application needs a database password somewhere. Writing it into the code is dangerous. AWS offers safer places to keep secrets and settings.

**AWS Secrets Manager** helps you manage, retrieve and rotate database credentials, application credentials, tokens, API keys and other secrets. Instead of hard-coding a credential in your source code, your application makes a call to Secrets Manager at run time and gets the secret when it needs it.

Secrets Manager can also rotate a secret automatically on a schedule you set. Because the credential is no longer stored with the application, rotating it does not mean changing and re-deploying the application. You pay only for what you use.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Secrets Manager** — a service that stores secrets and can rotate them automatically.
- **AWS Systems Manager** — a service for viewing and managing servers at scale, with several tools.
- **Parameter Store** — a Systems Manager tool that stores configuration values as named parameters.

### AWS Systems Manager

**AWS Systems Manager** helps you centrally view, manage and operate nodes (servers) at scale, in AWS and on-premises. Its tools include Run Command, Session Manager, Automation and Parameter Store. They let you patch servers, run commands remotely and connect to a node without opening inbound ports.

### Parameter Store

**Parameter Store** is a centralized store for configuration data kept as named values called parameters. A parameter can be plain text, a list, or a SecureString, a value that Parameter Store encrypts (scrambles) for you. The standard tier is free.

For real secrets, such as database passwords or API keys, AWS recommends Secrets Manager, because it adds automatic rotation. Parameter Store has no credential rotation.

blocks.title: Which one?
blocks.content:
| Need | Use |
|---|---|
| Database password with automatic rotation | Secrets Manager |
| An app setting such as a website address the app calls | Parameter Store |
| Patching and managing many servers | Systems Manager |

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Companies often use many AWS accounts, for example one per team or environment. Organizations lets you manage them as one group instead of one by one.

**AWS Organizations** helps you centrally manage and govern many AWS accounts. You can create accounts, group them, apply rules to them and get a single consolidated bill.

You group accounts into **organizational units** (OUs). An OU is a group of accounts that serve one application or service, such as Production or Development. Rules applied to an OU reach every account inside it.

The account that owns the organization is the management account. The others are member accounts.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Organizations** — a service for managing many AWS accounts together.
- **organizational unit** — a group of accounts inside an organization, such as Production.
- **service control policy** — a rule that sets the maximum permissions for the accounts it is attached to.

blocks.content:
### Service control policies

A **service control policy** (SCP) is a rule for your organization. It sets the maximum permissions available to the IAM users and roles in the accounts it covers. It acts as a fence around what is possible.

Key facts:

- An SCP never grants permissions. To allow something, the account still needs its own policies.
- What an identity can really do is what both the SCP and its own policies allow.
- An SCP limits the member accounts, including their root users. It does not affect users or roles in the management account.
- AWS recommends testing SCPs on a small OU before attaching them to the whole organization.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Companies already have a list of employees somewhere. Creating a second set of users inside every AWS account would be slow and risky. Federation reuses the list they already have.

A **federated identity** is an identity that is managed outside AWS and trusted by AWS. The system that holds those identities and vouches for them is the **identity provider**, for example your company's directory.

With **single sign-on** (SSO), a person signs in once and then reaches many applications or accounts without signing in again.

AWS recommends that human users get access through federation, using temporary credentials by assuming roles, instead of long-term IAM users.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **federated identity** — an identity managed outside AWS, such as in your company's directory, that AWS trusts.
- **identity provider** — the system that stores identities and vouches for who they are.
- **single sign-on** — signing in once to reach many applications or accounts.
- **AWS IAM Identity Center** — the AWS service for giving your workforce single sign-on access to many accounts and applications.

### AWS IAM Identity Center

**AWS IAM Identity Center** is the AWS solution for connecting your workforce to AWS accounts and AWS managed applications (AWS's own applications that use it for sign-in). You connect your existing identity provider and synchronize its users and groups, or you create users directly in Identity Center. AWS recommends it for centralized access management.

It gives you one point of federation. You can create permission sets, ready-made sets of permissions for common jobs such as administrator, provision them across accounts and assign them to users and groups. People use a web portal, the AWS access portal, to reach everything assigned to them.

An organization instance, the recommended kind, covers the accounts of your whole organization and is set up in its management account. It was called AWS Single Sign-On until July 26, 2022.

items.term: Amazon Cognito and AWS Directory Service

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Your employees and your app's customers are different groups of people, and many companies run Windows directories. AWS has a service for each case.

**Amazon Cognito** is an identity platform for web and mobile apps. It answers two questions, with two parts:

- **User pool:** "Who is this user?" It is a user directory with sign-up and sign-in. It can also let users sign in with social providers such as Google or with company identity providers.
- **Identity pool:** "What AWS resources may this user reach?" It swaps a trusted sign-in token for temporary, limited AWS credentials, so an app can call services such as Amazon S3 on the user's behalf. (A token is a small digital proof that someone has signed in.)

You can use them together: sign in with a user pool, then trade that token with an identity pool for AWS credentials.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Cognito** — the AWS service for sign-up, sign-in and access for the users of your web and mobile apps.
- **AWS Directory Service** — the AWS service for using Microsoft Active Directory with AWS.

### AWS Directory Service

Active Directory is Microsoft's directory for the users, groups and devices of a company. **AWS Directory Service** provides several ways to use it with AWS.

- **AWS Managed Microsoft AD** runs a real Windows Server Active Directory, managed by AWS in the cloud. Choose it when you need real Active Directory features for AWS applications or Windows workloads.
- **AD Connector** is a proxy. It forwards sign-in requests from AWS applications to your existing on-premises directory, with no directory synchronization needed.

### Choosing

blocks.title: Who are the users?
blocks.content:
| The users are | Use |
|---|---|
| Your employees, needing access to AWS accounts | AWS IAM Identity Center |
| Customers of your web or mobile app | Amazon Cognito |
| People in a Windows Active Directory | AWS Directory Service |

sections.title: Chapter 11: The shared responsibility model
sections.note: Who secures what on AWS: AWS secures the cloud itself, you secure what you put in it, and how the split shifts for EC2, RDS and Lambda.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Moving to the cloud does not hand all of security to AWS. If you think it does, you will leave your own part undone, and that is where most mistakes happen.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **shared responsibility model** — AWS's description of which security jobs belong to AWS and which belong to you, the customer.

Security on AWS is a shared responsibility between AWS and the customer. AWS looks after some parts of security. You look after the other parts. Neither side does everything.

Think of renting an apartment. The landlord looks after the building, the roof and the main door lock. You look after your own front-door key, who you let in, and what you leave on the table. A good lock does not help if you hand out copies of the key.

AWS says this model can relieve the customer's operational burden, because AWS operates, manages and controls the components from the host operating system and virtualization layer down to the physical security of the facilities in which the service operates.

blocks.title: Why the split depends on the service
blocks.content: Earlier you met IaaS, PaaS and SaaS: the more of the stack the provider runs, the less you run. The shared responsibility model follows the same idea. Customer responsibility is determined by the AWS Cloud services that a customer selects. AWS gives Amazon EC2 as an example of IaaS, so with EC2 the customer performs all of the necessary security configuration and management tasks for the parts it controls. The next lessons name the two halves and then walk through EC2, RDS and Lambda.

items.term: Why not let AWS do everything?
items.text: You decide what to build, who gets access, and what data goes in. AWS cannot know those choices. So the choices, and their security, stay with you. AWS runs the shared foundation, the same for every customer.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You need to know exactly what AWS protects, so you do not waste effort on it and so you can trust it when an auditor asks.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **security of the cloud** — the part of security that AWS is responsible for: the hardware, software, networking and facilities that run AWS Cloud services.

**Security of the cloud** is AWS's half. AWS is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs all of the services offered in the AWS Cloud. That infrastructure is composed of the hardware, software, networking, and facilities that run AWS Cloud services.

In plain words, AWS looks after the buildings (data centers, in every Availability Zone and at edge locations), the physical servers, the network cables, and the software layer that runs the services, including the hypervisor that splits one server into virtual machines.

Figure 10-1 below shows the two layers: AWS below the dashed line, you above it.

blocks.content: You do not have to visit a data center to trust it. Third-party auditors regularly test and verify the effectiveness of AWS security. Later in this module you will see how to download their reports.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: A visitor walks into an AWS data center and tries to reach a server. Who must stop them? AWS, because physical security of the facilities is security of the cloud. You cannot, and do not need to, guard a building you do not own.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> This is the half that is yours. If you skip it, AWS cannot do it for you, and a mistake here can expose your data even though AWS's side is perfect.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **security in the cloud** — the part of security that the customer is responsible for: your data, your permissions, and how you configure and use the services you choose.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: A team stores customer files in S3 and, by mistake, writes an IAM policy that lets everyone read them. Did AWS fail? No. The data and the permissions are security in the cloud, so the mistake is the customer's.

items.text: When you run your own server, the operating system inside it is also yours to keep updated. The next lessons show that this part moves to AWS as you use more managed services.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some security tasks exist on both sides. If you assume AWS did your side too, you leave a gap, for example an unpatched server.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **shared controls** — security controls where both AWS and the customer have a job, each in their own layer: for example patching, configuration and training.

A **control** is a safeguard that reduces a security risk, such as patching or training. AWS says the shared model extends to IT controls: just as the responsibility to operate the IT environment is shared, so is the management, operation and verification of IT controls.

**Shared controls** apply to both the infrastructure layer and the customer layer, but in completely separate contexts. AWS provides the requirements for the infrastructure, and the customer must provide their own control implementation within their use of AWS services.

AWS lists three examples:
- **Patch management.** AWS patches and fixes flaws within the infrastructure. You patch your guest OS and applications. (A patch is a software update that fixes a flaw.)
- **Configuration management.** AWS maintains the configuration of its infrastructure devices. You configure your own guest operating systems, databases and applications.
- **Awareness and training.** AWS trains AWS employees. You must train your own employees.

blocks.title: Same name, two jobs
blocks.content: Patch management is on both lists. AWS patching its infrastructure does not patch your guest operating system. Awareness and training also repeats: AWS training its staff does not train yours.

blocks.title: Two other kinds, for contrast
blocks.content: AWS also names controls a customer fully inherits from AWS, such as physical and environmental controls. And it names customer specific controls, which are solely the customer's responsibility, such as zone security that may require a customer to route or zone data within specific security environments.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> With EC2 you get the most freedom, and also the most security work. Knowing this tells you what to do after you launch an instance.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **responsibility shift: EC2** — with an EC2 instance you manage the guest operating system, the software on it, the network access rules and the permissions; AWS manages the hardware layers.

blocks.caption: For EC2, AWS looks after the data center and virtualization layer. You look after everything from the guest operating system upward.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: You launch an EC2 instance running a web server. A flaw is announced in the web server software. AWS will not fix it for you: the software is on your guest operating system, so patching it is your job.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> RDS is a managed service, so AWS takes on more work than with EC2. You need to know which jobs moved to AWS and which stayed with you.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **responsibility shift: RDS** — with Amazon RDS, AWS takes over operating system and database software installation and patching, backups and high availability; you keep your data, access permissions, and tuning your queries.

Amazon RDS is a managed database service. AWS's RDS guide compares who is responsible when you run a database on-premises, on EC2, or on RDS.

With RDS, AWS manages: scaling, high availability, database backups, database software installation and patching, and operating system installation and patching, as well as server maintenance, hardware, and power, network and cooling. On EC2 those database and operating system jobs are the customer's.

What stays with you: application optimization. AWS says you are responsible for query tuning, which is adjusting SQL queries to improve performance, and that monitoring and tuning are individualized processes that you own for your RDS databases. You also still control access with IAM and can protect databases with security groups and a virtual private cloud.

blocks.title: EC2 database versus RDS database
blocks.content: Running a database on EC2: you patch the operating system, install and patch the database software, and set up backups. Running it on RDS: AWS does those. Your share gets smaller, but it is not zero.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: Your RDS database is slow because one query is badly written. AWS manages the database engine, but tuning your own queries is yours.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Serverless takes even more off your plate. Seeing the full range from EC2 to Lambda shows the pattern behind the whole shared responsibility model.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **responsibility shift: Lambda** — with AWS Lambda, AWS manages the infrastructure, operating system and application platform; you are responsible for the security of your code and for IAM permissions.

For AWS Lambda, AWS manages the underlying infrastructure and foundation services, the operating system, and the application platform. You are responsible for the security of your code and AWS IAM to the Lambda service and within your function.

Serverless means you run code without provisioning or managing servers. AWS handles patching the underlying servers and operating systems. By default, Lambda applies security updates to managed language runtimes automatically.

blocks.title: The pattern
blocks.content: The more abstract the service, the more AWS manages and the less you do. EC2: you manage the guest OS and software. RDS: AWS adds the OS and database software. Lambda: AWS adds the application platform too. Whatever the service, your data and your IAM permissions stay with you.

items.term: Why does your share never reach zero?
items.text: Because AWS cannot choose for you who may use your data or what your code does. Those choices are yours in every service.

sections.title: Chapter 12: Security, governance and compliance
sections.note: The vocabulary of governance and compliance, and the AWS services that encrypt data, record activity, detect threats and enforce rules.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many organizations may only run workloads if they can prove they follow certain rules. These words describe that proof, and AWS gives you tools for it.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **governance** — setting rules for how your cloud is used and making sure they are followed.
- **compliance** — following the laws, standards and policies that apply to you.
- **audit** — an independent check of whether you follow the rules, based on evidence.
- **compliance program** — a named set of checkable requirements, such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 or PCI DSS.
- **compliance varies by location and industry** — which rules apply to you depends on the country you operate in and the kind of business you run.

**Governance** is how an organization sets its rules and makes sure people follow them: who may create what, which settings are required, and who checks.

**Compliance** means following the rules and standards that apply to you. Those can be laws (such as privacy laws), industry standards, or your own company policies.

An **audit** is a check, often by an independent outsider, of whether you really follow the rules. Auditors ask for evidence: reports, logs, settings.

A **compliance program** is a named set of requirements that can be checked, such as ISO 27001, SOC 2 or PCI DSS. AWS publishes a list of the compliance programs it supports. AWS says certifications and attestations are assessed by a third-party, independent auditor and result in a certification, audit report, or attestation of compliance.

blocks.title: Compliance varies by location and industry
blocks.content: A hospital, a bank and a games studio face different rules, and so do companies in different countries. So there is no single AWS setting that makes you compliant. Customer responsibility varies based on many factors, including the AWS services and Regions they choose, and the laws and regulations applicable to their organization and workload.

blocks.title: What AWS does and does not do
blocks.content: AWS customers remain responsible for complying with applicable compliance laws, regulations and privacy programs. For laws and regulations, no formal certification is available to, or distributable by, a cloud service provider. AWS offers functionality (such as security features), enablers and legal agreements to support customer compliance.

blocks.title: Where your data lives
blocks.content: As a customer, you determine where your content is stored, including the geographic Region of that storage. AWS will not move or replicate your content outside of your chosen AWS Region(s) without your agreement, except as necessary to comply with the law or a binding order of a governmental body. So choosing the right Region is one way to act on a data sovereignty rule.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> An auditor asks, "Can you prove the infrastructure you run on is audited?" AWS Artifact is where you get that proof, without writing to anyone.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Artifact** — the AWS place where you download AWS compliance documents and manage agreements with AWS.
- **compliance reports** — documents, such as SOC and ISO-related reports, in which independent parties describe how AWS controls were checked.
- **compliance requirements vary among services** — not every AWS service is covered by every compliance program, so check the services-in-scope list for the program you need.

**AWS Artifact** provides on-demand downloads of AWS security and compliance documents. On demand means you get them yourself, when you want them.

Examples AWS names are reports on compliance with ISO standards and PCI standards, and System and Organization Controls (SOC) reports. Artifact also provides certifications from accreditation bodies that validate the implementation and operating effectiveness of AWS security controls.

You can submit these documents to your auditors or regulators as audit artifacts. You can also use them as guidelines to evaluate your own cloud architecture and to assess the effectiveness of your company's internal controls.

You can also use Artifact to review, accept, and track the status of your agreements with AWS. AWS provides Artifact documents and agreements free of charge.

blocks.title: Not every service for every program
blocks.content: AWS's EC2 security guide points to a page named AWS Services in Scope by Compliance Program to learn which compliance programs apply to Amazon EC2. So before you rely on a program for a workload, check that the services you use are in scope for it.

blocks.title: What Artifact does not do
blocks.content: AWS customers are responsible for developing or obtaining documents that demonstrate the security and compliance of their companies. Artifact gives you AWS's documents, not yours.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: Your company must show an auditor that the infrastructure under its app has passed a SOC audit. You open AWS Artifact, download the SOC report, and hand it over as an audit artifact.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> If someone steals a disk or listens on a network cable, encryption makes what they get unreadable. It is one of your jobs in the shared responsibility model.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **encryption** — scrambling data so only someone with the right key can read it.
- **encryption at rest** — encrypting data while it sits in storage.
- **encryption in transit** — encrypting data while it moves over a network.
- **encryption key** — the secret value used to encrypt and decrypt data.

**Encryption** means scrambling data so that only someone holding the right **encryption key** can read it. A key is a secret value used to lock and unlock the data.

Data can be at two stages:

**Encryption at rest** protects data in storage. Data at rest is data you have in storage, such as on a hard drive, in the cloud, or in a database.

**Encryption in transit** protects data being transferred from one system to another over a network. When your browser talks to a secure website, the browser and server use in-transit encryption called Transport Layer Security (TLS). Someone could intercept the data, but it would be unreadable.

Without the key, encrypted data is only noise. That is why protecting the key matters as much as encrypting the data.

blocks.title: What AWS offers
blocks.content: AWS says to always encrypt your data both at rest and in transit. You can use TLS to encrypt the data in transit. Encryption at rest is achieved through data encryption capabilities available in AWS storage services such as Amazon EBS, Amazon S3 and Amazon RDS. Amazon S3 encrypts new objects by default.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: Customer records sit in an S3 bucket. If the storage is encrypted at rest, a stolen copy is unreadable. The page that customers use to fetch them is served over TLS, so someone on the network cannot read the traffic.

items.term: Keys and certificates: KMS, CloudHSM, ACM

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Encryption needs keys, and secure websites need certificates. AWS has three services that look after them so you do not have to build that yourself.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS KMS** — managed service to create and control encryption keys; the usual starting point.
- **AWS CloudHSM** — your own dedicated hardware security modules in the cloud, for when you need full control of keys and algorithms.
- **AWS Certificate Manager** — creates, stores and renews TLS certificates for your websites and applications.
- **TLS certificate** — a digital document that proves a website's identity and enables an encrypted HTTPS connection.

**AWS KMS** (Key Management Service) is an AWS managed service that makes it easy for you to create and control the keys used to encrypt and sign your data. KMS keys are protected by hardware security modules (HSMs) validated to FIPS 140-3 Security Level 3, and they never leave KMS unencrypted. You can also create key policies so that only trusted users have access to a key.

**AWS CloudHSM** gives you your own hardware security modules in the AWS Cloud. An HSM is a computing device that processes cryptographic operations and provides secure storage for cryptographic keys. With CloudHSM you have complete control, and the HSMs are single tenant, meaning they are not shared with other customers. The trade-off AWS states is that you have more responsibility than with a managed AWS service.

**AWS Certificate Manager (ACM)** handles creating, storing and renewing public and private SSL/TLS certificates and keys. A **TLS certificate** is a digital document that lets a browser check that a website is who it claims to be, and enables the encrypted HTTPS connection. AWS says there is no additional charge for the SSL/TLS certificates you manage with ACM.

blocks.title: Which one do I pick?
blocks.content: Need keys for encrypting your AWS data and want AWS to run the hardware? KMS. Need your own single-tenant hardware and full control of keys and algorithms, and accept the extra responsibility? CloudHSM. Need a certificate so your website uses HTTPS and renews on time? ACM. AWS itself suggests KMS if you want a managed service for your keys but do not want or need to operate your own HSMs.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: A company encrypts its S3 data with a key it controls in KMS, and puts a certificate from ACM on its website so visitors connect over HTTPS. That is encryption at rest plus encryption in transit.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You cannot run a system you cannot see. CloudWatch shows how your resources are doing and warns you when something goes wrong.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon CloudWatch** — the AWS service that collects metrics and logs and raises alarms so you can watch your resources and applications.
- **metric** — a number measured over time, such as processor use.
- **log** — a written record of events from a system or application.
- **alarm** — a rule that watches a metric and alerts you or acts when it crosses a threshold.

**Amazon CloudWatch** monitors your AWS resources and the applications you run on AWS in real time. It gives you visibility into application performance, operational health and resource use.

Three basic parts:
- A **metric** is a number tracked over time, such as how busy an EC2 instance's processor is. Many AWS services send basic metrics to CloudWatch automatically, for free. You can also publish your own.
- A **log** is a written record of events produced by a system or application. CloudWatch Logs stores logs from AWS services and your applications in log groups. A log group is a named collection of logs, kept together for easy organization.
- An **alarm** watches a metric against a threshold you choose, and can alert you or trigger an automated action when the threshold is breached.

CloudWatch also offers dashboards, which show your metrics and logs in one place.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: An EC2 instance's processor use stays near its limit. A CloudWatch alarm on that metric notifies the team before users complain, and can also trigger an automated action.

blocks.title: What CloudWatch does not tell you
blocks.content: CloudWatch answers: how is my system performing right now? The next lessons cover questions it does not answer: who changed something, and how a resource was set up.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> When something changes in your account, an auditor or a security team asks who did it and when. CloudTrail keeps that record.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS CloudTrail** — the service that records actions taken in your AWS account as events, so you can audit who did what.
- **API activity log** — the record of the API calls made in your account, whether from the console, the CLI or an SDK.

**AWS CloudTrail** helps you with operational and risk auditing, governance and compliance of your AWS account. Actions taken by a user, role or an AWS service are recorded as **events** in CloudTrail. These include actions taken in the AWS Management Console, the AWS CLI, and the AWS SDKs and APIs.

So every call to the AWS API, whichever way it was made, can leave a record: an **API activity log**. You can identify who or what took which action, what resources were acted upon, when the event occurred, and other details.

Figure 11-1 below shows the idea: a caller makes an API call on a resource, and CloudTrail writes down the facts.
