blocks.title: How long can I look back?
blocks.content: Event history gives you a viewable, searchable, downloadable and immutable record of the past 90 days of management events in an AWS Region, and viewing it has no CloudTrail charge. For a longer record, create a trail, which delivers events to an Amazon S3 bucket.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: A security group rule was changed overnight. CloudTrail shows which user or role made the call and at what time. CloudWatch would only show you that something was behaving differently.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> CloudTrail tells you who made a change. Often you also need to know what a resource looked like last week, and whether it breaks your rules today.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Config** — the service that records how your AWS resources are configured and how that changes over time.
- **configuration history** — the saved record of how a resource was set up in the past.
- **Config rule** — a check that compares a resource's settings with a condition you define and flags the resource as noncompliant if it fails.

**AWS Config** provides a detailed view of the configuration of your AWS resources: how they are related to one another and how they were configured in the past, so you can see how the configurations and relationships change over time. A resource's configuration is how it is set up, for example which port rules a security group has open.

That record is the **configuration history**. It helps with troubleshooting, because you can reach the last known good configuration of a problem resource. It also supports compliance: to demonstrate compliance, you need access to the historical configurations of your resources.

A **Config rule** evaluates the configuration settings of your resources. When Config detects that a resource violates the conditions in a rule, it flags the resource as noncompliant and sends a notification. It evaluates continuously, as resources are created, changed or deleted.

blocks.title: CloudTrail versus Config
blocks.content: CloudTrail records the actions: someone called an API at a certain time. Config records the state: what the resource looked like before and after. Use CloudTrail to find who, and Config to see what the setting was.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: Your rule says no security group may leave a risky port open to everyone. You add a Config rule for it. When someone opens that port, Config flags the security group as noncompliant and sends a notification.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Old users and unused permissions are open doors. Two IAM reports show you which doors exist so you can close them.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **IAM credential report** — a downloadable spreadsheet listing every IAM user and the status of their passwords, access keys and MFA devices.
- **IAM access advisor** — an IAM console tab showing which services a user, group, role or policy can access and when they were last used, to help remove unused permissions.

**IAM credential report.** You can generate and download a credential report that lists all users in your account and the status of their credentials, including passwords, access keys and MFA devices. It is a CSV file, which opens in any spreadsheet. You can provide it to an external auditor. A report can be generated as often as once every four hours.

**IAM access advisor.** When you view a user, group, role or policy in the IAM console, the **Access Advisor** tab shows which services the permissions allow and when each service was last accessed. AWS says this last accessed information helps you identify unused permissions so you can remove them, which supports the principle of least privilege.

Together: the credential report asks "which users and credentials exist, and what is their status?" Access advisor asks "which permissions are actually used?"

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: An auditor asks which employees still have active access keys. You download the credential report and filter the access key columns. Then you check Access Advisor for a role and see it has not used a service for months, so you remove that permission.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Logs hold the clues of an attack, but no person can read them all. GuardDuty reads them for you and tells you when something looks wrong.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon GuardDuty** — a service that watches your logs and activity and reports suspicious or malicious behavior.
- **threat detection** — looking for signs that someone is attacking, or has already broken into, your environment.

**Amazon GuardDuty** is a **threat detection** service. Threat detection means looking for signs that someone is attacking, or has already got into, your environment. GuardDuty continuously monitors, analyzes and processes AWS data sources and logs in your environment. It uses threat intelligence feeds (such as lists of malicious IP addresses and domains), and machine learning models (software that learns patterns from data), to identify suspicious and potentially malicious activity.

When you enable GuardDuty, it automatically starts ingesting foundational data sources: AWS CloudTrail management events, VPC flow logs from EC2 instances, and DNS logs. VPC flow logs are records of the IP traffic going to and from network interfaces in your VPC. You do not need to turn anything else on for it to begin analyzing them.

AWS lists threats it can help you detect, for example: compromised and exfiltrated AWS credentials; unauthorized cryptomining activity on EC2 instances and container workloads; and malware on EC2 instances and container workloads. GuardDuty reports what it finds as findings.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: An access key from your account is suddenly used from an unusual place to call many APIs. GuardDuty can recognize that pattern as possible compromised credentials and report it, so you can disable the key.

blocks.title: GuardDuty versus CloudTrail
blocks.content: CloudTrail keeps the record of what happened. GuardDuty reads that record, and other logs, looking for signs of attack. One is the diary; the other is the detective reading it.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Each security service reports in its own place. If you must open six consoles to see how safe you are, you will miss things. Security Hub puts them in one place.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Security Hub** — a service that collects security findings from many AWS services and partner products into one place, so you can prioritize and respond.
- **security finding** — a report of one security issue found by a service: what, where and how serious.

**AWS Security Hub** is a unified cloud security solution that prioritizes your critical security issues and helps you respond at scale. It automatically correlates and enriches security signals from multiple sources, including Amazon Inspector (vulnerability findings), Amazon GuardDuty (threat detection), and posture management.

A **security finding** is a report of one security issue: what was found, where, and how serious. Each service that finds something produces findings. Security Hub gathers them so you see one list instead of many.

blocks.content:
Part of Security Hub checks your configuration against security standards and best practices. AWS names this posture management capability AWS Security Hub CSPM, which supports standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, CIS, PCI DSS and NIST. Each standard includes several security controls, each representing a security best practice, and failed checks become findings.

Security Hub also offers automation, for example automation rules that update findings when a security check fails.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: GuardDuty reports a suspicious key. Inspector reports a vulnerable instance. Security Hub shows both in one list, so the team can decide which one to fix first.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A website can be knocked offline not by a break-in but by sheer traffic. Shield protects against that kind of attack.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Shield** — AWS's protection against DDoS attacks, in two levels: Standard and Advanced.
- **DDoS attack** — an attack in which many compromised systems flood a target with traffic so real users cannot reach it.

A **DDoS attack** (distributed denial of service attack) is one in which multiple compromised systems try to flood a target with traffic. It can prevent legitimate users from reaching the target service and can even make the target crash under the load.

**AWS Shield** provides protection against DDoS attacks for AWS resources, at the network and transport layers and at the application layer. It comes in two levels:

- **Shield Standard** is provided automatically and at no extra charge when you use AWS.
- **Shield Advanced** is for higher levels of protection. You subscribe to it. It gives expanded DDoS protection for the resources you add to it. AWS's FAQ lists protected resources such as EC2, Elastic Load Balancing, CloudFront, Global Accelerator and Route 53.

blocks.title: Standard versus Advanced
blocks.content: Standard: automatic, no extra charge, nothing to turn on. Advanced: you subscribe and add protection to chosen resources, for more protection against sophisticated and larger attacks. AWS also lists extras with Advanced, such as DDoS cost protection for scaling, which protects your AWS bill against higher fees from usage spikes during a DDoS attack. Check the current AWS Shield pricing page for costs.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: A small blog on CloudFront gets Shield Standard automatically. A large online shop, which cannot afford to be offline during a sale, subscribes to Shield Advanced for its load balancer and CloudFront distribution.

items.term: Guardrails and limits: Control Tower, Service Catalog, Service Quotas

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> With many accounts and teams, rules written on paper are not enough. These three services help enforce standards and limits automatically.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Control Tower** — sets up and governs a multi-account AWS environment using best-practice rules.
- **AWS Service Catalog** — a catalog of IT services approved for your organization, from which users can launch only approved products.
- **Service Quotas** — a central place to view your limits on AWS services and request increases.
- **guardrail** — a high-level rule that provides ongoing governance for your cloud environment.

**AWS Control Tower** offers a straightforward way to set up and govern a multi-account AWS environment, following prescriptive best practices. It orchestrates other services, including AWS Organizations, AWS Service Catalog and AWS IAM Identity Center, to build a landing zone. A **landing zone** is a well-architected, multi-account environment based on security and compliance best practices.

A **guardrail** is a high-level rule that provides ongoing governance for your environment, written in plain language. Control Tower calls these controls (sometimes called guardrails). They come in preventive, detective and proactive kinds. Control Tower also offers Account Factory, a configurable template for creating new accounts with pre-approved settings.

**AWS Service Catalog** lets organizations create and manage catalogs of IT services that are approved for AWS. Users browse the catalog and launch only approved products, within constraints that administrators set.

**Service Quotas** lets you view and manage your quotas (limits) for AWS services from a central location, and request increases.

blocks.title: Same goal, three tools
blocks.content: Control Tower: set up accounts and apply rules to them. Service Catalog: let people launch only approved things. Service Quotas: see and raise the maximum numbers of resources you can use. All three support governance, which you met at the start of this chapter.

blocks.title: Tiny scenario
blocks.content: A company has twenty teams. With Control Tower every new account starts with the same required rules. With Service Catalog teams launch only approved server setups. When a team needs more servers than the default limit allows, they request an increase in Service Quotas, and the request may be approved, denied or partially approved.

sections.title: Chapter 13: Security components and resources
sections.note: The extra AWS security tools, the Marketplace, and where AWS publishes security guidance.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some attacks arrive as ordinary-looking web requests. A firewall for web traffic lets you inspect each request and refuse the harmful ones before your application sees them.

**AWS WAF** is a web application firewall: it inspects the web requests (HTTP or HTTPS, the messages a browser sends to a website) that are forwarded to your application, and decides what happens to each one.

You attach it to a resource it protects, such as an Amazon CloudFront distribution or an Application Load Balancer. That resource forwards each incoming request to AWS WAF for inspection.

The inspection rules live in a **web ACL** (web access control list). Each rule describes what to look for, for example the IP address a request comes from or a value in its query string, and what to do on a match: allow it, block it, count it, or run a CAPTCHA or challenge check to verify a human. The web ACL also has a default action for requests that no rule matched.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS WAF** — a web application firewall that inspects the web requests sent to your application and allows, blocks or counts them by rule.
- **web ACL** — the set of rules (plus a default action) that you attach to the resources AWS WAF protects.
- **SQL injection** — an attack where someone sneaks malicious SQL code into a web request to change or steal what is in your database.
- **cross-site scripting** — an attack where someone uses a weakness in a harmless website to run malicious scripts in other visitors' browsers.

When AWS WAF blocks a request, the protected service answers with an HTTP 403 (Forbidden) status or with a custom response that you chose.

### Two attacks the rules can look for

AWS WAF has rule types for well-known attacks. A **SQL injection** rule looks for malicious SQL code in a request. Attackers insert such code to modify your database or extract data from it.

A **cross-site scripting** rule (XSS) looks for malicious scripts in a request. In an XSS attack, the attacker uses weaknesses in a benign website as a vehicle to inject malicious client-side scripts into other legitimate browsers.

You do not have to write every rule yourself. Managed rule groups, ready-made bundles of rules, are provided by AWS Managed Rules and by other sellers.

blocks.title: WAF versus Shield: one question each
blocks.content: **AWS Shield** answers the question: is someone flooding me with traffic (a DDoS attack)? **AWS WAF** answers a different question: what does this one request contain, and should it be allowed in? They work on different problems, and a public website can use both.

items.term: Where a web ACL is attached
items.text: AWS WAF protects specific resource types, and the list is longer than CloudFront and load balancers. For the exam, remember the two main ones above and that you attach a web ACL to the resource. Check the current AWS WAF page for the full list, because AWS adds new ones.

items.term: Why WAF does not replace secure code
items.text: A firewall in front of an application filters known bad patterns. It does not fix a weakness inside the application. Think of it as a guard at the door, not a repair of the room.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Setting up AWS WAF by hand is fine for one account. With dozens of accounts, hand work leaves gaps. Firewall Manager sets a protection once and applies it everywhere, even to accounts added later.

**AWS Firewall Manager** simplifies administration across multiple accounts and resources for several protections, including AWS WAF, AWS Shield Advanced and VPC security groups. You set up your protections just once, and the service automatically applies them across your accounts and resources, even as you add new ones.

It works with AWS Organizations, the service that groups many AWS accounts into one organization. Firewall Manager is particularly useful when you want to protect your entire organization rather than a small number of specific accounts and resources.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **AWS Firewall Manager** — a service that sets up firewall-style protections once and applies them across all the accounts and resources of an organization.

### What it can do for you

- Protect all resources of a particular type, such as all Amazon CloudFront distributions.
- Protect all resources that carry specific tags.
- Automatically add protection to resources that are added to your account later.
- Subscribe all member accounts in an organization to AWS Shield Advanced, and automatically subscribe new accounts that join.
- Apply security group rules to all member accounts, or to chosen subsets of them.

**A small scenario.** A company has 30 accounts and a rule: every CloudFront distribution must sit behind an AWS WAF web ACL. Checking 30 accounts by hand is slow and a new account is easy to forget. With Firewall Manager, the company writes the rule once, and any new distribution that appears is covered automatically.

blocks.title: What it costs
blocks.content: The charges incurred by AWS Firewall Manager are for the underlying services, such as AWS WAF and AWS Config. Check the current AWS Firewall Manager pricing page for details before you plan a budget.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A bucket can hold names, card numbers or passwords without anyone noticing. You cannot protect data you do not know you have.

**Amazon Macie** is a data security service that discovers sensitive data by using automated analysis and pattern matching, and gives you visibility into data security risks. It works on data stored in Amazon S3.

**Sensitive data** is data that would hurt people or the business if it leaked. Macie looks for types such as personally identifiable information (personal data that can identify one person, such as an address, bank account number or phone number), financial information, and credentials data.

Macie does two jobs. First, it keeps an inventory of your S3 buckets and monitors them for security and access control. If it spots a potential issue, such as a bucket that becomes publicly accessible, it generates a finding for you to review. Second, it looks inside objects for sensitive data and generates a sensitive data finding when it detects some.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Macie** — a service that uses automated analysis and pattern matching to find sensitive data in Amazon S3 and to flag risky bucket settings.
- **sensitive data** — data that would cause harm if exposed, such as personal information, financial information or credentials.

### Two ways to look for sensitive data

- **Automated sensitive data discovery:** Macie keeps checking your bucket inventory and samples representative objects to give you broad visibility.
- **Sensitive data discovery jobs:** deeper and more targeted. You choose the buckets and how deep to look, and you can run a job once or on a recurring schedule.

Macie finds data with managed data identifiers, which are built-in criteria for common types of sensitive data. You can add your own custom data identifiers, which are patterns (regular expressions) you define for data that is specific to your business.

You can send Macie findings to AWS Security Hub, so they sit next to findings from other services. If you have many accounts, a Macie administrator can manage Macie for all of them through AWS Organizations.

items.term: Policy finding versus sensitive data finding
items.text: Macie produces two kinds of findings. A policy finding is about the bucket itself, for example it became publicly accessible. A sensitive data finding is about the content of an object, for example it contains personal data.
An allow list tells Macie to ignore specific text, such as your company's public phone number or sample data used for testing, so you get fewer needless findings.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A threat alert tells you that something suspicious happened. The next questions are what exactly happened and how far it spread. Detective helps you answer them.

**Amazon Detective** helps you analyze, investigate, and quickly identify the root cause of security findings or suspicious activities. The **root cause** is the first thing that started the problem.

Detective automatically collects log data from your AWS resources. It then uses automated analysis, including statistical analysis and graph theory, to generate visualizations that help you run faster and more efficient security investigations.

Picture the hand-off between two services. Amazon GuardDuty continuously monitors your account for threats and raises security findings. Detective starts where that alert ends: you take a finding and dig into the activity around it. Detective links changes in activity to GuardDuty findings, and it gives you access to up to a year of historical event data.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Detective** — a service that gathers log data and shows it as visual summaries so you can investigate a security finding and find its root cause.
- **root cause** — the first thing that started a problem, as opposed to the symptoms you notice later.

blocks.title: Three things Detective offers
blocks.content:
- **Finding groups:** a group of related findings, because an attacker usually performs a sequence of actions that generates several findings. You examine them together.
- **Detective Investigation:** checks IAM users and IAM roles for indicators of compromise, which are signs that can identify malicious activity with a high level of confidence.
- **VPC flow volume:** visual summaries of the network traffic of your EC2 instances, built from VPC flow logs that Detective collects automatically.

items.text: Think of GuardDuty as the smoke alarm and Detective as the person who walks through the building afterwards to find where the fire started. Different jobs, so teams commonly want both.
Detective's source data includes AWS CloudTrail management events, the record of who called which AWS API. That is how it can show what an IAM user or role did around the time of a finding.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Copying a resource into every account means keeping many copies identical. Sharing one copy is simpler, and one set of rules is easier to keep secure.

**AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM)** helps you securely share your resources across AWS accounts, within your organization or organizational units (OUs, groups of accounts inside an organization), and with IAM roles and users for supported resource types.

You create a resource once and use AWS RAM to make it usable by the other accounts. This removes the need to build duplicate resources in every account.

Here is a concrete case. If you share an Amazon VPC subnet with another account, users in that account can see the subnet in their own VPC console, as if it were native to their account. The account that owns the resource is the owning account, and the account that uses it is the consuming account.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **AWS Resource Access Manager** — a service that lets you create a resource once and securely share it with other accounts, organizational units or an entire organization.

### Why share instead of copy

- **Less operational work:** one resource, not a duplicate in each account.
- **Security and consistency:** everyone using a share is managed by one set of policies and permissions, instead of identical policies you must keep identical in many accounts.
- **Visibility:** you can view the usage of shared resources through the integration with Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail.

### Who can receive a share

If your account is managed by AWS Organizations, you can share with all accounts in the organization or only with chosen OUs, without listing every account ID. You can also share with specific accounts by ID. If you share with an account outside your organization, AWS RAM sends an invitation, and the recipient must accept it before gaining access.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You cannot fix a problem nobody told you about. Trusted Advisor looks over your account and tells you where it looks risky, fragile or wasteful.

**AWS Trusted Advisor** inspects your AWS environment and makes recommendations when opportunities exist to save money, improve system availability and performance, or help close security gaps.

Each inspection is called a check. Checks are grouped into categories: Cost optimization, Performance, Security, Fault tolerance, Service limits, and Operational Excellence. These echo the pillars you met earlier, but they are not the same list. Service limits covers the quotas on how much of a service your account may use.

The Security category holds checks you can picture easily, for example MFA on the root account, Amazon S3 bucket permissions, security groups with specific ports unrestricted, and public snapshots of EBS volumes or RDS databases.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **AWS Trusted Advisor** — a service that checks your AWS environment against best practices and recommends improvements in cost, performance, security, fault tolerance, service limits and operations.

### Which checks do you get?

It depends on your support plan, which is the level of help you pay AWS for.

- With the entry-level support plan (the AWS page calls it Basic) you can use the Trusted Advisor console to see all checks in the Service limits category and selected checks in the Security and Fault tolerance categories. The Security checks you get include the ones named above.
- Every check is available with the higher, paid support plans. AWS's Trusted Advisor page names them as Business Support+, Enterprise Support and Unified Operations.

Confirm the current plan names on the AWS Trusted Advisor page before the exam.

You open Trusted Advisor in the AWS Management Console. With a paid plan you can also reach the checks through the Trusted Advisor API.

blocks.title: A worked example
blocks.content: A new team member creates a security group that leaves a risky port open to everyone. You never looked at it. Trusted Advisor's check for security groups with unrestricted ports flags it, so you see the gap and can close it. Trusted Advisor tells you where to look; it does not replace GuardDuty, which watches for active threats.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> AWS builds many security services, but not everything. If your company already trusts a security product from another company, you can often buy and launch it through AWS.

**AWS Marketplace** is a curated digital catalog that you can use to find, buy, deploy, and manage third-party software, data, and services. Third-party means made by a company other than AWS.

Sellers include independent software vendors (ISVs, companies that build and sell software). The catalog lists thousands of software products in categories such as security, networking, storage and database.

**Third-party security products** are the security entries in this catalog: tools from other companies that you can add next to AWS's own services. AWS's security pages point to security solutions in AWS Marketplace from hundreds of independent software vendors.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Marketplace** — an online catalog where you can find, buy and launch software, data and services from other companies, billed through your AWS bill.
- **third-party security products** — security tools made by companies other than AWS and sold through AWS Marketplace.

### How you receive them

Products come in several forms:

- an Amazon Machine Image (AMI) that you launch as an EC2 instance in your own account,
- a SaaS product, software you use over the internet,
- a web ACL, rules or conditions for AWS WAF, which tie back to the managed rule groups from AWS Marketplace sellers you met in the AWS WAF lesson.

### How you pay

Pricing options include free trial, hourly, monthly, annual and multi-year terms. AWS handles billing and payments, and the charges appear on your AWS bill. Every software product in AWS Marketplace has been through a curation process.

blocks.title: The exam point
blocks.content: If a question says a company wants to use a security product from another vendor on AWS, think AWS Marketplace. AWS's own services are not the only option.

items.term: Where to read about AWS security

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Security advice goes out of date. AWS publishes its own guidance and answers, so you can check the source instead of an old article.

AWS runs the security of the cloud, the part of the shared responsibility model that belongs to AWS. You still run the security of what you build in it, and AWS publishes places to learn how.

**AWS Knowledge Center** is a collection of answers to questions from AWS customers.

**AWS Security Blog** publishes AWS security articles. The posts on its front page when this was read covered topics such as GuardDuty threat detection and AWS IAM Identity Center.

**AWS Security Center** is the name the exam guide uses. AWS's own security home page is titled AWS Cloud Security and links to Security Services, Use Cases, Compliance, Data Protection, the Blog, Partners and Resources.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Knowledge Center** — a collection of answers to questions from AWS customers.
- **AWS Security Blog** — AWS's blog for security articles.
- **AWS Security Center** — the exam guide's name for AWS's security information hub; AWS's own home page for it is titled AWS Cloud Security.

Figure 12-1 below groups this chapter's security tools by the job each does. It is one helpful way to sort them, not an official AWS chart. Use it to answer exam-style questions: first decide the job (stop an attack, spot one, dig into one, or check and share safely), then pick the service.

blocks.content:
### Which resource for which question

| You want to... | Go to |
|---|---|
| a how-to answer from AWS to a specific problem | AWS Knowledge Center |
| news and deep dives on security topics | AWS Security Blog |
| the overall security hub, learning material and partner links | AWS Security Center (AWS Cloud Security page) |

items.text: AWS renames pages and services. The exam guide says AWS Security Center. Other AWS pages link to AWS Cloud Security Center. If a question says Security Center, it means AWS's central security information site.

items.term: Learning resources on the security home page
items.text: The AWS Cloud Security page also points to a course called AWS Security Fundamentals and to guidance called AWS Security Reference Architecture, and it says where to report vulnerabilities and suspicious emails.

sections.title: Chapter 14: AI/ML and analytics
sections.note: The AWS services that add artificial intelligence and machine learning to applications, and the services that collect, query and visualize data.

items.term: AI, ML, deep learning and generative AI

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> These four terms are often used as if they meant the same thing. They do not, and the exam expects you to know which one sits inside which.

**Artificial intelligence (AI)** is technology that enables machines to perform human-like problem-solving tasks, from recognizing images to making predictions from data.

**Machine learning (ML)** is a type of AI that performs data analysis tasks without explicit instructions. It processes large quantities of historical data, identifies patterns, and predicts new relationships between previously unknown data. Machine learning is AI, but not all AI is machine learning.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **artificial intelligence** — technology that lets machines do human-like problem solving, such as recognizing images or making predictions.
- **machine learning** — a type of AI that finds patterns in historical data and uses them to predict, without being given step-by-step instructions.
- **deep learning** — a kind of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks, which are loosely inspired by the human brain.
- **generative AI** — a type of AI that creates new content, such as text, images, video or music.
Figure 13-1 below shows how the four terms nest: each inner circle is a more specific kind of the circle around it.

blocks.content:
### The two inner circles

**Deep learning** is an AI method that teaches computers to process data in a way inspired by the human brain. It is a specialized form of machine learning that uses artificial neural networks, and it is good at complex jobs such as image and speech recognition.

**Generative AI** is a type of AI that can create new content and ideas, including conversations, stories, images, videos, and music. It is a subset of AI that generates new content, rather than only labelling or predicting.

Deep generative learning is the basis of modern generative AI and foundation models. Foundation models are large generative AI models trained on a broad spectrum of text and image data. They can perform a wide variety of general tasks, like answering questions, writing essays, and captioning images.

blocks.title: Quick way to remember
blocks.content:
- Is it a machine doing something that looks like human problem solving? That is **AI**.
- Does it learn patterns from data instead of following written rules? That is **machine learning**.
- Does it use layered artificial neural networks? That is **deep learning**.
- Does it produce new text, images or music? That is **generative AI**.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Every AI/ML service in this chapter has two phases: it learns once, then it answers many times. If you can tell the phases apart, the service descriptions become much easier to read.

A **dataset** is a collection of examples. In machine learning, you give an algorithm a dataset of known input and output pairs.

**Training** is the phase where the algorithm studies those examples and works out the relationship between input and output. The result is a **model**: the learned pattern, ready to apply.

**Inference** is the process of an AI model generating outputs from unseen data inputs. After training, the model uses inference to apply what it learned to new data.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **dataset** — a collection of examples that a model learns from.
- **training** — the phase where an algorithm studies a dataset and learns the relationship between inputs and outputs.
- **model** — the result of training: the learned pattern that you apply to new data.
- **inference** — using a trained model to produce an output, such as a prediction, for new data it has not seen.
Figure 13-2 below shows the flow: the dataset feeds training, training produces a model, and inference uses the model on new data to give a prediction.

blocks.title: A tiny worked example
blocks.content:
AWS explains it with numbers. You train an algorithm with these input and output pairs: (2, 10), (5, 19) and (9, 31). The algorithm works out the relationship: output = 3 x input + 4. That learned relationship is the model.

Now you give it a new input, 7, and ask for an output. The model works out 25. That step is inference.

items.term: Why training is the expensive part
items.text: Training needs lots of data and computing power, and you do it occasionally. Inference is what happens each time someone uses the model, so it happens far more often. The two phases are often paid for and scaled separately.
If the data changes, you retrain a new model with the new dataset. Retraining is simply running the training phase again.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Sometimes no ready-made AI service fits, and you need a model trained on your own data. SageMaker AI is where you build, train and run it without managing the machines yourself.

**Amazon SageMaker AI** is a fully managed machine learning service. Data scientists and developers use it to build, train, and deploy ML models into a production-ready hosted environment.

Fully managed means AWS handles the underlying servers. SageMaker AI also provides managed ML algorithms that run against extremely large data in a distributed environment, and it has built-in support for bring-your-own algorithms and frameworks.

Within a few steps you can deploy a model into a secure and scalable environment from the SageMaker AI console. In terms of the previous lesson, SageMaker AI covers training and also the hosting that does inference.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **Amazon SageMaker AI** — a fully managed service for building, training and deploying your own machine learning models.

### A naming trap

On December 3, 2024, Amazon SageMaker was renamed to Amazon SageMaker AI. The name change does not apply to existing features.

On the same date AWS released the next generation of **Amazon SageMaker**, a unified platform for data, analytics and AI. It includes Amazon SageMaker AI, formerly Amazon SageMaker, for building, training and deploying ML and foundation models, plus other capabilities such as Amazon SageMaker Lakehouse. The exam guide's service list says Amazon SageMaker AI.

blocks.title: When to pick it
blocks.content: Choose SageMaker AI when you want to build or train your own model. If the task is common, such as reading text from a scanned document, a ready-made AI service may do the job with no training. Those services are the next lessons.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many AI jobs, such as spotting objects in a photo or reading a scanned form, are common enough that AWS has already trained the model. You just send your data and get the answer back.

A **pre-trained AI service** is an AI service whose model AWS has already trained. You call it through an API and get results, with no machine learning expertise needed.

The two services in this lesson work with pictures. They rely on **computer vision**, the field of AI that enables computers to derive meaningful information from digital images, videos, and other visual inputs.

**Amazon Rekognition** is an image and video analysis service. Its API can analyze image and video files stored in Amazon S3. You can detect objects, text, and unsafe content, and compare faces.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **pre-trained AI service** — a ready-made AI service with a model AWS has already trained; you use it through an API.
- **Amazon Rekognition** — a service that analyzes images and videos, for example to detect objects, text and unsafe content, or compare faces.
- **Amazon Textract** — a service that reads text, forms and tables out of documents.
- **computer vision** — the field of AI that lets computers get information from images and videos.
- **OCR** — optical character recognition: turning an image of text into text a computer can search and edit.

**Amazon Textract** adds document text detection and analysis to your applications. It can detect typed and handwritten text, and it can extract text, forms and tables from documents. It also has operations for invoices and receipts, and for ID documents such as passports and drivers licenses.

What Textract does is **OCR** (optical character recognition): the process that converts an image of text into a machine-readable text format. A scanned receipt is only an image. After OCR, its contents are text data that you can search and count.

blocks.title: Which one for which job?
blocks.content:
| The input is... | Use |
|---|---|
| a photo or video: find objects, faces or unsafe content | Amazon Rekognition |
| a scanned invoice, receipt or form: pull out the text, fields and tables | Amazon Textract |

Rekognition can also detect text in images, but Textract is built for documents such as forms and tables.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Companies hold huge amounts of written text: reviews, emails, tickets. Two ready-made services can tell you what the text is about and translate it, with no model to train.

**Natural language processing (NLP)** is technology that allows computers to interpret, manipulate, and comprehend human language.

**Amazon Comprehend** uses NLP to extract insights about the content of documents. It develops insights by recognizing the entities, key phrases, language, sentiments, and other common elements in a document.

The insights it can return include entities (names of people, places and items), key phrases, personally identifiable information, the dominant language, sentiment (positive, neutral, negative or mixed), and syntax (the parts of speech of each word). It is a pre-trained AI service, so its model is already trained, and you can also train custom models for classification and entity recognition.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **natural language processing** — technology that lets computers interpret and understand human language.
- **Amazon Comprehend** — a service that finds insights in text, such as entities, key phrases, language and sentiment.
- **Amazon Translate** — a service that translates text between languages using machine learning.

**Amazon Translate** is a text translation service that uses advanced machine learning to provide high-quality translation on demand. You can use it to translate unstructured text documents or to build applications that work in multiple languages.

### Using them together

Translate's documentation lists Comprehend as a partner: translate text first, then extract named entities, sentiment and key phrases from it, for example from social media posts written in many languages.

blocks.title: A small scenario
blocks.content: A shop receives product reviews in several languages. It wants to know whether customers are happy. Comprehend can report each review's sentiment. Translate can turn reviews into one language for the team to read. Neither service needs the shop to train a model.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Voice is data too. Two ready-made services convert between spoken audio and written text, one in each direction.

**Speech to text** means turning spoken audio into written words. **Text to speech** means turning written words into spoken audio.

**Amazon Transcribe** is an automatic speech recognition service that uses machine learning models to convert audio to text. You can use it as a standalone transcription service or to add speech-to-text to any application. You can transcribe media in real time as it is spoken, or transcribe media files located in an Amazon S3 bucket.

**Amazon Polly** is a cloud service that converts text into lifelike speech. It supports multiple languages and a variety of lifelike voices, and you only pay for the text you synthesize.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Transcribe** — a service that turns spoken audio into written text.
- **Amazon Polly** — a service that turns written text into lifelike spoken audio.
- **speech to text** — converting spoken audio into written words.
- **text to speech** — converting written words into spoken audio.

Both are pre-trained AI services, so you call them through an API without training anything.

Common uses for Polly include newsreaders in mobile apps, games, eLearning platforms and accessibility applications for visually impaired people. You can also cache and replay the speech Polly generates at no additional cost.

blocks.title: Two directions, side by side
blocks.content:
| You have... | You want... | Use |
|---|---|---|
| a recording of a call | the words as text | Amazon Transcribe |
| an article as text | an audio version to listen to | Amazon Polly |

The services can work together with Translate: Translate's documentation describes making subtitles in many languages with Transcribe, and speaking translated content with Polly.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Customers ask the same questions all day. A chatbot can answer them at any hour. Lex lets you build one without deep learning skills.

A **chatbot** is a program or application that users can converse with using voice or text.

**Amazon Lex** is an AWS service for building conversational interfaces for applications using voice and text. It provides natural language understanding (NLU), which grasps what the user means, and automatic speech recognition (ASR), which turns speech into text.

With Lex, no deep learning expertise is necessary. To create a chatbot, you specify the basic conversation flow in the console, and Lex manages the dialog and dynamically adjusts the responses in the conversation.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Lex** — a service for building chatbots that talk with users by voice or text.
- **chatbot** — a program that users can have a conversation with by voice or text.

You can build, test and publish a text or voice chatbot in the Lex console, then add it to mobile devices, web applications and chat platforms. Lex integrates with AWS Lambda, so a bot can run your own code to fulfil a request.

AWS's own pages call the current version Amazon Lex V2. The exam guide just says Amazon Lex.

blocks.title: Lex compared with Transcribe and Polly
blocks.content: Lex understands the intent behind what a user says or types and carries on a conversation. Transcribe only converts audio to text, and Polly only turns text into speech. A voice chatbot needs the whole loop: hear, understand, answer. Lex provides speech recognition and language understanding together, so you do not have to assemble them yourself.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Generative AI is most useful when it sits where you already work. Amazon Q is AWS's family of generative-AI assistants.

An **AI assistant** is software you talk to in everyday language that answers questions and helps with tasks. **Amazon Q** is AWS's name for assistants powered by generative AI. Two members matter here.

**Amazon Q Developer** is a generative AI powered conversational assistant that can help you understand, build, extend, and operate AWS applications. You can ask about AWS architecture, your AWS resources, best practices and documentation. In an IDE (the program developers write code in), it can chat about code, give inline code completions, generate new code, and scan your code for security vulnerabilities.

**Amazon Q Business** is a fully managed, generative AI powered assistant that you configure to answer questions, provide summaries, generate content, and complete tasks based on your enterprise data.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Q** — AWS's family of generative AI powered assistants.
- **AI assistant** — software you talk to in everyday language that answers questions and helps with tasks.

Q Business gives permissions-aware responses from enterprise data sources with citations, for use cases such as IT and HR help desks. That means each person sees answers only from the data they are allowed to see.

### Two notices to know (read 21-10-26)

- AWS will end support for the Amazon Q Developer IDE plugins on April 30, 2027, and points to Kiro, an AWS agentic development environment, for similar capabilities.
- Amazon Q Business is no longer open to new customers from July 31, 2026, and AWS points to Amazon Quick, an AWS AI assistant for work (covered at the end of this chapter), for similar capabilities.

AWS keeps changing this area, so check the current AWS pages before relying on details.

blocks.title: Picking between the two
blocks.content:
- You build software on AWS and want help with code, errors and AWS questions: **Amazon Q Developer**.
- You want employees to ask questions about the company's own documents and systems: **Amazon Q Business**.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Every analytics service in the next lessons does one job in a chain. If you know the chain and its vocabulary, you can tell which service fits a question.

**Data analytics** converts raw data into actionable insights. It includes the tools, technologies and processes used to find trends and solve problems using data.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **data analytics** — turning raw data into insights you can act on.
- **batch vs streaming data** — batch data is collected and processed together on a schedule; streaming data flows in continuously and is processed as it arrives.
- **data lake** — a central store that keeps all your data, structured or not, in its original form.
- **data warehouse** — a central store of cleaned, organized data built for reports and analysis.
- **ETL** — extract, transform, load: pulling data out of its sources, cleaning and reshaping it, and loading it into a central store.
Figure 13-3 below shows a simple way to picture the chain: data is brought in, stored, processed, analyzed, and finally shown as charts. This five-step picture is a teaching aid, not AWS's own list.

blocks.content:
### Batch versus streaming

**Batch processing** is the method computers use to periodically complete high-volume, repetitive data jobs. An online shop might collect all the day's orders and hand them over in one batch at the end of the day.

**Streaming data** is data emitted at high volume in a continuous, incremental manner, often requiring low-latency processing. An example is the readings of sensors on a factory floor.

The difference is when you work with the data: on a schedule in groups, or constantly as it arrives.

### Lake versus warehouse

| | Data lake | Data warehouse |
|---|---|---|
| Holds | all structured and unstructured data, as it is | data organized into tables with a structure |
| Structure | none needed up front | defined in advance |
| Built for | many kinds of analytics, from dashboards to machine learning | reports and fast SQL queries |

A **data lake** is a centralized repository that allows you to store all your structured and unstructured data at any scale. You can store your data as-is, without having to first structure the data.

A **data warehouse** is a central repository of information that can be analyzed to make more informed decisions. Data flows into it from transactional systems, relational databases, and other sources, typically on a regular cadence. Using a separate warehouse keeps analytics processing away from transactional databases, which improves the performance of both systems.

### ETL

**ETL** (extract, transform, load) is the process of combining data from multiple sources into a large, central repository. It uses a set of business rules to clean and organize raw data and prepare it for storage, data analytics, and machine learning.

items.term: ELT, the same steps in another order
items.text: In ELT (extract, load, transform) the data is first loaded into storage and then transformed into the required format. AWS describes ETL and ELT as the two ways data collection can follow.

AWS's own explanation of big data analytics lists five steps: data collection, data storage, data processing, data cleansing and data analysis. The figure above is a simplified version that ends with showing the results.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Your data already sits in files in S3. Athena lets you ask questions of it in SQL right where it is, without loading it into a database first.

**Amazon Athena** is an interactive query service that makes it easy to analyze data directly in Amazon S3 using standard SQL. You point Athena at your data in S3 and begin running ad hoc queries, one-off questions, and get results in seconds.

Athena is **serverless**: there is no infrastructure to set up or manage, and you pay only for the queries you run. Athena scales automatically, running queries in parallel, so results are fast even with large datasets and complex queries.

That is why Athena is a natural partner for a data lake built on S3.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Athena** — a service that lets you query data stored in Amazon S3 using standard SQL, with no servers to manage.
- **serverless query** — running a query without setting up or managing any servers, paying only for the queries you run.

### A small scenario

An analyst has years of log files sitting in S3 and needs one answer: how many errors happened last Tuesday? Without Athena, she might build a database and load the files into it first. With Athena she points the service at the S3 data and writes an SQL question. She pays for that query and nothing sits idle afterwards.

Athena can also run Apache Spark applications (Spark is an open-source tool for processing large amounts of data), again without planning or managing resources.

blocks.title: What Athena is not
blocks.content: Athena does not store your data. The data stays in S3, and Athena reads it when you ask a question. Think of it as a question-asking tool, not a place to keep data.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Raw data is scattered and messy. Glue finds it, describes it, cleans it and moves it, so tools such as Athena can use it.

**AWS Glue** is a serverless data integration service that makes it easy to discover, prepare, move, and integrate data from multiple sources. You can use it for analytics, machine learning, and application development.

A **data catalog** is a central list of what data you have and what shape it has. In Glue it is the AWS Glue Data Catalog, where you manage your data in one place.

Glue crawlers automatically infer schema information and integrate it into the Data Catalog. A **schema** describes a table's structure, such as its columns and the type of data in each.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **AWS Glue** — a serverless service that finds, prepares and moves data so it is ready for analytics.
- **data catalog** — a central list that records what data you have and its structure, so tools can find and query it.

Glue also lets you visually create, run, and monitor ETL pipelines to load data into your data lakes. It is serverless, so there is no infrastructure to manage, and you pay as you go.

You can immediately search and query cataloged data using Amazon Athena.

### A small scenario

Files from several sources land in S3. A Glue crawler scans them and records their columns in the Data Catalog. A Glue job then cleans them. Because the data is now cataloged, an analyst can query it with Athena.

blocks.title: Glue and Athena, side by side
blocks.content:
- **Glue:** prepares and describes the data (ETL and the catalog).
- **Athena:** asks questions of the data.

They are often used together, but each does one job.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some data cannot wait for the nightly job. Click events, sensor readings and logs arrive nonstop and often need an answer within seconds.

**Amazon Kinesis** is the AWS streaming data platform. Its best-known part, Kinesis Data Streams, lets you collect and process large streams of data records in real time. The platform also includes Firehose, Kinesis Video Streams, and Managed Service for Apache Flink.

A **streaming data pipeline** has three parts: stream producers, a stream broker, and stream consumers. Producers are software components in applications and IoT systems (connected sensors and devices) that generate data. The broker ingests the data and gives each piece a sequence number so it can be processed in order. Consumers process and analyze the stream, for example by filtering or aggregating it.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Kinesis** — AWS's family of services for collecting and processing streaming data in real time.
- **streaming data pipeline** — the path streaming data follows: producers send it, a stream holds it in order, and consumers process it.

### What Data Streams is typically used for

- **Log and data feed intake:** producers push system and application logs directly into a stream, and they are available for processing in seconds.
- **Real-time metrics and reporting:** analyze data while it streams in, rather than wait for a batch.
- **Real-time analytics:** for example, processing website clickstreams, the trail of clicks users make on a site, as they happen.

The data types can include IT infrastructure logs, application logs, social media, market data feeds, and web clickstream data.

blocks.title: Streaming versus batch, again
blocks.content: Use a streaming service when the data keeps arriving and the answer is needed quickly. Use batch jobs when a delay is fine and the data can be collected first.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Business reports ask big questions over years of data. A data warehouse is built for exactly that, and Redshift is the AWS one.

**Amazon Redshift** is a fully managed, petabyte-scale data warehouse service in the cloud. A petabyte is 1,000,000 gigabytes, so petabyte-scale means it is built for very large amounts of data.

You load data and start querying right away in the Amazon Redshift query editor v2 or in your favorite business intelligence (BI) tool (software that turns data into charts and reports), using SQL. The same SQL-based tools and BI applications you already use can work with it.

**Amazon Redshift Serverless** lets you access and analyze data without all of the configuration of a provisioned data warehouse. Resources are automatically provisioned and capacity is scaled for you, and you do not incur charges when the data warehouse is idle.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content: - **Amazon Redshift** — AWS's fully managed data warehouse service for running fast SQL analytics on very large amounts of data.

### Why not just use the application's database?

A relational database is tuned to run an application. A warehouse is tuned to answer large analytical questions. Keeping the two apart improves the performance of both systems.

### Redshift or Athena?

| | Amazon Athena | Amazon Redshift |
|---|---|---|
| Where the data is | in S3, where it already sits | in the warehouse |
| Typical use | a quick one-off SQL question | repeated reports and dashboards on organized data |

A warehouse typically receives data on a regular cadence from transactional systems and other sources, so it holds data prepared for analysis.

blocks.title: Two ways to run it
blocks.content: You can use Redshift Serverless, or you can manage resources yourself by creating provisioned clusters (groups of servers that you size yourself). The serverless option removes the configuration work.

items.term: Amazon EMR and Amazon OpenSearch Service

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Two jobs do not fit a simple SQL query: crunching enormous datasets with open-source tools, and searching through huge piles of logs. These two services handle them.

**Big data processing** means processing very large sets of data, typically measured in terabytes or petabytes.

**Amazon EMR** is a managed cluster platform that simplifies running big data frameworks, such as Apache Hadoop and Apache Spark, on AWS to process and analyze vast amounts of data. A cluster is a group of servers working together. Amazon EMR was previously called Amazon Elastic MapReduce.

EMR can also move large amounts of data into and out of other AWS data stores and databases, such as Amazon S3 and Amazon DynamoDB. Amazon S3 is one place it can read from and write to.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon EMR** — a managed service for running big data tools such as Apache Spark and Hadoop to process very large datasets.
- **Amazon OpenSearch Service** — a managed service for running OpenSearch, a search and analytics engine.
- **big data processing** — processing very large sets of data, typically terabytes or petabytes.
- **search and log analytics** — finding things in large amounts of text records, such as logs, and analyzing them.

**Amazon OpenSearch Service** is a managed service that makes it easy to deploy, operate, and scale OpenSearch clusters in the AWS Cloud. OpenSearch is a fully open-source search and analytics engine for use cases such as log analytics, real-time application monitoring, and clickstream analysis.

**Search and log analytics** means that you search through logs and similar text records and analyze them, for example to find which servers produced an error.

The service provisions all the resources for your cluster and launches it. It also automatically detects and replaces failed nodes. Each EC2 instance in the cluster acts as one node. You can load data from Amazon S3, Amazon Kinesis, and Amazon DynamoDB.

blocks.title: Which one?
blocks.content:
- Process a huge dataset with Spark or Hadoop: **Amazon EMR**.
- Search and analyze logs or text records: **Amazon OpenSearch Service**.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Numbers in tables are hard to read. A dashboard turns them into charts that decision makers can understand at a glance.

A **dashboard** is one screen that brings together charts and key numbers about your data, so people can read the state of the business quickly.

**Amazon Quick Sight** is the AWS service for interactive data visualization and business intelligence (BI). You connect it to data sources, build dashboards, and can embed analytics in your own applications.

Quick Sight is the last step of the data analytics pipeline from earlier in this chapter: after data has been stored, processed and queried, Quick Sight shows the results as charts.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
- **Amazon Quick Sight** — an AWS service for building interactive charts and dashboards from your data.
- **dashboard** — a single screen of charts and key numbers that summarizes data.

### A naming trap

Amazon Quick Sight used to be called Amazon QuickSight. AWS now has a wider product named **Amazon Quick**, an AI-powered service for automating tasks, analyzing data, building web applications, and conducting research.

AWS says Amazon Quick evolved from Amazon QuickSight. QuickSight continues as Amazon Quick Sight, a feature within Quick, and all existing QuickSight APIs, SDKs, and integrations continue to work without changes.

The exam guide lists Amazon Quick Sight, so when a question asks about charts and dashboards, that is the service.

blocks.title: What else is in Amazon Quick
blocks.content: Besides Quick Sight, Amazon Quick includes Quick Flows (AI-powered workflows), Quick Automate (business process automation), Quick Index (connects your documents so AI answers are grounded in them), Quick Research (cited research reports) and Apps in Amazon Quick (web apps built by describing what you need). For the exam, remember Quick Sight for dashboards.

sections.title: Chapter 15: Other in-scope service categories
sections.note: Messaging, workflows, APIs, business apps, developer tools, virtual desktops, app building and IoT services that the exam asks you to recognise and choose between.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> When one part of an application calls another directly, a slow or broken part drags the whole app down.
>
> A queue lets the parts work at their own pace.

**Decoupling** means building an application so that its parts depend on each other as little as possible. If one part is slow, busy or down, the other parts keep working.

The AWS service for this job is **Amazon SQS** (Amazon Simple Queue Service).

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **decoupling**: building an application so its parts depend on each other as little as possible.
- **message queue**: a waiting line that holds messages until a program is ready to handle them.
- **Amazon SQS**: the AWS service that runs a message queue for you.
- **message**: a small piece of data that describes a job, for example "order 1042 was placed".
- **producer and consumer**: a producer is a program that sends messages; a consumer is a program that receives them.

Amazon SQS is a hosted queue that lets you integrate and decouple distributed software systems and components. *Hosted* means AWS runs the queue servers for you.

A producer sends a message to the queue. A consumer asks the queue for messages when it is ready, handles one, and then deletes it. Figure 14-1 below shows the three parts.

blocks.title: Worked example: a shop during a sale
blocks.content:
A web shop takes orders much faster than its billing program can charge cards. Without a queue, the shop has to wait for billing, and orders fail when billing is slow.

With a queue, the shop drops each order into the queue and moves on. Billing takes orders out at its own speed. If billing is down for a while, the orders wait in the queue.

blocks.title: How a message is kept safe
blocks.content: SQS stores each message on multiple servers. While a consumer is working on a message, the message stays in the queue but is hidden from other consumers for a set time called the visibility timeout. The consumer deletes the message when it is done, so it is not processed twice. A message nobody deletes is removed after the retention period, which is 4 days by default and can be set from 60 seconds up to 14 days.

blocks.title: Standard and FIFO queues
blocks.content: Standard queues support at-least-once delivery, which means a message can occasionally arrive more than once. FIFO (first in, first out) queues support exactly-once processing, and suit work where order and not losing messages matter.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A queue gives each message to one consumer. Sometimes many parties must hear about the same event at once.
>
> SNS sends one message to everyone who signed up for it.

**Publish/subscribe** (pub/sub) is a messaging style where a sender does not address its messages to anyone in particular. It publishes them to a channel, and anyone who has subscribed to that channel gets a copy.

**Amazon SNS** (Amazon Simple Notification Service) is the AWS service that does this.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **publish/subscribe**: a style where a sender publishes to a channel and every subscriber of that channel gets a copy.
- **Amazon SNS**: the AWS service for publish/subscribe messaging and notifications.
- **topic**: the channel in SNS that publishers send to and subscribers listen to.
- **notification**: a short message that tells a person or a program that something happened, such as an alarm or an order confirmation.

Amazon SNS is a fully managed service that delivers messages from publishers to subscribers. Publishers send messages to a topic, which is a logical access point and communication channel.

Subscribers can be an Amazon SQS queue, a Lambda function, an HTTP(S) endpoint, an email address, a mobile push notification or a mobile text message (SMS). SNS can send messages between applications and also straight to people.

Each subscriber gets its own copy of the message. Figure 14-2 below shows one message fanning out.

blocks.title: Worked example: a new order
blocks.content:
An application publishes one message to an SNS topic whenever an order is placed. One SQS queue subscribed to the topic feeds the program that fulfils the order. Another queue feeds a program that analyses all orders. Both receive identical copies, so the publisher sends once and does not need to know who is listening.

This pattern, one message copied to many subscribers, is called fanout.

items.text: A queue and a topic are often used together. If a subscriber is offline, a message sent straight to it could be missed. When the subscriber is an SQS queue, the message waits in the queue until the subscriber is ready.
SNS can send an alert by email or text message when something crosses a threshold you chose, for example a metric alarm in Amazon CloudWatch.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> An AWS service or your own app often needs to react the moment something happens, such as a file arriving or an order being placed.
>
> EventBridge connects the thing that happened to the code that should respond.

An **event** is a record that something happened. An **event bus** is a router that receives events and sends each one on to the right place. **Amazon EventBridge** is the serverless AWS service built around event buses.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **event bus**: a router that receives events and delivers them to zero or more targets.
- **Amazon EventBridge**: the serverless AWS service that uses events to connect application components.
- **choosing among SQS, SNS and EventBridge**: picking the messaging service whose style matches the job; Figure 14-3 below gives the rule of thumb.

EventBridge uses events to connect application components together. Events can come from your own applications, from AWS services and from third-party software, and the bus routes them to consumer applications.  Each place an event is delivered to is called a target.

Event buses suit routing events from many sources to many targets. EventBridge also has pipes for one-to-one links and a scheduler that runs tasks on a schedule. Figure 14-3 below compares the three messaging services.

blocks.title: Choosing: one question each
blocks.content:
**Must each job be handled by one worker, at the worker's pace?** Use SQS.

**Must many parties be told about the same message, or must people get an alert?** Use SNS.

**Must something react to events from AWS services or your applications, with rules deciding where each event goes?** Use EventBridge.

They differ in style: SQS is a waiting line, SNS is a broadcast channel, and EventBridge is a rule-based router.

items.text: All three keep parts of an application loosely linked. They can also be combined: SNS can copy one message into several SQS queues, as the SNS lesson showed.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Real jobs have many steps in a set order, with decisions and retries. Writing that order inside one program gets messy.
>
> Step Functions lets you draw the steps and runs them for you.

**Workflow orchestration** means coordinating several steps, in the right order, so a bigger job gets done. A good picture is a recipe: do this, then that, and if the dough is too dry, do something else.

**AWS Step Functions** is the AWS service that runs such workflows.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **workflow orchestration**: coordinating many steps of a job, in order, with decisions, so the whole job completes.
- **AWS Step Functions**: the AWS service that lets you build and run workflows made of steps.

With Step Functions you create workflows, also called state machines, to build distributed applications, automate processes and orchestrate microservices (applications built from many small, separate services). Each step in a workflow is called a *state*. A Task state does a unit of work, such as calling a Lambda function or another AWS service. A running copy of a workflow is an *execution*.

A Choice state adds conditional logic, which means it looks at the data and sends the workflow down one path or another. Figure 14-4 below shows a small workflow with a branch.
