blocks.title: Worked example: Lambda steps without Step Functions
blocks.content: Suppose three Lambda functions must run in order: check the order, charge the card, send the receipt. You could make each function call the next, but then every function has to know about the others, and the order is hidden inside code. In Step Functions the order is the workflow, and the console lets you visualize it and see the state of each step.

blocks.title: Standard and Express workflows
blocks.content: Standard workflows suit long-running, auditable work: they run each step exactly once and can run for up to one year. Express workflows suit high-event-rate work such as streaming data processing and IoT (connected-device) data ingestion: a step can run more than once, and a workflow can run for up to five minutes.

blocks.title: Working with other services
blocks.content: Step Functions can call AWS services such as Lambda to perform tasks, and it can control services such as AWS Glue to build extract, transform and load workflows.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Your code in Lambda or on a server is not much use if outside programs have no safe, managed way to reach it.
>
> API Gateway is the front door that receives those requests.

**Amazon API Gateway** is an AWS service for creating, publishing, maintaining, monitoring and securing APIs at any scale. An API, as you learned, is the agreed way one program asks another for something. API Gateway gives your backend a public address and handles the traffic coming to it.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **Amazon API Gateway**: the AWS service that builds and runs the front door for your APIs.
- **API endpoint**: the web address (hostname) of an API that you deployed in API Gateway to a specific Region.

API Gateway acts as a front door for applications to reach data, business logic or functions in your backend. The backend can be workloads on Amazon EC2, code running on AWS Lambda or any web application. Together with Lambda, it forms the app-facing part of the AWS serverless infrastructure.

It handles tasks such as traffic management, authorization and access control, and monitoring. It can create REST, HTTP and WebSocket APIs. REST and HTTP APIs are stateless (each request stands alone, with nothing remembered between requests), and WebSocket APIs keep a two-way connection open.

blocks.title: Worked example: a mobile app and Lambda
blocks.content: A mobile app needs to ask for a customer's order list. The app sends a request to the API endpoint. API Gateway checks who is asking, then passes the request to a Lambda function that looks up the orders. The function's answer goes back through API Gateway to the app. The app never talks to Lambda directly.

blocks.title: What the endpoint looks like
blocks.content: An API endpoint is a hostname for an API that is deployed to a specific Region. API Gateway can also use Amazon CloudFront to make an API faster to reach for far-away clients; that is called an edge-optimized endpoint.

blocks.title: Ways to secure it
blocks.content: API Gateway can check callers with AWS Identity and Access Management policies, Lambda authorizer functions (your own function that decides who may call) or Amazon Cognito user pools.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A company that talks to customers by phone and chat needs agents, queues and routing. Building that from scratch is a large project.
>
> Amazon Connect gives you a ready contact center as a service.

A **contact center** is the team and the system a company uses to talk with its customers, for example by phone, chat or text message. **Amazon Connect** is the AWS service that provides a cloud contact center, so you use a cloud service instead of running a phone system yourself.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **Amazon Connect**: the AWS cloud contact center service. AWS's current guide names the product Amazon Connect Customer; the exam guide uses the name Amazon Connect.
- **contact center**: the people and the system a business uses to talk with its customers.

Amazon Connect Customer is the current name for the product previously called Amazon Connect. It helps you build and manage customer communication experiences: connect customers to agents, enable intelligent routing and track performance in real time.

You begin by creating an instance, which is a virtual contact center. You then claim a phone number, set up channels, add agents and set up routing. With Amazon Connect you pay only for what you use.

blocks.title: Who uses it
blocks.content: **Customers** contact the center. **Agents** help them. **Managers** watch team numbers. **Administrators** set up phone numbers, queues and routing. All four roles use the same cloud service.

items.text: When a question describes a business that needs a cloud contact center with voice or chat, agents and routing, the matching service is Amazon Connect.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Applications often must send email: order confirmations, newsletters, password resets. Running your own mail servers is hard.
>
> SES lets an application send and receive email at scale.

**Amazon SES** (Amazon Simple Email Service) is an email platform that makes it easy and cost-effective to send and receive email using your own email addresses and domains.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **Amazon SES**: the AWS service for sending and receiving email from your applications and your own domain.

With SES you can send marketing emails such as special offers, transactional emails such as order confirmations, and other correspondence such as newsletters. You can also receive email, for example to build autoresponders, unsubscribe systems or tools that turn incoming emails into customer support tickets.

Without SES you must handle email server management, network configuration and IP address reputation yourself. With SES you pay based on the volume of emails sent and received.

blocks.title: SES or SNS?
blocks.content: Both can send an email, but they do different jobs. **SNS** is a notification and fanout service: it tells people and programs that something happened, and email is one of its delivery types. **SES** is a full email service for sending and receiving email under your own address and domain, including marketing and transactional mail. If the question is about newsletters or order confirmation emails from your own domain, think SES. If it is about alerts to a topic's subscribers, think SNS.

items.text: An application on Amazon EC2 can send mail through SES. You can set up Amazon SNS to tell you about emails that bounced, produced a complaint or were delivered. Received email can be stored in Amazon S3 or can trigger a Lambda function.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Releasing software by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. Every change must be built, tested and deployed the same way each time.
>
> These two services automate that routine.

**Continuous integration** is a practice where team members frequently combine their work in one place, and each change is built and verified automatically to catch problems early. **Continuous delivery** goes further and automates the whole release process up to production. Together they are often called **continuous integration and delivery**.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **continuous integration and delivery**: automatically building, testing and releasing every software change.
- **AWS CodeBuild**: a managed service that compiles your code, runs tests and produces files ready to deploy.
- **AWS CodePipeline**: a managed service that models, visualizes and automates the steps needed to release your software.

AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed build service. It compiles your source code, runs unit tests and produces artifacts that are ready to deploy, so you do not need to provision, manage and scale your own build servers. You pay only for the build minutes you use.

AWS CodePipeline is a continuous delivery service. A pipeline is a workflow that describes how code changes go through a release process, and you can add CodeBuild as a build or test action in it. Figure 14-5 below shows the idea.

blocks.title: Worked example: a small team
blocks.content: A developer saves a change. The pipeline notices it, CodeBuild builds the code and runs the tests, and if everything passes the change moves on to deployment. Nobody has to remember the steps or keep a build server running.

items.term: CodeBuild and CodePipeline are different jobs
items.text: CodeBuild does work: it builds and tests. CodePipeline organizes work: it decides what runs in what order and moves results between stages. In continuous delivery a person, an automated test or a business rule decides when the final push to production happens.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> When a request crosses many services and ends up slow or failing, logs from one service do not show where the time went.
>
> X-Ray follows a request through the whole path.

**Distributed tracing** means following one request as it travels through the different parts of an application, and recording what happened at each part. **AWS X-Ray** is the AWS service that collects and displays this data.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **distributed tracing**: following a single request through all the parts of an application that handle it.
- **AWS X-Ray**: the AWS service that collects data about requests your application serves and shows where problems and delays are.

X-Ray collects data about requests that your application serves and gives you tools to view, filter and gain insights into that data. For a traced request you can see not only the request and response, but also the calls your application makes to downstream AWS resources, microservices, databases and web APIs.

From this data X-Ray builds a trace map. The map shows the client, your front-end service and the backend services it calls, so you can spot bottlenecks and latency spikes. Some AWS services, such as AWS Lambda and API Gateway, work with X-Ray.

blocks.title: Worked example: a slow checkout
blocks.content: Customers say checkout feels slow. The request goes from the app through an API, a Lambda function and a database. Amazon CloudWatch tells you that something is slow overall. The X-Ray trace map shows which of those calls takes the most time, so you know where to look.

blocks.title: X-Ray and CloudWatch
blocks.content: Amazon CloudWatch watches numbers and logs from your resources. X-Ray follows individual requests across parts. They answer different questions: is something wrong, and where in the path is the delay.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Employees need a desktop or an application on whatever device they have, without IT shipping and patching hardware.
>
> These services run the desktop or app in AWS and show it on the user's screen.

A **virtual desktop** is a full desktop, with its operating system, that runs on a virtual machine in the cloud and appears on the user's own device. **Application streaming** sends just one application's screen to the user instead of a whole desktop.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **virtual desktop**: a full desktop that runs in the cloud and is shown on the user's own device.
- **application streaming**: running an application in the cloud and sending its screen to the user.
- **Amazon WorkSpaces**: the AWS service that provides virtual, cloud-based desktops.
- **Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser**: a hosted browser service for safely reaching private websites and web apps; it was previously named Amazon WorkSpaces Web.
- **Amazon AppStream 2.0**: the exam guide's name for the AWS application streaming service; AWS's current guide page for it is titled Amazon WorkSpaces Applications.

**Amazon WorkSpaces** lets you provision virtual, cloud-based desktops for your users. They can run Microsoft Windows, Ubuntu Linux, Rocky Linux or Red Hat Enterprise Linux. WorkSpaces Personal gives persistent desktops (they keep the user's files and settings between sign-ins) for one user each, like a physical computer assigned to a person. WorkSpaces Pools give non-persistent desktops (a fresh desktop at each sign-in). AWS states that WorkSpaces Pools no longer accepts new customers from July 31, 2026, and that its support ends on December 31, 2027.

**Amazon AppStream 2.0** is a fully managed application streaming service. Your applications run on AWS compute resources and are streamed to your users' devices. You maintain a single version of each application.

blocks.title: Amazon WorkSpaces Secure Browser
blocks.content:
Secure Browser is a fully managed hosted browser service used to securely access private websites and software-as-a-service web applications. Web content is streamed to the user's own browser while the actual browser runs isolated in AWS, and no sensitive company data is sent to the local machine.

Check availability before relying on it: AWS states that it will no longer be open to new customers starting October 29, 2026, and that existing customers can continue to use it.

blocks.title: Which one?
blocks.content:
**A whole desktop for an employee:** WorkSpaces.

**Just one desktop application for many users, with one copy to maintain:** AppStream 2.0.

**Safe access to web apps and private websites from any browser:** WorkSpaces Secure Browser.

items.text: AWS renames services from time to time. The exam guide still uses AppStream 2.0 while the current AWS guide page for the same service is titled Amazon WorkSpaces Applications. If a question or a page uses either name, treat them as the same service.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A frontend developer wants a web or mobile app online with login, data and storage, without learning every AWS service first.
>
> Amplify packages those pieces for frontend developers.

**Frontend web and mobile development** means building the part of an app that people see and touch: the website in a browser or the app on a phone. **AWS Amplify** is a set of AWS tools for building and hosting such apps.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **frontend web and mobile development**: building the part of an app that users see and use, in a browser or on a phone.
- **AWS Amplify**: AWS tools to host web apps and to add backend features such as login, data and storage.

Amplify Hosting provides a Git-based workflow for hosting full-stack serverless web applications with continuous deployment. It deploys your app to the AWS global content delivery network. Git is a tool that records every change to code, and continuous deployment means each approved change goes live automatically.

Amplify also helps you add backend features. AWS lists Data (secure real-time APIs backed by AWS databases), Auth (authentication flows and control of access), Storage and Functions. You describe them in TypeScript, and Amplify sets up the right cloud resources.

blocks.title: Worked example: a new web app
blocks.content: A developer keeps a React web app (React is a popular toolkit for building web pages) in a Git repository. They connect the repository to Amplify Hosting. Each time they push a change, Amplify deploys it. Later they add sign-in with Amplify's Auth feature and a place to keep user files with Storage. The same backend can serve a web app and a mobile app.

blocks.title: Features around hosting
blocks.content: Amplify Hosting lists feature branches, custom domains, pull request previews and atomic deployments. Atomic deployments mean a site is updated only after the entire deployment finishes.

blocks.title: Frameworks it supports
blocks.content: Amplify Hosting supports single-page application frameworks such as React, Angular and Vue.js, server-side rendering frameworks such as Next.js and Nuxt, and static site generators.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Sensors, meters and machines produce data, but they are not computers in the usual sense. They need a safe way to talk to the cloud.
>
> IoT Core is that connection point.

The **Internet of Things** (IoT) is the idea of ordinary objects, such as sensors, meters and appliances, connected to a network so they can send and receive data. An **IoT device** is one such object. **AWS IoT Core** is the AWS service that connects IoT devices to AWS.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **Internet of Things**: ordinary objects with network connections that send and receive data.
- **IoT device**: one connected object, such as a sensor or a smart meter.
- **AWS IoT Core**: the AWS service that connects IoT devices to other devices and AWS services.

AWS IoT provides the cloud services that connect your IoT devices to other devices and to AWS cloud services. AWS IoT Core includes a device gateway and a message broker, which connect and process messages between your devices and the cloud. The device gateway is the entry point for devices, and the message broker passes each message on to whoever subscribed to it.

Devices can publish and subscribe to messages using the MQTT protocol, a light message format for small devices. IoT Core can also be used with HTTPS and LoRaWAN (a long-range, low-power wireless network for small devices). IoT Core's management tools include jobs, rules and device defender features for managing devices in the field.

blocks.title: Worked example: a temperature sensor
blocks.content: A cold-storage room has a temperature sensor. The sensor sends a reading to IoT Core every few minutes. A rule passes each reading on to a Lambda function that stores it and, if the room is too warm, triggers an alert. AWS IoT Core is the part that safely receives readings from many sensors.

items.text: The IoT Core message broker works with the publish/subscribe idea from the SNS lesson: devices publish messages and others subscribe to them.

sections.title: Chapter 16: Migration and the Cloud Adoption Framework
sections.note: Why organizations move to AWS, how the AWS Cloud Adoption Framework guides them, the phases and seven strategies of a migration, and the AWS tools that help.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Before choosing how to move to the cloud, you need to know why. The reasons decide which route is worth the effort.
>
> This lesson links the cloud benefits you already know to a real move.

**Migration** to AWS is the process of moving applications and data from one location, usually your own on-premises environment or another cloud provider, into the AWS Cloud. The **benefits of migrating** are the reasons an organization gives for making that move.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **benefits of migrating**: the business reasons for moving applications and data to AWS, such as lower spending, faster delivery and better security.

AWS calls these reasons *migration drivers*. Typical drivers are:

- reducing up-front spending on hardware
- decreasing ongoing cost
- improving scalability and elasticity
- improving time-to-market, meaning how fast a new idea reaches customers
- improving security and compliance

Each driver connects to a benefit of the cloud you already know. Elasticity is the ability to grow and shrink with demand, and agility is the ability to try and ship things quickly.

blocks.title: Worked example: an ageing server room
blocks.content: A company runs its applications in its own server room. The hardware is old, and during busy weeks the servers are overloaded. Buying more takes months. The company's drivers are scalability and elasticity (add capacity when needed), time-to-market (stop waiting for hardware) and decreasing ongoing cost (stop running its own room). Those drivers, written down at the start, tell the team what a good migration looks like.

blocks.title: Write the goal down first
blocks.content: AWS suggests identifying migration key performance indicators at the start, after you set migration goals. These are measurements that show whether the goals were met, so the project can be judged later.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A move to the cloud fails more often because of people and process than because of technology.
>
> The Cloud Adoption Framework is AWS's checklist of what an organization must get ready, beyond the servers.

The **AWS Cloud Adoption Framework** (AWS CAF) uses AWS experience and best practices to help you digitally transform and accelerate business outcomes through innovative use of AWS. You can use it to identify and prioritize opportunities, evaluate and improve your cloud readiness, and keep updating your roadmap.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **AWS Cloud Adoption Framework**: AWS's guidance on the organizational abilities (capabilities) a company needs for a successful move to the cloud.
- **CAF perspective**: one of the six areas of the framework, each owned by a related group of stakeholders.

AWS CAF groups its capabilities in six perspectives: Business, People, Governance, Platform, Security and Operations. Business, People and Governance focus on the organization. Platform, Security and Operations cover the technical side.

Each perspective has its own stakeholders. For example, the Security perspective is of most interest to security officers, auditors and security engineers. Figure 15-1 below shows the six perspectives around one business goal.

blocks.caption: The six CAF perspectives, three about the organization (green) and three about the technology (blue).

blocks.title: What each perspective is for
blocks.content:
**Business:** helps ensure that cloud investments accelerate your business outcomes.

**People:** a bridge between technology and business, with a focus on culture, organizational structure, leadership and workforce.

**Governance:** orchestrate cloud initiatives while maximizing benefits and minimizing transformation-related risks.

**Platform:** build an enterprise-grade, scalable, hybrid cloud platform, modernize existing workloads and implement new cloud-native solutions (built from the start to use cloud services).

**Security:** achieve the confidentiality, integrity and availability of your data and cloud workloads.

**Operations:** ensure that cloud services are delivered at a level that meets the needs of your business.

blocks.title: CAF is not the Well-Architected Framework
blocks.content: They are easy to mix up. The **Well-Architected Framework** helps you understand the pros and cons of the decisions you make when building a workload, using six pillars. The **Cloud Adoption Framework** is about the organization's readiness to move: people, process, governance and platform.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Leaders approve a migration for results they can name. The framework names four.
>
> Knowing them helps you explain why a cloud move is worth doing.

AWS describes four benefits, or value outcomes, that the Cloud Adoption Framework aims to help you reach. The exam guide words them as reduced business risk, improved environmental, social and governance (ESG) performance, increased revenue and increased operational efficiency.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **CAF value outcomes**: the four business results the framework aims for: less risk, better ESG performance, more revenue and better operational efficiency.
- **ESG**: environmental, social and governance: how a company affects the environment and society and how openly it is run.

blocks.title: The four outcomes
blocks.content:
**Reduce business risk:** lower your risk profile through improved reliability, increased performance and enhanced security.

**Improve environmental, social and governance performance:** use insights to improve sustainability and corporate transparency.

**Grow revenue:** create new products and services, reach new customers and enter new market segments.

**Increase operational efficiency:** reduce operating costs, increase productivity and improve employee and customer experience.

A quick way to remember them is risk, ESG, revenue and efficiency. Three of the four are about how well the business runs and how it is seen. Only one, grow revenue, is about making more money.

In a question, match the words in the scenario. A company that wants fewer outages and stronger security is aiming at reduced business risk. A company that wants to launch a new product for new customers is aiming at increased revenue.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.content: A retailer says: "Our site goes down in sales weeks, our staff spend hours on manual updates, and we want to enter new markets." Fewer outages map to reduced business risk, fewer manual updates to increased operational efficiency, and new markets to increased revenue.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Moving hundreds of applications at once is a recipe for chaos. AWS recommends doing it in phases, so each phase builds on the last.
>
> You will see these three phase names in exam questions.

A **migration journey** is the whole path an organization follows from deciding to move, to running its workloads on AWS. AWS recommends a three-phase process, and each **migration phase** has a different purpose.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **migration journey**: the whole path from deciding to move to running on AWS.
- **migration phases**: the three stages AWS recommends: assess, mobilize, and migrate and modernize.
- **landing zone**: the baseline cloud environment you prepare before moving applications into it.

**Assess** is the first phase. You assess your organization's current readiness to operate in the cloud and, most importantly, identify the business outcomes you want and develop the business case for migration.

**Mobilize** is the process of creating a migration plan and refining the business case. You address the gaps found in the assess phase, build your baseline environment (the landing zone), drive operational readiness and develop cloud skills. Think of it as a pilot migration project.

**Migrate and modernize** is the phase where each application is designed, migrated and validated. Figure 15-2 below shows the path.

blocks.caption: The three phases AWS recommends. Each builds on the one before.

blocks.title: Do not mix the two lists of phases
blocks.content: The Cloud Adoption Framework has its own four transformation phases: Envision, Align, Launch and Scale. They describe the broader cloud transformation of the organization. The three-phase process of assess, mobilize, and migrate and modernize describes moving applications. If a question lists assess and mobilize, it is about the migration process.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.content: A company with 200 applications first assesses readiness and builds a business case (assess). It then builds its landing zone, trains staff and moves a few low-risk applications as a pilot (mobilize). Finally it moves the rest, application by application, validating each one (migrate and modernize).

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Not every application should be moved the same way. Each route trades speed against how much you improve along the way.
>
> Three routes keep the application mostly as it is.

A **migration strategy** is the approach used to migrate a workload into the AWS Cloud. AWS lists seven, known as the 7 Rs. This lesson covers the first three, which change the least: **rehost**, **relocate** and **replatform**.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **migration strategy**: the approach used to move one workload to AWS.
- **rehost**: move the application as it is, with no changes. Also called lift and shift.
- **relocate**: move servers or objects to a cloud version of the same platform, or to another VPC, Region or account, without changing the architecture.
- **replatform**: move the application and make some improvements, such as using a managed service. Also called lift, tinker and shift.

**Rehost**, also known as lift and shift, moves an application from the source environment to the AWS Cloud without making any changes to it. For example, you move an application stack from on-premises to AWS. It is fast, but it does not by itself add cloud optimizations. Applications are easier to optimize once they already run in the cloud.

**Relocate** transfers a large number of servers at a time to a cloud version of the platform, or moves instances or objects to a different VPC, AWS Region or AWS account. For example, you can move an Amazon RDS database instance to another VPC or account. It does not impact the overall architecture of your application.

**Replatform** moves the application and adds some optimization to run it efficiently, reduce costs or use cloud capabilities. For example, you might move a Microsoft SQL Server database to Amazon RDS for SQL Server.

blocks.title: Side by side
blocks.content:
| Strategy | What changes | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Rehost | nothing in the application | move the app stack from on-premises to AWS as it is |
| Relocate | where it runs, not the architecture | move an RDS database instance to another VPC or account |
| Replatform | some optimization | move a SQL Server database to Amazon RDS for SQL Server |

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.content: A company has three applications. It rehosts the first, because it must leave its data center quickly and the application should not change. It replatforms the second by moving its database to a managed database service so it no longer has to patch the database. It relocates the third, a set of servers already running on a compatible platform, to the cloud version of that platform.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> The first three strategies keep the application. The other four replace it, redesign it, stop it or leave it alone.
>
> Many exam questions ask you to name the strategy from a short story.

Four more strategies complete the seven. **Repurchase** replaces the application with a different version or product. **Refactor** (also called re-architect) redesigns the application to take advantage of cloud-native features. **Retire** decommissions it. **Retain** keeps it where it is for now.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **repurchase**: replace the application with a different product, often a SaaS one. Also called drop and shop.
- **refactor**: change the application's architecture to use cloud-native features. Also called re-architect.
- **retire**: shut the application down because it is no longer needed.
- **retain**: keep the application in its current environment, perhaps to move later.

**Repurchase** is also known as drop and shop. A common case is moving from a traditional license to SaaS, which means software you use as a service without running its infrastructure. It typically reduces the costs of maintenance, infrastructure and licensing.

**Refactor** is the most complex and costly strategy, because you modernize the application during the migration. It suits cases like a monolith (one big application built as a single block) that slows down delivery, or a legacy application nobody knows how to maintain. It is driven by strong business demand to scale and release faster.

**Retire** is for applications you want to decommission or archive, for instance when there is no business value in keeping them or when they run on unsupported software. **Retain** is for applications you are not ready to move, for example because of data residency rules, dependencies on other applications or hardware with no cloud equivalent. blocks.title: Worked example: four stories
blocks.content:
**"We now use the vendor's hosted version and stopped running our own copy."** Repurchase.

**"Nobody has used this application for months, so we switched it off."** Retire.

**"It needs special factory hardware that has no cloud equivalent, so it stays."** Retain.

**"We rebuilt the monolith as separate cloud-native services."** Refactor.

blocks.title: A note for large moves
blocks.content: For a large migration, refactor is not recommended because it is the most complex and hard to manage across many applications. AWS suggests rehosting, relocating or replatforming first and modernizing afterwards.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A database is changing every second, so you cannot copy it once and switch over without losing recent data.
>
> Replication keeps the new copy up to date until you are ready.

In a **database replication migration strategy** you first copy the existing database to AWS, then keep copying every new change, so the new database stays in sync with the old one until the day you switch applications over to it. AWS Database Migration Service (AWS DMS) is the tool for this.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **database replication migration strategy**: moving a database by copying it to the target and then continuously replicating changes, so source and target stay in sync until cutover.

AWS DMS is a cloud service for migrating relational databases, data warehouses, NoSQL databases and other types of data stores. You can run one-time migrations, or replicate ongoing changes to keep sources and targets in sync.

At a basic level, AWS DMS is a server in the AWS Cloud that runs replication software. You create a source and a target connection, then schedule a task that moves the data. A task can capture ongoing changes while the migration runs, which is called ongoing replication or change data capture.

blocks.title: Worked example: an orders database
blocks.content: A shop's orders database must move to Amazon RDS. The team starts a DMS task that copies the full database, then keeps applying new orders to the copy. The shop keeps running on the old database. When the copy has caught up and has been checked, the team points the application at the new database and stops the old one.

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.content: AWS notes that change data capture does not provide real-time replication: delay varies and has no guaranteed limit. If you move to a different database engine, AWS DMS Schema Conversion or the AWS Schema Conversion Tool can convert the source schemas first. AWS DMS fits the replatform idea too, for example moving a database to a managed service.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You cannot plan a move if you do not know what you have. Three AWS tools cover finding the servers, tracking the move and building the business case.
>
> Exam questions give a need and ask for the tool.

**AWS Application Discovery Service** collects usage and configuration data about your on-premises servers and databases to help plan the move. **AWS Migration Hub** is one place to discover servers, plan migrations and track the status of each application. **Migration Evaluator** builds a business case for moving.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **AWS Application Discovery Service**: a service that collects configuration and usage data about on-premises servers and databases.
- **AWS Migration Hub**: a single place to see your servers, plan a migration and track each application's progress.
- **Migration Evaluator**: a service that creates a data-driven business case for moving to AWS.

**Application Discovery Service** can collect data in three ways: an agentless collector installed through VMware vCenter, an agent installed on each virtual machine or physical server, or a file import. The data can include server settings and how heavily they are used, and it can show network connections between servers to help group them into applications. VMware vCenter is the management tool for VMware virtual machines.

**Migration Hub** lets you view discovered servers, group them into applications and track each application's migration status. It supports status updates from migration tools, including AWS DMS and the server migration service in the next lesson.

blocks.title: Migration Evaluator
blocks.content: Migration Evaluator is a complimentary service for building data-driven business cases for cloud planning and migration. It starts from an inventory of your on-premises servers, models their use, and outputs a business case comparing the current state with several future configurations on AWS. It also gives insight into reusing existing software licensing to reduce costs.

blocks.title: Which tool for which need
blocks.content:
**"Collect data about our servers."** Application Discovery Service.

**"One place to track each application's migration."** Migration Hub.

**"Show me a business case for moving."** Migration Evaluator.

blocks.title: Availability changes
blocks.content: AWS notes that Application Discovery Service and Migration Hub are no longer open to new customers, and points to AWS Transform for similar capabilities. They are still listed in the exam guide's scope. For current availability, check the AWS pages.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> After you plan, something has to move the servers and the data. The right tool depends on what you are moving.
>
> This lesson links each need to a tool you already met.

**AWS Application Migration Service** automates rehosting: it copies physical, virtual and cloud servers to AWS so they run natively. AWS's current guide page for it is titled AWS Transform MGN, where MGN is short for migration. **Data transfer options** are the different ways to move files and data to AWS.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Each term below is new in this lesson.

- **AWS Application Migration Service**: the AWS service that automates lift-and-shift migration of servers to AWS. Its current AWS guide page is titled AWS Transform MGN.
- **data transfer options**: the different ways to move files and data to AWS, each suited to a different need.

AWS Application Migration Service performs continuous block-level replication of your source servers and converts them to launch on AWS. It automates the migration of physical, virtual and cloud servers to AWS with minimal downtime, typically with cutover windows of minutes. The stages are: install the replication agent on the source servers, wait for the first sync, launch and test instances on AWS, and cut over.

AWS describes this service as the primary one recommended for lift-and-shift migrations. That is the rehost strategy from earlier.

blocks.title: Options for moving data
blocks.content:
**Over the internet or a private line.** AWS Direct Connect links your network to AWS through a private connection that bypasses internet providers.

**A gateway that looks like local storage.** AWS Storage Gateway's S3 File Gateway lets your on-premises applications store and retrieve objects in Amazon S3 using file protocols such as NFS and SMB.

**An online copy service.** AWS DataSync is an online data movement service that moves data between on-premises storage and AWS storage services.

**Databases.** AWS DMS, from the previous lesson, migrates databases.

**Physical devices.** AWS has stated that it will no longer offer Snow Family devices to new customers, so older study material that lists them may be out of date.

blocks.title: Where to get help
blocks.content: Three kinds of help come up in migration talk. **AWS Professional Services** is a global team of AWS experts that helps you reach your business outcomes in AWS. **AWS Partners** belong to the AWS Partner Network, a global community of organizations that build solutions and services for customers. **AWS Prescriptive Guidance** is a library of guides, strategies and step-by-step patterns for migration and modernization. A later chapter covers them in more detail.

sections.title: Chapter 17: Cloud economics
sections.note: How fixed and variable cost, on-premises cost, scale, rightsizing, automation and licensing shape what the cloud costs.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Every cost lesson in this book rests on one idea: some bills stay the same whatever you do, and some bills follow your use.
> Knowing which is which explains why the cloud changes the way you pay.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **fixed cost** — a cost that stays the same no matter how much you use, such as a server you bought.
- **variable cost** — a cost that goes up and down with how much you use.
- **capital expense** — spending money up front on things that last for years, such as servers and buildings. Often shortened to capex.
- **operating expense** — spending money on running things, paid as you use them, such as a monthly cloud bill. Often shortened to opex.

A fixed cost does not move with your use, and a variable cost does.

**The question this lesson answers:** why do people say the cloud trades a fixed expense for a variable expense?

On-premises, you buy servers before you know how much capacity you will need. That purchase is a capital expense. You pay it in full whether the servers are busy or idle, so it behaves like a fixed cost.

With pay-as-you-go, the bill follows your use. That is an operating expense, and it behaves like a variable cost.

AWS lists this as the first of its six advantages of cloud computing: instead of having to invest heavily in data centers and servers before you know how you are going to use them, you can pay only when you consume computing resources, and pay only for how much you consume.

Figure 16-1 below shows the two shapes over time. In the figure, the gap between the fixed steps and the use line is capacity that is paid for but unused.

blocks.title: Figure 16-1

blocks.title: A tiny scenario
blocks.content: A small team launches an app. On-premises, they would buy enough servers for the busiest day they can imagine and pay for them all year. In the cloud, they start with a few instances, add more when visitors arrive, and remove them afterwards, paying only for the hours they ran.

items.term: Why the words capex and opex matter
items.text: AWS notes that, in some organizations, the cloud lets you transition from making capital expenditures on IT to operational expenses, which can result in cost savings. It says "in some organizations", not all.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Comparing the price of one server with a cloud bill is not a fair test.
> You can only judge the cloud if you first count everything that running your own data center really costs.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **on-premises cost components** — the separate items that make up the cost of running your own IT: hardware, paid software, facilities, power and cooling, and the people who run it all.
- **total cost of ownership** — TCO for short: the full cost of owning something over its whole life, counting purchase, running costs and staff, not only the price tag.

The true cost of on-premises is much more than the price of the servers.

**The question this lesson answers:** which costs must you count when you compare your own data center with the cloud?

AWS describes a total cost of ownership analysis as looking at your assets: physical machines, servers, labor, storage, paid software and data centers. A fair comparison counts them all:

- **Hardware**: servers, storage and network equipment. This is a capital expense, and AWS advises spreading it over its life, because it is usually replaced on a refresh cycle.
- **Paid software**: the operating system, databases and other products you must pay to use.
- **Facilities**: the data center space and racks.
- **Power and cooling** for the physical servers.
- **People** who manage and maintain compute, storage and network.
- **Unused capacity**: you must plan for spikes in demand, so you buy more than the average need and part of it sits idle.

blocks.title: Hidden costs people forget
blocks.content: AWS also points to indirect costs that are hard to calculate, such as downtime and lost productivity. Skipping them makes on-premises look cheaper than it is. A TCO assessment helps you avoid being surprised by a bill higher than you budgeted when you move to the cloud.

items.term: Capacity planning is itself a cost
items.text: On-premises, you must predict demand and buy equipment ahead of time. AWS says this planning must account for the spikes in the demand curve, which leads to over-provisioning and underused resources. In the cloud you can add or remove resources as the need changes.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A company running its own servers buys at its own small size. AWS buys at a very large size.
> This lesson explains why that difference can lower the price you pay.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **economies of scale** — the effect where doing something in very large volume makes each unit cheaper, because costs are spread over many customers and bought in bulk.

Economies of scale means that a provider serving a huge number of customers can offer lower prices than any one customer could achieve alone.

**The question this lesson answers:** why can AWS offer a lower variable cost than you can get on your own?

AWS puts it this way: because usage from hundreds of thousands of customers is aggregated in the cloud, providers such as AWS can achieve higher economies of scale, which translates into lower pay-as-you-go prices.

Think of buying in bulk. One household buying a single bag of flour pays the shelf price. A wholesaler buying for thousands of shops pays less per bag, and can pass part of that saving on.

blocks.title: What this does and does not promise
blocks.content: It lowers the variable cost per unit of what you use, which is the pay-as-you-go price. It does not mean every bill is automatically small. An AWS enterprise-strategy blog article says your actual savings depend on your success at managing your cloud costs, which is called cost optimization.

items.term: Where else the scale shows up
items.text: The same AWS article lists a second reason costs can be lower: your own data center has unused capacity that you pay for, while in the cloud you can adjust your infrastructure as your needs change. A third reason is that the cost of building AWS's software services is spread over many customers.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> In the cloud you pick the size of what you rent, so you can pick wrongly.
> Too big wastes money every hour, and too small makes the application slow. Rightsizing is how you fix both.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **rightsizing** — choosing the instance type and size that fits what the workload really uses, and changing it when the usage changes.

Rightsizing means matching the size of your resources to what the workload actually needs, no more and no less.

**The question this lesson answers:** how do you stop paying for capacity you do not use?

An instance that is too big is over-provisioned: part of it sits idle and you pay for it anyway, under the variable cost model, every hour it runs. An instance that is too small is under-provisioned: it cannot meet the performance the workload needs.

AWS advises basing the choice on actual utilization, not on an exact copy of the old server. Its example: a physical server with 12 cores and 64 GB of memory that uses only 25 percent of each can be mapped to an instance with 4 vCPUs and 16 GB.

Figure 16-2 below shows the three cases.

blocks.title: Rightsize before you move, and keep checking
blocks.content: AWS warns that many organizations fail to consider rightsizing before migrating their workloads. If you rightsize properly, the resources you need for peak use are there when needed and you do not pay for more than you need. Workloads change over time, so rightsizing is a habit, not a one-off job.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Rightsizing by guesswork is slow and risky.
> This lesson introduces the AWS service that looks at how your resources are really used and suggests a better size.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Compute Optimizer** — an AWS service that analyzes the configuration and utilization metrics of your resources and gives rightsizing recommendations to cut cost and improve performance.

AWS Compute Optimizer reads your resources' configuration and their utilization metrics, then tells you whether each resource is the right size and what to change.

**The question this lesson answers:** how can you find over-provisioned resources without checking each one by hand?

For an EC2 instance, Compute Optimizer gives one of these findings:

- **Under-provisioned**: at least one specification, such as CPU, memory or network, does not meet the workload's needs. Performance may suffer.
- **Over-provisioned**: at least one specification can be sized down and the workload would still be served. It may cost more than needed.
- **Optimized**: every specification meets the need and nothing is oversized.

It also shows graphs of recent utilization and the projected utilization if you accept a recommendation, so you can compare price and performance. You decide what to change.

blocks.title: What it covers, and a limit
blocks.content: It analyzes resources such as EC2 instances, Auto Scaling groups, Lambda functions, EBS volumes and Amazon ECS services on AWS Fargate. It needs some history first: an instance gets no recommendation if it has been running for less than 30 hours or you opted in less than 12 hours ago. Compute Optimizer recommends. It is not a cost tool that charges you or changes things on its own.

items.text: If you opt in the main account of an organization, you can view findings and recommendations across multiple accounts, and across multiple Regions.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Clicking through a console to build the same thing twice invites mistakes, and idle machines keep costing money.
> This lesson lists what automation gives you, in money and in reliability.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **benefits of automation** — the gains from letting software do repeatable work: consistency, fewer manual errors, speed, and resources that scale up and down on their own.

Automation lets software create, change and remove resources for you, and that makes the work faster, repeatable and cheaper to run.

**The question this lesson answers:** what do you gain by automating instead of doing the steps by hand?

AWS lists these benefits of managing infrastructure as code and with automated delivery:

- **Consistency and repeatability**: the same definition builds the same result every time.
- **Fewer errors**: it reduces the risk of manual, error-prone tasks.
- **Reliable, fast changes**: you deploy updates without manual intervention.
- **Cost-efficient scaling**: by watching key metrics and applying predefined scaling policies, Auto Scaling can provision or deprovision resources as needed, which improves performance and cost-efficiency.
- **Quicker response**: AWS notes that infrastructure as code lets a team respond quickly to new business opportunities.

blocks.title: The money link
blocks.content: Without automation, someone must remember to remove capacity after a busy period, and the cost keeps running until they do. With a scaling policy, removal happens by itself. Automation also saves people's time, so they can work on the product instead of on infrastructure configuration.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some software on a server is not free, and who pays for its license changes your bill.
> You will be asked to tell the two main choices apart, and to pick one for a simple case.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **software license** — the vendor's permission to use their software under stated terms. Vendors often charge by core, socket, machine or user.
- **bring your own license** — BYOL: you use a software license you already own on AWS. You are responsible for staying within its terms.
- **license included** — the software license is part of the AWS price, so you do not buy a separate license.

With license included, you pay one AWS price that already covers the software; with bring your own license, you use a license you already own.

**The question this lesson answers:** when you run licensed software on AWS, who supplies the license?

License included: AWS has licensed the software. For example, when you run an EC2 instance from a Windows Server image, or Amazon RDS for SQL Server license included, AWS takes care of licensing costs and compliance for you. Amazon RDS for Oracle also offers license included, but only for the Standard Edition 2 license.

Bring your own license: you re-use licenses you already paid for. For SQL Server on EC2, AWS notes that you must manage the license compliance yourself.

blocks.title: Which one when?
blocks.content:
AWS guidance for SQL Server on EC2: use license included for variable workloads, short-term projects and when you want flexibility across instance types. Use BYOL if you already have licenses and plan to run large, predictable workloads.

Scenario: a company already owns database licenses and will run the database all year without much change. BYOL avoids paying for the license twice. A team testing a database for two weeks, with no licenses, picks license included.

items.text: Your license terms decide whether and how you can bring it. For some software, AWS describes options such as License Mobility through Software Assurance, a Microsoft licensing program. Always check the vendor's terms. License included also has a billing benefit for Oracle on RDS: you pay only for the hours the database runs, which suits test environments.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Owning licenses is easy; proving you use them within the rules is hard once servers appear in many accounts.
> This lesson introduces the AWS tool that counts and limits license use for you.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS License Manager** — an AWS service that helps you manage software licenses from vendors across Regions and accounts, tracks their use and enforces limits you set.

AWS License Manager tracks the software licenses you own, applies rules that match your license agreements, and warns you or blocks new servers before you break them.

**The question this lesson answers:** how do you stay within your license terms when you run software at scale?

AWS says License Manager makes it easier to manage software licenses from vendors such as Microsoft, SAP, Oracle and IBM across multiple Regions and accounts within an organization. You can:

- set **hard or soft limits** on new and existing cloud deployments;
- track software licensed by vCPUs, physical cores, sockets or number of machines;
- see ongoing usage on built-in dashboards, which also helps with vendor audits.

The rules can limit a licensing breach by stopping an instance from launching, or by notifying administrators about the infringement.

blocks.title: Why it ties to cost
blocks.content: If you use more licenses than you own, you risk penalties and extra costs. License Manager reduces the risk of licensing overages and non-compliance. It also supports BYOL, because it lets you re-purpose the license inventory you already have. An AWS article says there is no charge for using License Manager itself, only for the resources you create. Check the current pricing page before you rely on that.

sections.title: Chapter 18: Pricing models
sections.note: How AWS charges, and how to compare and choose the ways of paying for compute, data transfer and storage.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Before comparing any discount, you need the map of how AWS charges at all.
> This lesson gives the basic ways you pay, and how you can try services at no charge.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **pricing principles** — the basic ways AWS charges: pay as you go, pay less when you commit, pay less by using more, and flat-rate plans.
- **AWS Free Tier** — AWS's offers that let you try services at no charge, within limits. The offers include a free plan, always-free services and short trials.

AWS charges mostly by what you use, and offers cheaper prices if you commit or use more.

**The question this lesson answers:** in what ways can you pay for AWS?

AWS describes its pricing like paying for utilities such as water and electricity. For the vast majority of services, you pay only for the services you need, for as long as you use them, without long-term contracts. Once you stop, there are no termination fees.

AWS lists these ways to pay:

- **Pay as you go**: you pay for what you use.
- **Save when you commit**: you promise to use a set amount for a term, in exchange for a lower price than the pay-as-you-go price.
- **Pay less by using more**: for services such as S3, pricing is tiered, so the more you use, the less you pay per GB.
- **Flat rate**: plans that combine several services into one price with no overage charges.

blocks.title: The AWS Free Tier
blocks.content: On the page AWS shows today, a new customer chooses a free plan or a paid plan. The free plan gives credits to try select services and does not charge you unless you upgrade. The paid plan gives access to all services with pay-as-you-go pricing. Some services are always free within monthly limits, and some have short trials. Older accounts may still have the legacy 12-months-free offers. Amounts and rules change, so read the current Free Tier page before you rely on it.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> On-Demand is the simplest way to pay for a server, and every other option is described as a change from it.
> You need it as the baseline.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **On-Demand Instances** — EC2 instances you pay for as you use them, by the second or hour, with no long-term commitment.

On-Demand Instances let you pay for compute capacity by the hour or second, with no long-term commitment.

**The question this lesson answers:** what do you get, and what do you give up, when you simply launch an instance and pay as it runs?

AWS says per-second billing (minimum of 60 seconds) applies to Linux, Windows, RHEL and Ubuntu Pro instances, while SUSE Linux Enterprise Server instances are billed as a full hour. Pricing is per instance-hour consumed, from the time an instance launches until it is terminated or stopped.

AWS describes this as freeing you from the costs and complexities of planning, purchasing and maintaining hardware, and as transforming what are commonly large fixed costs into much smaller variable costs.

blocks.title: When On-Demand fits
blocks.content: Use it when you cannot predict how long or how much you will run: a new application, a test, or a short project. You can stop any time and the charges stop with the instance. The other options in this chapter trade some of that freedom for a lower price, so On-Demand is the price you compare them against.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> If a server runs all year, paying the flat pay-as-you-go price for every hour is wasteful.
> This lesson shows how a promise of time can lower the price, and what the promise costs you.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Reserved Instances** — a billing discount for EC2 in exchange for a commitment. They are not physical machines.
- **commitment term** — the length of time you promise to pay, which is 1 year or 3 years for Reserved Instances.

Reserved Instances give you a lower price on EC2 if you commit to a one-year or three-year term.

**The question this lesson answers:** how does a Reserved Instance lower the bill, and what do you give up?

AWS says Reserved Instances are not physical instances, but rather a billing discount applied to the use of On-Demand Instances in your account. Those instances must match certain attributes, such as instance type and Region.

You choose the term. The three-year commitment gives a bigger discount.

You also choose a payment option:

- **All Upfront**: you pay the full term at the start.
- **Partial Upfront**: you pay part now, then a discounted hourly rate.
- **No Upfront**: you pay a discounted hourly rate every hour, with nothing at the start.

Generally, a higher upfront payment saves more money.

blocks.title: The catch
blocks.content: With a Reserved Instance you pay for every hour in the term whether or not the instance runs. After you buy one, you cannot cancel the purchase, though you might be able to modify, exchange or sell it. Reserved Instances do not renew automatically: when they end, matching instances are charged at On-Demand rates. You moved some of your cost from variable back toward fixed, which is the price of the discount.

items.text: AWS publishes the discount as up to a percentage, and the real figure depends on the term, the payment option, the instance family and the Reserved Instance type. Check the current pricing page for a real number.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A Reserved Instance that does not match what you run saves you nothing.
> This lesson shows the two choices that decide how easily your discount finds your usage.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Reserved Instance flexibility** — how much a Reserved Instance lets your usage change and still get the discount: its scope (Region or Availability Zone) and its class (Standard or Convertible).

Reserved Instance flexibility comes from two choices: the scope and the class.

**The question this lesson answers:** how can you buy a Reserved Instance and still change your setup later?

**Scope** says where the discount applies:

- A **regional** Reserved Instance applies to usage in any Availability Zone in the Region. It also applies across sizes in an instance family, but only for Linux and Unix with default tenancy (the normal setup, on hardware shared with other customers). It does not reserve capacity.
- A **zonal** Reserved Instance applies to one Availability Zone and one instance size. It does reserve capacity in that zone.

AWS gives an example: a regional m5.2xlarge Linux Reserved Instance in US East (N. Virginia) can cover two m5.xlarge instances in one zone or four m5.large instances in another.

blocks.title: Class: Standard or Convertible
blocks.content:
**Standard** gives the most significant discount, but can only be modified. It cannot be exchanged.

**Convertible** gives a lower discount, but can be exchanged for another Convertible Reserved Instance with different instance attributes. It can also be modified.

Simple rule: the more freedom you want to change later, the lower the discount.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Reserved Instances ask you to promise a specific machine, and your needs change.
> Savings Plans promise an amount of spending instead, which is easier to keep.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Savings Plans** — a discount model: you commit to a consistent amount of usage, measured in USD per hour, for 1 or 3 years (Database Savings Plans: 1 year only), and get lower prices in return.

A Savings Plan lowers your price in exchange for a commitment to spend a set amount per hour for one or three years.

**The question this lesson answers:** how is a Savings Plan different from a Reserved Instance?

With a Reserved Instance you commit to a specific instance configuration. With a Savings Plan you commit to a consistent amount of usage, measured in USD per hour. Usage up to the commitment is charged at the Savings Plans price, and anything beyond it is charged at regular On-Demand rates.

AWS says it recommends Savings Plans over Reserved Instances because they are the easiest and most flexible way to save on compute costs. A Savings Plan does not reserve capacity: it changes the price, but it does not guarantee that an instance is available when you want to launch one.

blocks.title: The types
blocks.content:
AWS lists four types: **Compute**, **EC2 Instance**, **Database** and **SageMaker AI**. Database Savings Plans are sold for a 1-year term only.

**Compute Savings Plans** are the most flexible. They apply to EC2 whatever the instance family, size, Region, operating system or tenancy (shared or dedicated hardware), and also to AWS Fargate and AWS Lambda. You can move a workload from EC2 to Fargate or Lambda and keep the Savings Plans price.

**EC2 Instance Savings Plans** give lower prices in return for committing to one instance family in one Region, for example m5 in Virginia. Size and operating system can change.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> AWS has spare computing capacity, and it sells it cheaply.
> The price you pay for the bargain is that AWS can ask for it back, so you need to know which jobs can live with that.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Spot Instances** — EC2 instances that use spare capacity at a steep discount, which AWS can take back.
- **interruption** — the moment EC2 reclaims a Spot Instance because it needs the capacity back.

Spot Instances let you use unused EC2 capacity at a steep discount, on the condition that EC2 can take it back.

**The question this lesson answers:** which jobs can use Spot, and which cannot?

AWS describes Spot Instances as spare capacity for up to a 90 percent discount compared to On-Demand pricing. When EC2 needs the capacity back, it interrupts the Spot Instance. Depending on the behavior you chose, the instance is terminated, stopped or hibernated. Hibernated means its memory is saved to disk so it can resume later.

AWS issues a Spot Instance interruption notice two minutes before the interruption. That is the time to save your work.

blocks.title: Good fit and bad fit
blocks.content:
Good fit: work that is fault-tolerant and flexible about when it runs, such as a batch job that can restart. A common pattern is to save the job's progress to storage such as Amazon S3 so another instance can continue.

Bad fit: something that must never stop, such as a database serving customers, or a task that cannot restart safely. Use another option for that.

AWS says demand for Spot capacity changes from moment to moment, so it is always possible that a Spot Instance might be interrupted.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Normally your instances share physical servers with other customers' instances, kept apart by virtualization.
> Some rules and some licenses need the server to be yours alone, and these two options provide that.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Dedicated Hosts** — a physical server fully dedicated to you, with control over placement, so you can use licenses tied to sockets or cores.
- **Dedicated Instances** — EC2 instances that run on hardware dedicated to a single customer, billed per instance.

Both options give you hardware that no other customer uses; a Dedicated Host also gives you the whole server to control.

**The question this lesson answers:** when do you need dedicated hardware, and which of the two do you pick?

Dedicated Instances run on hardware dedicated to a single customer, and are physically isolated from instances that belong to other AWS accounts. They may share hardware with other instances from the same account. AWS bills them per instance, plus an extra per-Region hourly fee.

A Dedicated Host is a physical server fully dedicated for your use. It gives you visibility of sockets and physical cores, affinity between a host and an instance, and targeted placement. It is billed per host. A socket is a processor slot on the server, and a core is a processing unit inside a processor.

blocks.title: Why choose a Host
blocks.content:
AWS says Dedicated Hosts let you use your existing per-socket, per-core or per-VM software licenses, such as Windows Server and SQL Server, subject to your license terms. That can save money, and it can also help meet corporate compliance and regulatory needs.

In short: if you need to see the sockets and cores, pin an instance to a server, or use a server-bound license, pick a Dedicated Host. If you only need isolated hardware, Dedicated Instances are enough.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A discount does not guarantee that a server is available when you ask for it.
> If an application must always be able to launch, you need to reserve the room itself.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Capacity Reservations** — a way to reserve EC2 capacity in one Availability Zone for as long as you need it, without a discount by itself.

A Capacity Reservation holds compute capacity for you in one specific Availability Zone, for any duration.

**The question this lesson answers:** how do you make sure the capacity is there when you need it?

AWS recommends it if you have strict capacity requirements for business-critical workloads, to help ensure you always have access to EC2 capacity when you need it, for as long as you need it.

If you create one for immediate use, there is no term commitment: you can modify it at any time and cancel it to release the capacity and stop incurring charges. You can also create a future-dated reservation, and then you commit to keeping it for the length you specify.

Instances that match its attributes use it: instance type, platform, Availability Zone and tenancy. Platform means the operating system, and tenancy means shared or dedicated hardware.

blocks.title: Reservation, discount, or both?
blocks.content:
A Capacity Reservation by itself gives no billing discount. You can combine it with a Savings Plan or a regional Reserved Instance to receive a discount.

From AWS's comparison: Capacity Reservations reserve capacity in one zone and need no term for immediate use. Zonal Reserved Instances reserve capacity and give a discount for a 1 or 3 year term. Regional Reserved Instances and Savings Plans give a discount for a term but no capacity.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You now know seven options, and the exam asks you to pick the right one for a story.
> This lesson turns the details into a small set of questions you can ask.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **choosing a compute purchase option** — matching a workload to a way of paying for EC2 by asking how steady it is, how much freedom you need, whether it can be interrupted, and whether it needs capacity, licenses or isolated hardware.

Pick the purchase option by asking what your workload can promise and what it cannot live without.

**The question this lesson answers:** given a workload, which option fits?

AWS's purchasing guidance gives these matches:

- You can commit to an amount of usage but not to a specific instance configuration: a Savings Plan.
- You require a capacity reservation: Reserved Instances in one zone, or Capacity Reservations.
- You can be flexible about when your applications run and they can be interrupted: Spot Instances.
- You need to meet compliance requirements, or use existing server-bound software licenses: Dedicated Hosts or Dedicated Instances.

One more match comes from the On-Demand lesson above: if you cannot predict your use or commit to anything, use On-Demand Instances.

Figure 17-1 below compares four of the options on commitment, flexibility and discount.

blocks.title: Four small scenarios
blocks.content:
1. A web server that runs all year: commit with a Savings Plan.
2. A nightly job that can restart if stopped: Spot Instances.
3. A two-week test of a new idea: On-Demand Instances.
4. A database licensed per physical socket, which you already own: a Dedicated Host.

And for any of them, if you must be sure the instance can launch in one zone, add a Capacity Reservation.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A company often has many AWS accounts, and a discount bought in one may be left unused there.
> This lesson shows how the discount can follow the usage across the whole company.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Reserved Instance and Savings Plans sharing in an organization** — the way a Reserved Instance or Savings Plans discount bought in one account can also lower the bill for matching usage in other accounts of the same AWS Organization.

In an AWS Organization, Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts can be shared, so matching usage in any account can use them.

**The question this lesson answers:** if one account buys the discount, who gets it?

For billing, AWS can treat all accounts in an organization as if they were one account, which is called consolidated billing: one combined bill. AWS says combining the usage shares the volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts and Savings Plans, which can result in a lower charge than with individual standalone accounts.

The rules:

- The account that bought the discount gets it first. (One exception: unused zonal Reserved Instances from other accounts are applied before an account's own regional ones.)
- If that account has no matching usage, the discount goes to matching usage in another account of the organization.
- Sharing is turned on by default.

blocks.title: Turning sharing off
blocks.content: The organization's main account, the one that pays the bill, can control sharing for any account. If sharing is deactivated for an account, it only receives the discounts that it owns. The charges of that account still go on the organization's combined bill. AWS also lets you define groups of accounts for sharing, such as sharing first inside a group. Savings Plans discounts stop applying to the combined bill if the account that owns them leaves the organization.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Servers and storage are not the only items on an AWS bill: moving data costs money too.
> An architecture can look cheap on paper and still be expensive because of where its data travels.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **data transfer cost** — the charge for moving data into AWS, out of AWS, or between Regions and Availability Zones.

Data coming into AWS is free, while data going out, or across Regions, is charged.

**The question this lesson answers:** which data movements cost money?

AWS says data transfer IN is always free of charge. Data transfer OUT to the internet is charged, and the price is tiered: the more you use, the less you pay per GB. AWS also gives a free amount of data transfer out each month, aggregated across services. Check the current page for its size.

Between Regions, data crossing from one Region to another carries an inter-Region transfer charge.

Within a Region, data between Availability Zones is charged for services such as EC2 and RDS, and AWS says traffic inside the same Availability Zone is free. Some services, such as S3 to EC2 in the same Region, are free.
