blocks.title: A hidden cost of high availability
blocks.content: Suppose two application servers sit in different Availability Zones for high availability, and they talk to each other all day. AWS says data transfer charges apply for that cross-zone communication. It is worth the safety, but it is a cost to expect and estimate.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> The three storage services you met bill in different ways.
> Mixing them up leads to wrong cost guesses, and to questions you can answer once you see the pattern.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **storage pricing** — how a storage service charges: by what you store, by what you provision, by how often you read the data, and by the tier or class you choose.

Amazon S3 charges for what you store, Amazon EBS charges for what you provision, and Amazon EFS charges for what you store in each class.

**The question this lesson answers:** how does each storage service count the bill?

**Amazon S3**: you pay only for what you use, with no minimum charge. The cost parts are storage, requests and data retrieval, data transfer, and management features. The storage rate depends on object size, how long you stored it during the month, and the storage class. Classes meant for less frequent access cost less to store but add retrieval charges and, for some classes, a minimum storage duration.

**Amazon EBS**: you pay by the gigabyte-month of storage that you provision, even if you do not use it. A 100 GB volume holding 10 GB of data is billed for 100 GB-month. Snapshots are also billed by GB-month, in a standard or an archive tier.

blocks.title: Amazon EFS and the pattern
blocks.content:
**Amazon EFS**: you pay for the data in each storage class: EFS Standard, EFS Infrequent Access and EFS Archive. Reading from the Infrequent Access or Archive classes, and moving data between classes, adds data access charges.

The pattern is tiers: keep frequently used data in the faster, pricier class and move rarely used data to a cheaper class, for example with a lifecycle policy. The fine print for each service sits on its pricing page.

items.text: The EBS example shows why unused provisioned space is a waste. AWS suggests auditing volumes and migrating to smaller ones if you do not use most of the space. S3 and EFS do not work this way: you pay for the data you actually store.

sections.title: Chapter 19: Billing, budgets and cost management
sections.note: How to read your AWS bill, estimate and analyze costs, set budget alerts, tag costs, get detailed reports and combine accounts into one bill.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> AWS is pay-as-you-go, so your charges change every month. You need to know where to read what you owe and who to ask when a number looks wrong.

The AWS Billing and Cost Management console is the place in the AWS Management Console where you read your bills and invoices and ask for billing help.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Billing and Cost Management console** — the part of the AWS Management Console where you see your charges, download invoices, and use the cost tools of this chapter.
- **bill and invoice** — the bill is the list of what you used and what it cost. An invoice is the formal PDF document AWS issues when a billing period closes or when you make a one-time purchase.
- **billing support** — help with questions about your charges and your account. Every AWS account owner gets it free of charge.
- **billing period** — the span of time one bill covers, normally one month.

To read your bill, open the AWS Billing and Cost Management console and choose **Bills** in the navigation pane. Then pick a billing period.

A month that is still running has the status **Pending**. Its totals are estimates based on the usage AWS has metered so far. The summary is not an invoice until the month closes.

When the month closes, the status becomes **Issued**. AWS then produces the invoice as a PDF file, and if you pay by credit card, it charges the card you have on file.

The Bills page also lists purchases made through AWS Marketplace, next to your AWS service charges.

blocks.title: One-time fees are billed at once
blocks.content: Not every charge waits for month end. You are charged immediately for one-time fees, such as the fee for buying a Reserved Instance paid all upfront. That purchase gets its own invoice straight away.

blocks.title: Billing support: who to ask
blocks.content:
Every AWS account owner has account and billing support free of charge. Start with the AWS Knowledge Center: open it, choose **Billing Management**, and scan the topics for a question like yours.

If you want a person to answer, open a support case. A support case is a request that you send to AWS's support staff. Choose **Account and billing support**, then pick **Web** for an email reply or **Phone** to ask for a phone call. Chat is not available for billing questions.

Only personalized technical support needs a paid plan. Billing questions and appeals do not.

items.term: Estimating cost: pricing pages and Pricing Calculator

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> The bill tells you what you already spent. Before you build, you want an idea of what a setup will cost each month.

AWS gives you two places to look: the pricing page of each service, and the AWS Pricing Calculator, a free tool that adds a whole setup up into one estimate.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **service pricing pages** — the page on the AWS website for one service that lists what that service costs and how it is charged.
- **AWS Pricing Calculator** — a free web tool where you describe the AWS services you plan to use and get a cost estimate.
- **estimate** — a calculated guess of a future cost, based only on what you type in.

Every AWS service has its own pricing page. It states the rates and what each one is charged for. AWS describes its pricing as pay as you go for most services: you pay only for the individual services you need, for as long as you use them, and without long-term contracts.

A pricing page prices one service. A real solution uses several. The AWS Pricing Calculator is the tool for that.

The AWS Pricing Calculator is a free web-based planning tool that you can use to create cost estimates for using AWS services. You open it in a browser at calculator.aws. You do not need an AWS account or any experience with cloud computing to use it.

What you can do with it:

- Model your solution before you build it, and plan your AWS spend.
- Explore the price of services and see the calculation behind each number.
- Sort services into groups that match your architecture.
- Save a link to an estimate to share it later, or export it as CSV or PDF.

Example from AWS: you want to add an EC2 instance for a weekly traffic spike. You enter the weekly peak, pick the instance and a payment option, and the calculator returns an estimate with upfront, monthly and annual costs.

blocks.title: Know its limits
blocks.content:
An estimate is only as good as what you enter. The calculator gives pricing details for only the information you enter, and its estimates do not include any taxes that might apply. If a price on the AWS marketing pages differs from the calculator, AWS uses the marketing page price when it generates your estimate.

There are two versions. The public Pricing Calculator website creates estimates with On-Demand rates. The Pricing Calculator inside the Billing and Cost Management console estimates planned costs using your own discounts and purchase commitments.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> One bill total does not tell you which service or which month made your spend go up. You need a way to look at the charges from different angles.

AWS Cost Explorer is a tool in the Billing and Cost Management console that draws your past costs as charts and forecasts future ones.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Cost Explorer** — a tool for viewing and analyzing your costs and usage with charts, filters and groupings.
- **cost forecast** — a prediction of how much you will spend in a future period, based on your past usage.

AWS Cost Explorer is a tool that enables you to view and analyze your costs and usage. You explore with a main graph, with ready-made cost and usage reports, or with reports about Reserved Instances. You can filter and group the data, for example by service, to see which service drives a rise.

You can view data for up to the last 13 months, and forecast how much you are likely to spend for the next 18 months. It can also recommend which Reserved Instances to buy.

Using Cost Explorer in the console is free of charge. You have to enable it first, and after enabling it you cannot disable it. Data for the current month is ready in about 24 hours, and AWS refreshes the data at least once every 24 hours.

A cost forecast is a prediction of how much you will use AWS services over a future period you select. It is based on your past usage.

Because it is a prediction, the amount is an estimate and may differ from your actual charges. Cost Explorer forecasts use an 80 percent prediction interval (a range around the forecast), shown as lines on each side of your costs. If AWS does not have enough data, there is no forecast. This is common for accounts that have less than one full billing cycle.

Think of a weather forecast: useful for planning, but not a promise.

blocks.title: Cost Explorer or Pricing Calculator?
blocks.content:
| | Cost Explorer | Pricing Calculator |
|---|---|---|
| Looks at | spend you already have | a setup you plan |
| Data | your real usage | what you type in |
| Forecast | yes, from past usage | an estimate you build |

Use Cost Explorer to find out where your money goes. Use the Pricing Calculator to find out what a new idea would cost.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Looking at charts after the fact is too late if a mistake is burning money now. You want a tool that warns you before the month ends.

AWS Budgets lets you set a spending or usage limit for your account and sends a budget alert when you reach it, or when AWS expects you to.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Budgets** — a service in which you set a target for cost or usage and get notified when you pass it.
- **budget alert** — a notification sent when your actual or forecasted cost or usage crosses a threshold (a percentage of the budget) that you chose.
- **threshold** — the level at which an alert fires, for example 80 percent of the budget.

You can use AWS Budgets to track and take action on your AWS costs and usage. It differs from Cost Explorer: Cost Explorer shows you the numbers, while Budgets watches the numbers against a target and tells you.

A typical example: set a monthly cost budget with a fixed amount for your whole account, and ask to be alerted for both actual spend (after it has accrued) and forecasted spend (before it has accrued).

The forecast part is why you can hear about a problem before you reach the limit. (Accrued means charges you have already incurred.)

There are six types of budget:

- **Cost budgets** and **usage budgets** track spend or usage of one or more services.
- **Reserved Instance utilization** and **coverage** budgets alert you when your reservations are used too little, or cover too small a share of your usage.
- **Savings Plans utilization** and **coverage** budgets do the same for Savings Plans.

Alerts go to an email address, to an Amazon SNS topic, or to both. Using SNS means a budget alert can reach other systems, not only a person's inbox.

blocks.title: An alert is not a spending cap
blocks.content: A budget warns you, it does not stop spending by itself. There can be a delay between the moment you incur a charge and the moment AWS Budgets notifies you, so you may pass your threshold before the alert arrives. Budgets can also take an action. For example, at 80 percent of the budget it can automatically apply a custom IAM policy that denies you the ability to provision additional resources in the account. Budget information is updated up to three times a day.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A bill that only says "EC2" and "S3" does not tell you which team or application spent the money. Labels on your resources can.

A cost allocation tag is a label on a resource that AWS can use to group your costs by team, application or owner.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **tag** — a label made of a key and a value, attached to an AWS resource. Example: key Stack, value Test.
- **cost allocation tag** — a tag that you have activated in the Billing and Cost Management console so that your costs can be grouped by it.
- **AWS-generated tag** — a tag that AWS (or an AWS Marketplace seller) creates and applies for you. Its key starts with aws:.
- **user-defined tag** — a tag that you create and apply yourself. Its key starts with user:.

A tag is a label that you or AWS assigns to an AWS resource. Each tag has a key and a value. For one resource, each tag key must be unique, and each key can have only one value.

Tags by themselves only organize resources. To track costs by tag, you activate them as cost allocation tags. Once activated, AWS organizes your resource costs by those tags, which makes it easier to categorize and track costs.

Pick tags that mean something to your business, such as cost centers, application names or owners. Then the total cost of one application is the sum of everything carrying its tag, whichever services it runs on.

There are two types:

- **AWS-generated tags** are defined, created and applied by AWS or by an AWS Marketplace seller. An example is createdBy, which records who created a resource. Their key uses the aws: prefix.
- **User-defined tags** are tags that you define, create and apply. Their key uses the user: prefix.

You must activate both types separately before they can appear in Cost Explorer or on a cost allocation report. After activation, a tag can take up to 24 hours to appear in the console.

blocks.title: What you get once tags are active
blocks.content:
AWS can generate a cost allocation report as a CSV file with your usage and costs grouped by your active tags. The report includes tagged and untagged resources, so nothing is hidden. At the end of the billing cycle its total matches the total on your Bills page. You can also use the tags to filter your views in Cost Explorer.

Two good habits. Do not put sensitive information in tags. And to create and update tags, use the AWS Tag Editor.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Sometimes the charts are not enough. You want every line item of your usage, so you can search it, join it and audit it.

AWS Cost and Usage Reports (AWS CUR) deliver the most detailed billing data AWS offers, as files in an S3 bucket you own.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR)** — report files with your detailed cost and usage data, delivered to an Amazon S3 bucket that you own.
- **line item** — one row of the report: one unique combination of AWS product, usage type and operation.
- **manifest file** — a small file that comes with the report files and describes them.

AWS Cost and Usage Reports contains the most comprehensive set of cost and usage data available. You publish your billing reports to an Amazon S3 bucket that you own. You can have the data broken down by hour, day or month, by product or product resource, or by tags that you define yourself.

Each report holds line items for each unique combination of AWS products, usage type and operation that you use in your account. A report is a CSV file or a collection of CSV files plus a manifest file. A report larger than about 1 million rows is split into several files in the same folder.

After you create a report, it can take up to 24 hours for the first one to arrive. After that, AWS updates the report at least once a day. Each update is cumulative, so it holds all billing data of the month so far.

These updates are estimates, and charges are subject to change as you keep using services. AWS finalizes the usage charges after it issues the invoice at the end of the month. After that, AWS may still update the report when it applies refunds, credits or support fees.

Tags tie in here. The report can be organized by the tags you defined, which is why activating cost allocation tags matters.

blocks.title: Three ways to use the report
blocks.content:
- Download it from the Amazon S3 console and open it in a spreadsheet.
- Query it with Amazon Athena, with plain SQL, straight from S3.
- Load it into Amazon Redshift, or into Amazon Quick (the wider AWS product that contains Quick Sight, the dashboard tool from the analytics chapter).

Cost Explorer uses the same dataset that generates these reports. Use Cost Explorer when charts are enough. Use CUR when you need the raw rows.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A company often has many AWS accounts. Paying and tracking each bill separately is slow, and separate accounts miss discounts that come with bigger combined usage.

Consolidated billing, a feature of AWS Organizations, adds the charges of many accounts into one bill paid by one account.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **consolidated billing** — the feature of AWS Organizations that combines the billing and payment of several AWS accounts.
- **management account** — the one account of an organization that pays the charges of all the other accounts.
- **member account** — any other account in the organization. Its charges are paid by the management account.

You can use the consolidated billing feature in AWS Organizations to consolidate billing and payment for multiple AWS accounts. Every organization has a management account that pays the charges of all the member accounts.

Figure 18-1 below shows the idea: several member accounts, one management account that pays, and one bill.

blocks.title: Figure 18-1
blocks.svg:
<svg viewBox="0 0 640 380" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-label="Three member accounts roll up to one management account and one bill">
<rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="380" fill="#f8fafc"/>

blocks.caption: Member accounts roll up to one management-account bill.

blocks.content:
Consolidated billing has four benefits:

- **One bill** for multiple accounts.
- **Easy tracking.** You can track charges across accounts and download the combined cost and usage data.
- **Combined usage.** Usage is combined across all accounts, so the organization shares volume pricing discounts, Reserved Instance discounts and Savings Plans. This can cost less than separate standalone accounts.
- **No extra fee.** Consolidated billing is offered at no additional cost.

Volume pricing means tiers: for services such as Amazon S3, the more you use, the less you pay per GB. Combined usage reaches the cheaper tiers sooner.

blocks.title: Who can see what
blocks.content:
If you have access to the management account, you can see a combined view of the charges the member accounts incur, and you can get a cost report for each member account. That is how costs are allocated back to teams or projects.

The bills of member accounts are for information only. The management account might reallocate the extra volume discounts, Reserved Instance or Savings Plans discounts that a member account receives.

If a member account leaves the organization, it can no longer access the Cost Explorer data generated while it was a member. The data is not deleted, and the management account can still access it.

sections.title: Chapter 20: Technical resources and AWS Support
sections.note: Where AWS publishes its official answers, how the AWS Support plans differ, and which partners and expert teams can help.

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> You will always have questions that this module cannot answer, and AWS changes often. You need to know where AWS itself publishes the current answers.

AWS publishes three kinds of official reading: documentation, whitepapers and blogs. Each answers a different kind of question.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Documentation** — the official guides for every service, with user guides, tutorials, code samples and API and CLI references. Its address is docs.aws.amazon.com.
- **whitepaper** — a longer technical paper that explains a topic in depth, written by AWS or the AWS community.
- **AWS Blog** — short posts on aws.amazon.com that announce new features and show how to use services.

AWS Documentation is where you go to learn how a service works and how to use it. It holds user guides, code samples, SDKs and toolkits, tutorials, and API and CLI references. It also has a getting-started area for the fundamentals and best practices.

Whitepapers sit on aws.amazon.com/whitepapers. AWS describes that page as technical content authored by AWS and the AWS community: technical whitepapers, decision guides, technical guides, reference material, and reference architecture diagrams. The Well-Architected lenses are published there too.

The AWS Blogs page at aws.amazon.com/blogs lists the newest posts. Use blogs to hear what is new, for example a launch of a new feature, and to see an idea explained in a worked example.

blocks.title: Which one do I open?
blocks.content:
| You want to | Open |
|---|---|
| know how one service works or how to set it up | Documentation |
| learn a design practice in depth | a whitepaper |
| hear what changed or launched | the AWS Blog |

Rule of thumb: the official address is the one to trust for AWS facts. Limits, names and prices change, so read the current page rather than an old copy of it.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Docs describe how a service works. They do not always answer "why does my setup fail?" or "how do I plan a migration?". Other official places do.

AWS re:Post is where people ask and answer questions. AWS Prescriptive Guidance gives step-by-step plans and patterns.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS re:Post** — a question and answer site run by AWS, where AWS customers, partners and employees ask and answer technical questions about AWS.
- **AWS Prescriptive Guidance** — expert-written guides and patterns from AWS for planning and carrying out cloud adoption, migration and modernization.

AWS re:Post is an AWS-managed Q&A service driven by the community of AWS customers, partners and employees. It offers crowd-sourced, expert-reviewed answers to technical questions, and it replaced the original AWS Forums.

You can browse without signing in. If you sign in with your AWS account, you can post questions and answers. AWS says re:Post is not intended for questions that are time-sensitive or that involve private information, such as customer account details.

The AWS Knowledge Center lives in re:Post too. It holds articles that answer questions AWS customers ask often, for example the billing topics from the previous chapter.

AWS Prescriptive Guidance has resources from AWS technology experts to help accelerate cloud adoption and modernization. It has two main kinds of content:

- **Guides** give planning and implementation guidance, with a focus on best practices and tools, for architects, managers, technical leads and executives.
- **Patterns** give steps, architectures, tools and code for common migration, optimization and modernization scenarios, for builders and other hands-on users.

blocks.title: Which one do I open?
blocks.content:
| Your situation | Go to |
|---|---|
| a technical question nobody has answered for you | re:Post |
| a common how-to question, answered in an article | Knowledge Center |
| a plan or a recipe for a migration or a modernization | Prescriptive Guidance |

None of these is a promise of an answer from AWS staff. For that you need a support case, which the next lessons explain.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Some problems need a person at AWS, not a forum. The kind of help you can ask for depends on the support you have.

AWS Support is the help AWS offers about your account and your workloads. Every account has Basic Support at no charge.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Support** — the help AWS gives its customers: answers about accounts and billing, and, with a paid plan, technical help from AWS engineers.
- **AWS Support Center** — the page in the AWS Management Console where you create and follow your support cases.
- **Basic Support** — the support every AWS customer has automatically, at no extra charge.
- **customer service and communities** — what Basic Support gives you: 24/7 customer service, plus documentation, whitepapers and AWS re:Post.

You open cases in the AWS Support Center. There are three types of case:

- **Account and billing** cases are available to all customers.
- **Service limit increase** requests are available to all customers. A service limit is the same as a service quota.
- **Technical** cases connect you to help with technical problems. If you have Basic Support, you cannot create a technical case.

So with Basic Support you can ask AWS about your bill and your quotas. For a technical problem you read the documentation and ask the community on re:Post, or you choose a paid plan.

blocks.title: A small example
blocks.content: Your web server on EC2 is slow. With only Basic Support you cannot open a technical case. You can search the documentation, ask on re:Post, and check Trusted Advisor core checks. If you need an AWS engineer to look at it, you need one of the paid plans in the next lessons.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> A production system that stops can cost a business more than the support fee. The first paid plan is where AWS engineers start to answer your technical cases.

AWS Business Support+ is the first paid AWS Support plan: AI help with your context at any hour, plus human engineers when it matters.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Business Support+** — the paid support plan that AWS names as the minimum recommended for production workloads. It adds 24/7 technical help from AI and from engineers, and the full set of Trusted Advisor checks.

blocks.content:
A case has a severity, and each severity has a first-response time. The plans below are Business Support+ or higher. The times are what AWS makes every reasonable effort to meet.

| Severity | First response |
|---|---|
| General guidance | 24 hours |
| System impaired | 12 hours |
| Production system impaired | 4 hours |
| Production system down | 1 hour |
| Business-critical system down | under 30 minutes with Business Support+ |

Pick the highest severity only for cases that cannot be worked around or that directly affect production.

blocks.title: Plan names you may still see
blocks.content:
Older material mentions Developer Support, Business Support and Enterprise On-Ramp. AWS has announced that Developer Support and Business Support will be discontinued on January 1, 2027, and Enterprise On-Ramp on the same date. Customers on them can keep their plan until then or move to Business Support+. They stay available in AWS GovCloud (US).

At the time of reading (October 2026) AWS stated a minimum of 29 USD per month per account for Business Support+. Prices change, so check the current AWS Support page before you decide.

items.term: AWS Enterprise Support and Unified Operations

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Large businesses run systems that cannot fail. They want a named person who knows their setup and a fast response, not only a queue of cases.

The two highest plans add designated experts. AWS Enterprise Support adds a designated person for guidance. AWS Unified Operations adds a designated team and monitoring for mission-critical workloads.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Enterprise Support** — the plan that includes everything in Business Support+ and adds a designated Technical Account Manager, faster response times and security incident help.
- **AWS Unified Operations** — the top plan, for mission-critical workloads, with a designated team of experts and 24/7 workload monitoring.
- **Technical Account Manager (TAM)** — an AWS expert assigned to your account who gives guidance on your architecture, costs and security and brings in other AWS experts.
- **mission-critical** — so important to the business that a failure is not acceptable.

blocks.title: Why the plan list changed
blocks.content: Older guides list Developer, Business, Enterprise On-Ramp and Enterprise. AWS states that throughout 2026 customers of Enterprise On-Ramp are being upgraded to Enterprise Support, and that On-Ramp ends on January 1, 2027. The current exam guide names Basic, Business Support+, Enterprise Support and Unified Operations. When an old source disagrees, trust the current AWS Support page.

items.term: AWS Health Dashboard and Health API

blocks.content:
> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Sometimes your application breaks because AWS has a problem, not because you made one. You want to know that fast, without opening a case.

The AWS Health Dashboard tells you about AWS events that affect the services and resources you use.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Health Dashboard** — the page that shows the health of AWS services and events that affect your own account. It is free and needs no setup.
- **AWS Health API** — the way to read the same Health events from code, so other systems can use them. It needs a paid support plan.

AWS Health gives you ongoing visibility into the performance of your resources and the availability of AWS services and accounts. AWS Health events help you learn how service and resource changes might affect your applications, and prepare for planned activities.

The AWS Health Dashboard is available to all AWS customers at no additional cost. You do not need to write code or perform any action to set it up.

It has two views. **Service health** shows the health of all AWS services, and you can open it without signing in or having an account. It shows only public events, and keeps a history of the last 12 months. **Your account health** shows events that are specific to your account and its resources.

The AWS Health Dashboard is powered by the AWS Health API. With the API, you can pull Health events into your own tools or third-party systems.

To use the Health API you need AWS Business Support+, AWS Enterprise Support or AWS Unified Operations. An account without one of those gets an error when it calls the API.

Every customer can also receive AWS Health events through Amazon EventBridge at no additional cost. And if your account is part of AWS Organizations, an organizational view collects Health events across all the accounts in the organization.

blocks.title: Dashboard or API?
blocks.content:
| | Dashboard | API |
|---|---|---|
| Who uses it | a person, in the console | a program |
| Plan needed | none | a paid plan |
| Cost | free | included in the paid plan |

If a person only needs to look, use the dashboard. If an alert must reach your own tools, use EventBridge, or the API with a paid plan.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Money leaks quietly: a load balancer nobody uses, a server that sits idle, a disk that no machine reads. A tool that scans for them pays for itself.

AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your account and lists where you could spend less. How much of it you see depends on your support plan.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **Trusted Advisor for cost optimization** — the group of Trusted Advisor checks that look for waste and savings, such as idle or underused resources.
- **Trusted Advisor by support plan** — which checks you can see depends on the support plan you have.

What you can see depends on the plan:

- **Basic Support:** all checks in the Service Limits category and selected checks in the Security and Fault tolerance categories. The full cost optimization checks are not part of this.
- **Business Support+, Enterprise Support or Unified Operations:** all Trusted Advisor checks in the console and in the Trusted Advisor API.

Some cost checks draw on AWS Compute Optimizer and AWS Cost Optimization Hub (a tool that gathers cost-saving recommendations from several AWS services in one place), and you must opt in to those first.

blocks.title: A warning before you delete
blocks.content: A finding like low utilization does not automatically mean the resource can be removed. It might be a test environment or a batch job that does not run all the time. In that case resizing the instance or adding an automatic shutdown can fix the cost. Read the recommendation, then decide.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Someone may use AWS resources to attack you, send spam, or host harmful content. Neither the Support plans nor re:Post is the place to report that.

The AWS Trust and Safety team handles abuse of AWS resources. You report abuse to it with an abuse report.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Trust and Safety team** — the AWS team that handles abuse of AWS services.
- **abuse report** — a report you send to that team, saying that AWS resources are being used in a harmful or rule-breaking way.
- **abuse** — any use of AWS services that violates the AWS Service Terms or the AWS Acceptable Use Policy.

How to report: use the form called Report abusive activity from AWS resources, which gives faster processing. You can also email trustandsafety@support.aws.com.

You do not need to be an AWS customer to report abuse. Anyone who suspects that AWS resources are being used for abusive activity or content can report it.

Give as much detail as you can. For network abuse that means the type of abuse, dates and times with the time zone, source and target IP addresses, ports and protocols, and log extracts. For content abuse, give the URL and a description.

blocks.title: Not the same as Support
blocks.content: Trust and Safety deals with AWS resources that are used against someone else. It does not fix your own technical problem. For your own account you use the Support Center, and for questions you use re:Post. If you suspect fraudulent activity using your own AWS account, AWS also points you to the same abuse reporting process.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Many companies do not build alone. They hire a firm to migrate them, or buy software built by another firm. AWS has a network of such organizations.

The AWS Partner Network is the community of companies that build on AWS and help customers use it.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Partner Network (APN)** — the global community of organizations that use AWS technologies, programs, funding and tools to build solutions and services for customers.
- **AWS Partner** — one company that is a member of the AWS Partner Network.
- **independent software vendor (ISV)** — a company that makes software that runs on or works with AWS.
- **system integrator (SI)** — a professional services firm that helps customers design, build, migrate and manage their workloads on AWS.
- **partner benefits** — what AWS gives to its Partners, such as training, certification, events and ways to sell.

The AWS Partner Network (APN) is a global community of organizations. Together with AWS they deliver solutions where and when customers need them.

Two kinds of Partner matter most here:

- **ISVs** are in the technology group. They provide software, such as SaaS products, that runs on or integrates with the AWS Cloud. They can offer it through AWS Marketplace.
- **System integrators** are consulting Partners. They are professional services firms that help customers design, architect, build, migrate and manage workloads and applications in AWS.

So as a customer you can buy software from an ISV, and hire a system integrator to carry out a migration.

blocks.title: Customer or Partner?
blocks.content: You are a customer when you use AWS for your own workloads. A company becomes a Partner when it builds solutions or services for other customers. A Partner can also be an AWS customer. The two roles are separate.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Buying software for a company means contracts, licenses, approvals and a separate invoice for each seller. AWS Marketplace tries to put all of that inside your AWS account.

AWS Marketplace offers three key services around buying software: cost management, governance and entitlement.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **cost management in AWS Marketplace** — charges for Marketplace products appear on your AWS bill, in one place, with flexible pricing options.
- **governance in AWS Marketplace** — controlling which products people in your organization may buy.
- **entitlement** — the right to use a product you have bought. It is tracked as a license.

AWS Marketplace is a curated digital catalog where you find, buy, deploy and manage third-party software, data and services. Sellers are often independent software vendors. Products come as Amazon Machine Images, SaaS and other forms.

**Cost management.** All pricing options are billed from one source. Options include free trial, hourly, monthly, annual, multi-year and Bring Your Own License. AWS handles billing and payment, and the charges appear on your AWS bill. Some tags on your costs are AWS-generated tags that a Marketplace seller applies.

**Governance.** AWS Private Marketplace lets administrators create sets of approved products and approve them for different accounts in their organization. Users find and deploy only approved products. For a product that is not approved, a user can send a request to the administrator.

**Entitlement.** An entitlement is the right to use a Marketplace product. Managed entitlements create licenses that match your product subscriptions, so you can see them at account level. You can distribute them to the accounts of your organization, and you manage them in AWS License Manager under Granted Licenses.

blocks.title: A short scenario
blocks.content: A company has twenty accounts. The security team approves three tools in Private Marketplace. A developer subscribes to one. The charge shows on the company's AWS bill, and License Manager shares the license with the other accounts. That is governance, cost management and entitlement working together.

> **🎯 Why?**
>
> Sometimes reading and asking are not enough, and you want experts to design or build with you. AWS offers people for that, not only documents.

Two kinds of technical help come from AWS itself: AWS Professional Services, who carry out projects with you, and AWS solutions architects, who help you design.

blocks.title: New words in this lesson
blocks.content:
Write these down. Each word below is used for the first time in this lesson.

- **AWS Professional Services** — an AWS consulting team that helps organizations design, build, migrate and manage their workloads on AWS.
- **AWS solutions architect** — an AWS technical expert who works with a customer to turn business needs into an architecture on AWS.

AWS Professional Services combines specialized solutions and industry expertise to help organizations design, build, migrate and manage their workloads and applications on AWS. Its focus areas include data and AI, migration, modernization, and scale and security, and it has industry-specific expertise.

It works together with AWS Partners, so you can combine AWS's own experts with a Partner's industry knowledge. Professional Services offerings are also listed in AWS Marketplace. To start, you contact AWS.

AWS solutions architects are the bridge between a customer's business challenges and technology. They start from what the customer wants to achieve, design the blueprint (system architecture diagrams and the services behind them), and guide the customer from the first idea to the implementation.

They are trusted technical advisors for companies of every size, from startups to large enterprises, and they help align technology choices with business goals.

blocks.title: Who do I ask for what?
blocks.content:
| You need | Ask |
|---|---|
| an answer to a technical question | re:Post or the documentation |
| help with a problem in your account | AWS Support, with a paid plan |
| a design for a new workload | an AWS solutions architect |
| a team to carry out a migration or build | AWS Professional Services or a Partner |
| ongoing named guidance | a Technical Account Manager, from Enterprise Support |

A building that supplies power and cooling for computers

Guaranteed elimination of all security vulnerabilities

quizData.question: A company needs a disaster recovery strategy where a scaled-down but fully functional version of its environment runs continuously in a secondary AWS Region, enabling rapid failover by scaling up to full capacity when a disaster occurs. Which disaster recovery strategy does this describe?
explanations: Incorrect. Backup and restore involves storing regular data backups and restoring them to a newly provisioned environment after a disaster, resulting in the longest recovery time of all DR strategies as infrastructure must be built from scratch during recovery rather than already being available. Pilot light keeps only the minimal core components of the environment running in the secondary Region, such as a replicated database, with other infrastructure shut down and requiring provisioning during failover, resulting in faster recovery than backup and restore but slower than warm standby since more infrastructure must be brought online. Multi-site active-active runs full production copies of the environment across multiple sites simultaneously, providing the fastest possible failover with essentially zero downtime, but at the highest ongoing cost since all sites must maintain full production capacity at all times.

quizData.question: A company must store critical business data in Amazon S3 with a backup to another AWS Region. How can this be achieved?

Taking Amazon S3 bucket snapshots is not a native S3 feature; S3 does not have a native snapshot capability like EBS, and the correct approach for S3 backup to another Region is cross-region replication rather than snapshots.

quizData.question: Which of the following can be used to protect data at rest on Amazon S3?
explanations: WARNING - flagged (ambiguous): Versioning and permissions are not data-at-rest protection per se; encryption is the usual answer and is not offered Check: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/security.html. Correct. Amazon S3 versioning retains multiple versions of objects, protecting against accidental deletion and allowing restoration of previous versions, and S3 permissions through IAM policies and bucket policies control who can access and modify objects. Both help protect data at rest on Amazon S3.

WARNING - flagged (ambiguous): Versioning and permissions are not data-at-rest protection per se; encryption is the usual answer and is not offered Check: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/security.html. Incorrect. Deduplication is a storage optimization technique that removes duplicate copies of data to save space, and is not a data protection mechanism for Amazon S3; S3 does not expose deduplication as a security feature. quizData.question: When should a company consider using Amazon EC2 Spot Instances?
options: For applications that cannot have interruptions
explanations: WARNING - flagged (ambiguous): 'Non-production applications' is a use case, not a Spot suitability criterion; keyed answer A is debatable. Check: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-spot-instances.html. Correct. Spot Instances are best for non-production applications that can tolerate interruptions and for fault-tolerant, flexible workloads that can checkpoint and resume. Stateful, high-uptime, or sensitive database workloads should not use Spot.

WARNING - flagged (ambiguous): 'Non-production applications' is a use case, not a Spot suitability criterion; keyed answer A is debatable. Check: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/using-spot-instances.html. Incorrect. Stateful workloads that maintain persistent connections or application state are not suitable for Spot Instances because an interruption would disrupt that state, requiring complex recovery mechanisms. Applications that cannot have interruptions require guaranteed availability that Spot Instances cannot provide, as AWS may reclaim Spot capacity at any time with a two-minute warning. Sensitive database applications require consistent availability, data integrity, and predictable performance, making them poorly suited to the interruption risk inherent in Spot Instance pricing.

quizData.question: A company has multiple AWS accounts within AWS Organizations and wants to apply the Amazon EC2 Reserved Instances benefit to a single account only. Which action should be taken?
options: Purchase the Reserved Instances from master payer account and turn off Reserved Instance sharing
Enable billing alerts in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console
Purchase the Reserved Instances in individual linked accounts and turn off Reserved Instance sharing from the payer level
Enable Reserved Instance sharing in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console
explanations: WARNING - flagged (ambiguous): Keyed A (buy in payer, disable sharing) vs C (buy in the linked account, disable sharing) both plausible. Check: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/ri-turn-off.html. Correct. To restrict Reserved Instance benefits to a single account, purchase the RIs from the master payer account and turn off Reserved Instance sharing in the billing settings, preventing the discounts from applying to other member accounts.

WARNING - flagged (ambiguous): Keyed A (buy in payer, disable sharing) vs C (buy in the linked account, disable sharing) both plausible. Check: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/ri-turn-off.html. Incorrect. Enabling billing alerts in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console creates notifications when spending exceeds thresholds, and has no effect on how Reserved Instance benefits are shared or restricted across accounts in an organization. Purchasing the Reserved Instances in individual linked accounts and turning off RI sharing from the payer level would apply RI restrictions organization-wide rather than limiting benefits to a single specific account. Enabling Reserved Instance sharing in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console would expand RI benefit sharing across all member accounts, which is the opposite of restricting the benefit to a single account.

quizData.question: How can a company separate costs for network traffic, Amazon EC2, Amazon S3, and other AWS services by department?
options: Add department-specific tags to each resource
Create a separate VPC for each department
Create a separate AWS account for each department
explanations: WARNING - flagged (ambiguous): Tags (A) also separate costs by department across services; keyed answer is separate accounts. Check: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awsaccountbilling/latest/aboutv2/cost-alloc-tags.html. Incorrect. Adding department-specific tags to each resource enables cost attribution within shared accounts through Cost Explorer, but tagging relies on consistent human application and does not provide the hard billing boundaries that separate accounts create.
